Question: How are software engineers and full-stack web developers different? I asked this question because I wanna do just something (solving problems, creating new features, and thinking about it) Without any domain specifics. How should I do?
Answer: It sounds like you're asking for some kind of “pure software engineering” in the same vein as “pure mathematics.” Such a thing might exist in academia, but at that point you're doing computer science research, not software engineering. Software engineers, kind of by definition, are building something. That's what engineers do. And you can't find people to pay you software engineer wages to build software that completely lacks a domain. In some cases the domain may be a software domain. Database development is itself a domain, for instance. Working on a web site that manages a to-do list might not require any industry domain knowledge, but it does require you to learn web or backend development and all of the relevant libraries and frameworks that you need to deal with. And even then you may need to understand user privacy laws like the GDPR. If you're just saying that you don't want to learn a million arbitrary rules to work on banking or PCI compliance software, or the huge set of rules surrounding medical compliance, or any other heavily regulated industry? Then in that case just learning engineering and picking up details on the job is all you'll likely need. But there is no getting around at least some form of domain learning if you want to work in software. As to your specific question: There's no generally agreed upon definition for software engineer or full stack developer. In my own definition, a software engineer uses software engineering principles and has a deep understanding of what it is they're building, whether it be a web site, server backend, mobile app, or firmware for an IoT device. Whereas a full stack developer can create a frontend and backend for a web site, and probably knows HTML, JavaScript/TypeScript plus maybe an additional server language, and how to interact with at least one database, but may or may not be a software engineer by my definition. Hint: A software engineer doesn't need to copy and paste code or use AI to generate code. I use AI all the time at this point, but it's generally as a semantic search of the docs. Aside from the template to start a new app, though, or the very occasional (like, once a week or less) block of code to do something obscure, it's literally multiple times faster for me to write the code to get the result I want than to try to convince an AI to produce that code. That doesn't mean I won't use autocomplete when it pops up, if it saves me some time and produces what I was going to type anyway. But the point is I could have typed the code. You can't engineer something if you don't understand the pieces you're using, and if you can't build something from scratch with those pieces, you don't really understand them. And when you understand software development at a deep level, you can pick up the domain knowledge you need as you need it. So endeavor to become a software engineer. The rest should follow.

Question: How do people with unusually high IQs go about solving a problem?
Answer: Ummm… Very quickly, usually? Let me ask you this: How do you run on rough terrain? You've just learned how, and your brain does the work, right? Maybe when you practice you lean specific ways to plant your feet or keep your center of balance closer to your center of mass so you are more stable. But you don't really think about it. Well, people with a high IQ have learned many techniques to solve problems, some by trial and error and others they pick up from seeing or reading about them. And the cool thing about having a high IQ is you can quickly identify which technique is likely best for the problem at hand—and often you can apply the technique quickly as well. There are tons of books and blogs and articles about problem solving hacks. The more you can learn and remember, the quicker you will be able to solve problems. What distinguishes the problem solver with a higher IQ from the rest is that they more easily remember all of the techniques and can apply them more quickly.

Question: Realistically, how deeply can the average CS undergrad - that is, not a top student but just an *average CS undergrad* - be expected to understand the Cook-Levin theorem and/or the notion of NP-completeness? Isn’t that beyond their capabilities?
Answer: It doesn't really matter? I mean, do your best to learn it well enough to pass your tests. But if you're planning to be a software engineer, don't stress over not understanding the concepts deeply. It's good to understand that some problems can't be solved deterministically. As far as I'm concerned, that's the real takeaway from that corner of the CS curriculum. “Some researcher proved that a bunch of problems map onto each other and that none can be solved as quickly at the solutions to those same problems can be verified.” So unless you are planning on doing research in that area, learn what you can and memorize enough of the rest to pass your tests. (Learn what P and NP stand for, and understand why NP gets so big so much faster than P). Will you miss a few questions on a test? Maybe. Would it be nice to get all As? Sure. But at least for me, no one ever asked to see my college transcript. As long as you pass (and keep up grade requirements for your major, if any) you're good. If you want to help your career, get as much practice actually programming that when you apply to your first internship or job, you can demonstrate real skill at programming. Good luck.

Question: I hate that honesty is shamed. Everyone, and I mean everyone has no issue being brutally honest towards me my whole life, but when I am more honest than them, I am considered an AH. Why is it backward like this? I hate lying to spare feelings.
Answer: How is this … “Backward” ? You’re saying that you should be able to be brutally honest but no one else should? No one should be mean. No one should be pointlessly cruel. It’s not “lying to spare feelings” to not be mean or cruel. And everyone around you has “no issue being brutally honest” with you? Maybe you’re surrounded by assholes. But there’s a saying: If you run into an asshole in the morning, you ran into an asshole. If you run into assholes all day, you're the asshole. There’s another option as well: You may be hyper-sensitive to criticism. To the point where someone making an entirely reasonable constructive suggestion gets interpreted by your brain as “brutally honest,” but then when you say something cruel to them in response, they (rightfully) respond as if you’re the asshole. There’s no simple way to fix this other than therapy to help center yourself and add stability and structure to your mental landscape. I promise you that honesty isn’t shamed. Unsolicited critical advice? Sure, that can be shamed. WTF does someone care about the unasked opinion of a rando? If someone you know asks for your honest opinion and you give it couched in the softest way you can manage, though? That isn’t shamed. If you respond in a way that’s pointlessly cruel? That is shamed. See the difference? I don’t “lie to spare feelings,” and people don’t treat me as an asshole. I feel like honesty is a really important value to me, and I am as truthful as I can figure out how to be. But that sometimes requires a bit of mental gymnastics to find something nice to say that isn’t a lie. “I hate lying to spare feelings” is the refrain of someone who really wants to strike out at the world with no consequences. It’s not a healthy thing to say. It implies that you’re in mental anguish and seek to spread the pain. You instead need to work on becoming more mentally healthy. Therapy, which can include group sessions that are free, is probably crucial for you. And don’t tell me “therapy doesn’t work.” Maybe a therapist or two wasn’t a good match for you, but even with the best possible therapist, the therapist is never the one doing the work. It’s all you. A therapist can only guide you and give you perspective. And maybe you need psychiatric help (i.e., prescription drugs). There are even prescriptions psychedelics that purportedly help with trauma and depression. I’m not a doctor, so I can’t recommend anything specific, but between therapy like EMDR and the various drugs available, there’s likely something that will help you. But you need to be willing to do the work. Drugs aren’t magic; you still need the therapy and to do the work. Nothing comes for free. And that means facing your own demons and defeating them. Good luck.

Question: As a software engineer, do you try to understand how the tools (IDE, CI pipelines, etc.) work under the hood?
Answer: Yes. And no. It depends on what you mean. Do I need to know exactly how every aspect of my IDE works? No. Do I want to know how it's performing linting and making suggestions? Yes. Because I want to know what tool or tools generated the various errors and warnings I'm looking at. Do I need to know exactly how the CI pipeline allocates workers and reacts to source control triggers? No. Do I need to understand how Docker exactly creates a virtual machine to run the CI processes? No. Do I need to know in general how Docker works, and how it encapsulates the build environment? Enough that I can run the same build environment on my system to help diagnose build system CI failures locally? Absolutely! Do I need to know exactly what optimizations my compiler can and can't do? Sometimes, yes. Do I have need to know exactly what kind of parser it uses? Not really. Is it useful to know how a compiler is written in general? Totally. Do I need to know exactly how React handles events internally in order to program in it reliably? Unfortunately, also yes. Do most React developers understand how events are handled internally? Apparently not, since every React project I've worked on has had bugs related to very subtle interactions between events. Things where it really really seemed like it should work. And the “solution” to said problem is often to layer more and more frameworks and libraries on top of React to better hide the design flaws in React rather than fixing the fundamental problems like they did in SolidJS. But I digress… I would go as far as to say that, to consider yourself a software engineer and not just a programmer, you should have some understanding of the tools you use and how they probably work, at least at an abstract level. You don't need to be an expert in all of them. You don't need to read source code from every tool you use. But the more you understand, the more you can apply engineering principles to the things you build and the environment you're building them in. Engineers don't just throw crap together and see if it works, moving the gears and levers around until the clock functions correctly. They plan out the device they're creating in advance and have some idea how it might fail, and how the parts will fit together, before they even start assembling. That's what software engineering should be. And in order for planning to be possible, you need to understand your tools. The pinned answer in my profile has my twelve most important “laws of programming”. Three of those laws are about understanding the tools you use. That's how important I think it is.

Question: Can Node.js handle a high traffic website, or is this affected by its single-threaded nature?
Answer: Node isn't really single threaded. I write more about that here: And yes, Node can handle “a high traffic web site.” At least up to a point. The way you worded your question implies that you mean a single web server running Node.js, and that's how I'm answering the question. If you are using multiple servers, then most any backend environment will work, as long as you're willing to pay to scale up your servers sufficiently. Yes, you may be paying 50x as much for some environments or frameworks, but that would be “handling” the server side. It would just be expensive. And in general it's best for redundancy to have multiple servers running with a load balancer in front of them. That way if there's an issue with one, another can take over. So what would limit a Node server? One thing is bandwidth. Remember that the server Node is running on can only handle so much data on its network. Generally, well-written code on Node can probably saturate a 1gbps network connection if it has enough RAM and CPU speed. But if the site is so high-traffic that you need to serve more than 1gbps worth of data, then you need to have multiple servers operating in parallel. Another bottleneck on a site is the database. Again, well-written code will give you more throughput than poorly written code, sometimes by several orders of magnitude. And there's nothing that any language or ecosystem can do if your code slams your database and your database starts causing high latency as a result. So a Node site with poorly designed code could have crap performance, even if the load isn't that high. And maybe your site does something like converting images for clients. Node can do that, and if you do it right, Node can even perform all the work in threads while dealing with other requests. But if you're using a lot of CPU on your application server, it can still impact the latency of your site. Finally, you might want your site to be even faster worldwide than any single server can support, simply due to latency of signals needing to travel around the world. In other words, your server should probably feed a CDN with current pages so they can be served to local viewers from multiple data centers around the world. That's also independent of Node.js, and will take significant load off of your Node.js servers. So yes, except for some narrow situations, Node is a fine choice.

Question: M28. I hate people who say, "You can get a girlfriend" Whenever I state girls would never find me interesting, all I can manage is being a brother to them. Why, do you guys think every man can be the typical guy that women want out of nowhere?
Answer: Assuming there is such a thing, why would you need to be “the typical guy women want”? Women aren't a monolith. You don't need to attract a significant fraction of women in order to get a girlfriend. Think of all the guys you know, from the most to the least attractive. From the most to the least interesting. Do they all want exactly the same women? Unless you're living in a bubble, the answer is no. You don't need a large percentage of women to find you attractive to get a girlfriend. You need one woman to find you attractive. What have you done to make yourself interesting? Do you have hobbies? Do anything outdoors? Have any interests at all outside of eating, sleeping, and (hypothetically) having sex? Even having sex can be a positive if you ensure the woman enjoys it enough. How would she know before you even touch? By how you treat her with respect and care. I'm not going to say you'll learn what you need to attract a woman overnight, but the three main components are to learn to like yourself to learn to enjoy yourself and to do what you enjoy, and to learn to respect and connect with a woman as something more than a sex object. And something that I was reminded of recently is that women also frequently are attracted to those who can show vulnerability. Hint: Politely asking a woman out or otherwise expressing interest is one way that can look. No, it's not easy. But unless you're a pretty extreme case, it's likely the person you're looking for is out there. You may need to perform maintenence on yourself first, but almost everyone can get there if they try. And that's why people say “you can get a girlfriend.” Not because you're necessarily even ready to try right now, but that if you can adopt the right mindset and do the work, you can find your way there. And yes, “do the work” might even involve some form of therapy. Almost everyone would benefit from some form of therapy, and the more you understand yourself, the better you can be as a partner.

Question: Can Node.js, TypeScript, and MongoDB be used as a backend for a full accounting software that heavily depends on transactions?
Answer: Everything is possible. Not everything is a good idea. As far as I know can tell, there's no good reason to use MongoDB for just about anything. I'm sure there are narrow use cases, but in general? Better to use PostgreSQL. Simply enforcing a schema and referential integrity is a minimal software engineering practice for full accounting software. Postgres has a decimal type for exact math. Queries on PostgreSQL with aggregation will be tremendously useful. And nothing that MongoDB offers is an advantage for an accounting system.

Question: Which should I choose for a social network website, Node.js, PHP, or Python? Why?
Answer: Of those three? Node.js with TypeScript is an easy answer. I think that's enough by itself. Python might be useful for machine learning analysis and AI, but once you have enough users for that to matter, add some Python to just do the ML. There's no real advantage to having the backend run Python; there can be servers that handle ML tasks, and they can provide the results to your backend. Each option above is like selecting a set of tools. The PHP toolbox, to borrow an analogy, has a lot of hammers and an assortment of oddly shaped tools with unfortunate ergonomics. The Python toolbox has a lot of tools, but they work best at solving one kind of problem—and you have several needs that their tools don't meet. There's only one hammer, for instance, and it works OK for some tasks, but not so great for others. Node.js is like having the entire hardware store and adjacent tool and machinery rental store in your back pocket. It might be harder to choose which tools to start with, but if you're careful you can pick the exact tools you need for the job.

Question: Why do some developers, juniors to mega seniors, develop the God complex?
Answer: Hmm. Let's see. According to Wikipedia: A god complex is an unshakable belief characterized by consistently inflated feelings of personal ability, privilege, or infallibility. The person is also highly dogmatic in their views, meaning the person speaks of their personal opinions as though they were unquestionably correct. Someone with a god complex may exhibit no regard for the conventions and demands of society, and may request special consideration or privileges. Consistently inflated feelings of personal ability? With respect to programmers, nearly the opposite is generally true. Impostor Syndrome is practically endemic. But for those of us who are confident in our ability, we are frequently accused of being overconfident. In public fora, I'm confident enough to often be accused of being arrogant, even. This never happens in “real life,” by the way. When I've asked people I work with if I seem arrogant, they've always told me either that I'm just being confident or that it's a “deserved” arrogance. I think this follows into the second point: Being called dogmatic. There's a concept: “Strong opinions, weakly held.” It shows up in popular culture as a signal of being wise[1], and also in industry blogs. [2] As Jeff Atwood points out in the latter link, writing about ideas in anything but a confident tone is difficult to wade through. If you want to write something worth reading, in other words, it needs to express an opinion. At the same time it's important to be open to new information; open specifically to changing your mind. Does it sound dogmatic when I say it? Sure. But it's not based on a dogma, a fixed set of unchanging beliefs that are immune to modification. So what about the last point? “…no regard for the conventions and demands of society, and may request special consideration or privileges.” I'll plead guilty on that point. Society seems to demand that I lie about what I observe in the industry to protect people's feelings. I think this is harmful to the same people it's allegedly protecting! If you're not familiar with my writing, I'm often making the point that not everyone is cut out for software engineering. This is absolutely unquestionably true. The only matter for debate is where one might draw the line to call someone “good enough”. There are people who struggle with basic math. Who can barely read. Some who can't even talk using grammar. You can't tell me that they would be able to contribute positively to a programming job. And yes, those are extremes, but every human trait exists as a spectrum. At some point on that spectrum a person is skilled enough, or has enough of the right aptitude, to contribute positively as a programmer. Society in general, and insecure programmers in particular, take issue with me pointing out this fact. But if the general attitude is “everyone can be a programmer,” then how does it make people feel when they try their hardest and fail? Lying to them to “encourage them” to try their hardest is likely to destroy as many lives as it helps out, maybe more, and I don't accept society's apparent position that sacrificing some so that others might benefit is ethical. Just because “everyone does it” doesn't mean it's the right thing to do. As to the privileges I request: I'll only take jobs where I work from home, and that pay pretty well. I also am not very patient with poor management decisions. So is that a “god complex”? Or is “they have a god complex” merely the latest in a stream of insults aimed at the competent programmers by the insecure? I would argue it's often the latter. I'm sure there are incompetent developers who are dogmatic and who act like prima donnas. They may even outnumber their competent and confident coworkers. But the fact that actually competent and confident developers get painted with the same brush stroke makes me wonder how much of the message is motivated by insecurity rather than the reality. Sometimes it's not a god complex as much as a non-neurotypical expressing themself in a confident manner. The phrase “god complex” itself isn't a psychological diagnosis, after all, but more of an insult. If you have a specific criticism of a specific developer, maybe it's better to describe it directly. Otherwise it seems more like your insecurities are showing.

Question: How important is mobile responsiveness in your website development process?
Answer: Important? Hmm. That seems insufficient. Really really important? Closer. Absolutely drop-dead critical? Yeah. That. More people use mobile phones to browse web sites than desktops and laptops. If your mobile experience is terrible, your customers will get a bad impression. It just takes understanding of how web pages really function, and a willingness to do a bit more work instead of lazily pasting in code from a hundred different services.

Question: Why do backend developers think frontend programming is a waste of time?
Answer: I doubt any, or at least many, backend developers actually think that all frontend programming is a waste of time. Maybe some Unix command line afficionados who don't see see past their own nose enough to realize that, even if they eschew all GUIs, other people need, use, and desire a clean modern user interface? It's a big world. I'm sure someone thinks this. But it's not a common sentiment. Much more likely is that backend developers consider most frontend development a waste of their time. Maybe also a waste of money for anyone who is paying them to work on frontend. Look. The skills and knowledge necessary to create backend code differ from the skills and knowledge necessary to produce frontend code. In addition, the temperament required to produce frontend code is different. Broadly speaking, backend leans harder on general computer science and optimization principles, while frontend leans more on creating and assembling many components just right. Frontend requires a certain category of patience with the client who will come back for the fifth time asking for a button to be a slightly different color and to be moved by three pixels to the left this time. It also needs patience in dealing with things like CSS formatting quirks, and either memorizing or frequently Googling how to get around specific issues with reactive formatting. I can work on frontend. I just really don't like it. As a result, I'm much slower at it than someone who specializes in it, so it doesn't really make sense for me to spend my time on it. And I've met other developers who do like it—and who prefer it to backend. And since they're also faster, it's just a huge win to let them do it. So we're all happier if we can work on the part of the code that we're better at and enjoy more.

Question: How do you solve the issue of electric car charging when many people can not charge at home suchas those in town or rowhouses or apartments etc? Will charging locations end up like current gas stations in the future?
Answer: Supply and demand will solve the issue, to some degree. Demand for EVs is going up on its own. It's an exponential curve, and a curve like that can start out seemingly nearly flat before it accelerates. See the nearly flat part on the left? That's where we are right now. As adoption starts to really accelerate, or more to the point, as it starts saturating the market to the point where even people in apartments and townhomes are buying them in large numbers, landlords will start installing EV chargers in equally large numbers. Right now there's little incentive. If they install a charger in an apartment lot, even if they charge for using it to pay for the electricity, it doesn't really make a meaningful difference to them financially. But after half of their prospective renters have EVs? The units that have guaranteed access to overnight charges will be in higher demand than those that don't. Those who offer “free” charging even more so. Higher demand means higher rents. Installing a “Level 1” charger is cheap. Many lots have the right kind of electricity nearby to install several with no electrical upgrades necessary. Minor/inexpensive upgrades can provide power to most of a small lot. If they decide to offer “free” power for simplicity, they might be paying $0.50–$1/night to charge each car on average, or $15–30/month, but then could possibly charge $80/month more on rent. If you do a lot of driving, how much would it be worth to you to be able to never need to go to a gas station again (unless you're on a road trip)? I'm sure a lot of people will consider it a good deal. If you're looking at paying $1500/month in rent vs $1580/month, and in one place you'll never need to pay to fuel your car for your daily commute? Seems like a no-brainer to be.

Question: What can I do to improve my logic in programming? Everyone keeps saying “code code code code”, but how can one code all the time when they can't even build a logic to tackle the issue easily?
Answer: There's a point when you're learning to program—a threshold that you cross—where on one side of the threshold everything is a blur, and even though you've been learning all of the syntax of some programming language, you have no idea how to put the pieces together to build things. Then you cross that threshold and suddenly it starts to all make sense. If you can cross the threshold. I think there is a lot of well meaning advice given on how to learn to program, but what it comes down to in reality is the fact that you need to do enough programming to get your brain to make the right connections. To cross the bridge from confusion to comprehension. The “Learn X The Hard Way” tutorials (based on Learn Python The Hard Way) model roughly how I learned to program. Or rather, learned to think like a programmer. They have you type in code and explain how it works. There are likely other approaches that are effective, but it's a kind of immersion approach like you'd use to learn a human language. But that's why people tell you to code code code. It takes exposure for your brain to cross that threshold. To gain that understanding. And the uncomfortable truth is that some people never manage to cross that bridge. That includes some people who work as professional programmers—the kind that only barely get along by Googling for code to modify, or by using ChatGPT to write code for them. I can't tell you whether you just haven't tried hard enough yet or if you'll never get there. It might take a full year of practice to have the right insights; if you've been trying much longer than that, you might want to consider a career pivot. Good luck.

Question: How do I start learning programming professionally, and how many programming languages should I learn? How much time does it take to learn one programming language?
Answer: Learning a programming language is never the challenge. The hard part is learning how to think like a programmer. I'd say you need at least a year, maybe two, to do that. During that time you'll be using a programming language, but as I said, it's not leaning the language that's the hard part. Question: Is it possible to memorise most of data structures and algorithms to crack the coding interview?

Question: Greenspun's Tenth Rule of programming states that “Any sufficiently complicated C or Fortran program contains an ad hoc, informally-specified, bug-ridden, slow implementation of half of Common Lisp.” Is Greenspun’s Tenth Rule correct?
Answer: It's certainly an amusing claim. And to some degree it may be true of C, and also of the Fortran version available when he coined that phrase. But that doesn't mean that we should all be using Lisp. Just that Lisp includes design ideas that should be imported into more modern languages. And I submit that those ideas do already exist in modern languages: Lisp was ahead of its time in many ways. There are few advantages to Common Lisp that we don't take for granted in more modern languages, though. I've heard it suggested that if you showed Ruby to Greenspun back then and told him it was a Lisp variant with an alternative syntax, he would have believed it. To be fair, there are at least two major things that a Lisp can do that modern languages can't: The first, in my opinion, is a wise omission. When you use macros to create a custom DSL, to some degree it doesn't matter how awesome the DSL is: By doing that you've now made it impossible for experts to immediately understand your code. In other words, keeping the syntax consistent is of more value than allowing it to be modified arbitrarily. It's already annoying enough to need to learn the quirks of several major programming languages to be able to get things done. If every single app had syntax quirks it would be exceedingly painful to ever start working on a new app. As to custom code generation: That's also almost always a bad idea. It's generally better to just write code that behaves flexibly than to write code to generate code. It's harder to debug a code generator. It's harder to reason about. It was valued back in the day because at the time they thought it would be the path to AI. They thought in the 50s that they'd be able to write code that reasoned like a human in only about 20 years. That didn't work out quite as they hoped. Lisp was also developed as a compiler target; ironically, it wasn't intended to be used directly by humans. And it shows. 😛 And even C has a plethora of libraries available to add many of the above features to a C application. C is still more susceptible to bugs that aren't even possible in a more modern language, but the amount of “reinventing” required today is much less than in the early nineties. So his rule is only “sort of” correct, and really only does apply at all to C and an outdated dialect of Fortran. Honestly, C should be retired and replaced with C++ or Rust. It will never happen, in large part because the majority of developers still using C don't want to learn a more complex language, or they don't like some of the features of C++. But aside from a steeper learning curve, C++ is strictly better than C, and can allow you access to many of the above features, even when used in an embedded/resource-constrained environment. And no one in their right mind would start a new C app today. Not something with a GUI and user facing features. People do it anyway, I'm sure, but it doesn't seem like it's a defensible practice.

Question: What does a software engineer do? I mean like in web development there are frontend engineer and backend engineer and there are full stack engineer. So where does this software engineer role fit in the software fronted and backend things?
Answer: A software engineer can do frontend, or backend, or full stack development. They probably can do any of the above, but may prefer one over the others. What they are creating (frontend, backend, IoT, etc.) isn't really constrained by the title. Question: Is doing software engineering in 2024 worth it? My term will end in 2029. Will there still be a demand of software engineers?
Answer: For the first question: Yes. But also, no. (If you feel the need to ask the question, odds are good the answer is no.) For the second question: Skilled and talented software engineers will be in demand for the foreseeable future. Full stop. Odds are good the demand will only increase relative to the supply over the next century. Here's the catch: Getting a degree doesn't make you skilled and talented. Spend some time trying to learn to program. Serious time: A year of regular effort should be enough. By the end of that year you should be able to tell whether software development is fun and interesting or if it seems like torture. Hint: If it seems like torture, you're not one of the skilled and talented. Related life hack: Don't pick the career that feels like torture. I'm not naive enough to suggest that everyone should love their job so much that they'd do it for free. That's a fantasy. But if you pick something you absolutely hate, you're setting yourself up for a life of misery—and don't expect particular success in your career, since you won't have the free energy to do what it takes to go the extra mile. If I were given a nickel for every time I saw someone complaining about how hard it was to keep up with current tech in programming…well, I'd probably be able to buy myself a dinner at an inexpensive restaurant. But talented developers who are successful don't complain about needing to learn. They generally like learning, so it's not a huge imposition to need to learn new ideas. The right aptitude makes it easy, in fact. Only you can answer the question as to whether you have that aptitude, though, and it might take a lot of work to figure it out. If you're asking the question, though, that's not a good sign. It indicates you might not really want to be studying software engineering, which implies that you really don't like the topic. If you're really just worried about whether it will continue to be a good career, then that's fine; it will, and frankly will probably be a good career for much longer than literally any other high paying job. By the time AI is ready to replace all software engineers, every single other career will already be able to be replaced by AI as well. Even careers requiring physical interactions like doctor, dentist, or surgeon.

Question: Can one do programming mostly without Google if they study basic methods in libraries and learn how to implement algorithms and data structures by those methods?
Answer: One does programming mostly without Google by… Wait for it… Learning to program. But you're conflating things in your question. “Basic methods in libraries” are learned not by studying them but by using them. You learn about them by reading the docs. How you read the docs doesn't matter: If you Google for docs, simply because the actual doc page has crap search functionality, that's fine. When people complain about programmers “coding with Google” the complaint is about copying and pasting code without fully understanding it. Code they wouldn't be able to write, not because they don't know the details of library calls, but because they never really became skilled at programming. You also asked about data structures and algorithms. You study data structures and algorithms as a means to practice—you guessed it!—learning to program. There is a profound misunderstand shared by many programmers: That learning how to code, for instance, a QuickSort, in college, was a misguided attempt to teach you how to code an algorithm you'd need to code for your job. As if you would need to write a sort when every single environment comes with sort built into its libraries. No. Academics can be a bit out of touch with industry, but I doubt anyone anywhere thinks you'll need to code a QuickSort for a job. The idea is, and has always been, that learning to code complex algorithms will teach you how to think about and code complex algorithms. You will probably never need to code a sort, but you might need to write code that's complex and that you can't just copy off the internet. For instance, it's frequent to need to convert between data in multiple formats, and sometimes the data relationship can be…rather obtuse. And if the brute force approach is too inefficient, you might not be able to convert the data at the speed the data comes in. Unfortunately, learning to code complex algorithms clearly doesn't always stick. Some people are clearly not cut out to be programmers, and even computer science graduates frequently don't really learn how to program. This is the elephant in the room in all discussions about retraining out-of-work people to code: Maybe only one in twenty in the overall population have what it takes, if that many, and very few of those people would have ended up in a low-skill job to begin with. It might be only one in a thousand or fewer who could transition from, say, coal mining to programming. Now there are a significant number of professional developers who only know how to “code” by copy-and-paste. I put code in quotes because that's no longer even coding, really, but simple scripting. And scripting has a place, and can be a productive part of a project, but building a complex project using only scripters is about as reliable as hiring only carpenters to build an apartment building. They might be able to get something nailed together, but it might fall over in the first stiff breeze—and have plumbing and ductwork sticking out in awkward places. So do your best to learn to program. Really learn. Type in the code yourself, and become adept at writing arbitrary algorithms without needing to look up examples for everything. And if you hit a wall, then just continue what you're doing, as long as you can continue to get paid for it. Honestly, there are too many jobs and not enough highly skilled programmers to fill them all, so do your best and keep food on your table. But you might want to consider a “Plan B” in case you have a hard time finding a job in the future. I have seen people claim that older developers are highly discriminated against, and while older, highly skilled programmers have enough options to continue to find jobs, less skilled developers tell stories of applying to hundreds of jobs over the course of multiple years to no avail. So finding another path to a good income is probably in your best interests if you can't make the leap to programming without Google. Good luck.

Question: Why don't more poor people with internet access teach themselves to code, and earn a more comfortable living? What other barriers may be in play here?
Answer: There are many reasons given in other answers. It's not easy to dig your way out of being poor. But even if someone overcomes the economic and psychological obstacles, there's still the elephant in the room that just “learning to code” is about as useful to getting a job as “learning math” is for getting a job as an accountant. Bootcamp claims aside, it really takes about three years of nearly full time learning to get to the point of being good enough to reliably get a job in software development. The competition at the low end of entry level jobs is intense. I hear stories of people applying hundreds of times over the course of a year or more and still not getting offers. In addition to the time required to really learn, you need the right aptitude and temperament to do the job. I'm good at math and understand rules well, but I could never be an accountant. Wrong temperament. And some people never really understand programming—even some people who have managed to get jobs in the industry. Which might make you think that “anyone” can do it, but lower skilled programming positions have much higher competition—with all of the associated racism and classism that enables. So if you don't know anyone, and you can't afford to pay some bootcamp to help you get your foot in the door, odds are poor you will get a reliable job. And how many poor people have the right kinds of connections to get that foot in the door? I fully support programs that help people learn to code. But frankly, it's a small percentage of the population who would be good at it—and unfortunately, some of that aptitude likely comes from nurture and early learning, nurture that poor kids don't receive. So it's great to see successes. People with the aptitude and temperament can and do beat the odds all the time. When I found out about programming, nothing could have stopped me from learning it. I was immediately hooked. (That said, I wasn't poor, so I wasn't forced to work long hours as a teen to make ends meet.) But it's not a one-size-fits-all solution to the job problem for the working poor.

Question: Why, despite widespread agreement on the flaws in tech company recruitment processes and candidate dissatisfaction, is there no collective action or mass boycott against these methods, targeting tech executives, CEOs, and investors directly?
Answer: Flaws? Yes. The current process is flawed, but likely not in the way that the asker implies. The current process is flawed in that it: I'm guessing that the asker is asking because they're one of the group who feels they need to game the interview process by practicing hundreds of Leetcode problems. That they go through dozens of interviews without getting an offer, and they blame the process for their lack of offers. Sorry, but no. That's a feature of the current process, not a bug. If you're failing that many interviews, then maybe you need to think seriously about a career pivot—at least to applying to jobs that require less programming skill and more design and scripting skill. Programmers who might want to practice a few Leetcode problems to get in the right mindset, but who haven't gotten rusty at programming because that's what they do in their day job. As other answers have pointed out, if everyone who hates the current interview process were to boycott companies that use it, there would be much rejoicing. Please, if you feel like interviews with programming challenges are terrible and you fail way more than you pass, boycott to your heart's content! We won't waste our time or yours on the interview. Everyone's happy. What it comes down to is that there is no known-better process. The behavioral style of interview apparently has some data backing it up as better than other approaches, but only in addition to the programming challenges, not instead of them. There's no better test to see if someone can program aside from having them program. This isn't rocket science. Because the truth is that some people are good at programming, and some aren't. Stories of needing to send out hundreds of resumes and go through dozens of interviews only to get one job offer are completely unfamiliar to my own experience and that of the other good developers I know. It's still the case that my friends can apply at a dozen or fewer companies, go through four interviews, and get 2–3 offers. The 1–2 that don't give them offers are a combination of cultural fit and false negative rate. One of my friends went through this process on the last year, looking only at companies that were 100% remote and high salaries. And yes, it's mildly annoying to need to do programming problems at Every. Single. Interview. But what can you do? The alternative is to work for companies where they don't apply that filter. And that would be a lot more than mildly annoying and well into intolerable. So by all means, boycott away. It will mean less stress for you in interviews, and less wasted time for many interviewers. Question: Where do you think programs begin to be a "big ball of mud"? That is where do you think programs get large enough that a person cannot track all the interactions between the parts, even if the parts are coherent abstractions?
Answer: At the point where the complexity of the program exceeds the ability of the lead developers on it to fully mentally model the problem at hand. Which is further influenced by the design skills of the lead developers, since the better the design, the more overall complexity the program can contain without resorting to inelegant spaghetti code. Look, for example, at sendmail, the classic Unix mail handler, vs Qmail. The complexity of sendmail is such that it takes a serious expert to configure, and it spent much of its youth having to fix major security holes at least monthly. It's monolithic, and arguably a big ball of mud. But Qmail is modular. It's broken into some six or seven smaller executables (I forget the exact number), and each one is practically a work of art. It was first written in 1995, and its final release, version 1.03, was released in 1998. 25 years later there are still no major security holes that have been found in Qmail, despite bug bounties available for much of that time. And while Qmail may not be the second most popular mail transfer agent any more, it's absolutely still in use. And Qmail is still arguably “one application,” simply with a modular design. Can sendmail do things that Qmail can't? Yes and no: Anything that you can do in sendmail can be done with Qmail, but some things require external tools or configuration. So you could say that part of the strength of the design is knowing when to stop adding features and to instead rely on the Unix philosophy of small tools each with a focused purpose. Extending that thought, imagine the standard ecosystem of tools available under a typical (non-minimalist) Linux install. Hundreds of small tools, spanning millions of lines of code, all designed to interface with each other. Each tool easy to understand, but fully isolated from each other tool, and therefore trivially not a “big ball of mud.” And yet that collection of tools is effectively a large single application, at least how it's used in practice. So my thesis is that there is no single threshold you can point to after which a program will necessarily become a big ball of mud. There are often practical reasons you end up with inelegant interdependencies that lead to a ball of mud, the most common being inability to hire software engineers with sufficient skill and rigor to keep your design clean, and the second most common being applying too much pressure to release new features and not allowing enough time to clean up technical debt. So it happens, and it's even common, but it's not inevitable. As a corollary, I dispute the claim in the question that a program getting too complex for a person to track all of a program's interactions among its various parts is the threshold across which it becomes a ball of mud. A good design will keep the various parts of a program isolated enough that a developer only needs to fully understand the interactions between a small number of modules within the program. If you have developers who are sufficiently skilled at design, and you give them sufficient time to implement features and clean up technical debt, then at no point will your application ever need to become a ball of mud, no matter the size.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Why do universities teach algorithms seldom used in the real world, and why do coding interviews primarily favor questions benefiting junior developers? What would be the impact if everyone were to boycott these practices?
Answer: Universities attempt to teach students how to program. The way they do this is to give them well defined, increasingly complex, algorithms to implement, and hope that the practice in implementing those algorithms will help them generalize to all problems they may encounter in the industry. This isn't always successful, obviously, or questions like this wouldn't exist. But I digress. The point of the algorithms they choose to teach is never, and has never been, that you may need to use those exact algorithms. A university attempts to impart a broad education. They want to teach students how to think in all situations. If you want to be taught “real world algorithms” by rote, then you don't want a university. You want a vocational school. And there are good reasons that a university education is granted more respect than that from a vocational school. Similarly, the algorithm questions in interviews are intended to determine whether a candidate knows how to program. And in some cases, how to reason about programming. It has never been, nor should it be, about memorizing algorithms. It shouldn't require that a candidate practice dozens or hundreds of Leetcode challenges. Because a candidate that is skilled at programming should be able to solve any Leetcode “easy” or “medium” hardness (with few exceptions) without much effort. The thing is that a significant fraction of the industry, as evidenced by the existence of questions like this, performs their jobs not by programming as much as regurgitating memorized algorithms. This can actually be fine for large categories of job, especially frontend development of basic UI/UX, but is not great for backend or full stack app development—or anything more complicated. Senior candidates who can really program are not at a disadvantage compared to junior developers. The opposite is true, in fact. Most developers I know and work with don't even bother practicing Leetcode for interviews, at least beyond a few warm-up problems, because we use our programming skills every day on the job. Senior developers who have been producing code by rote and copying and pasting everything they can't remember, on the other hand, are disadvantaged as compared to every developer who has actually recently been programming. So the question is whether those of us who really know how to program do a better job than those who produce code by rote. And the answer to that is an unequivocal “yes.” My personal brand is focused on rescuing small businesses from code disasters. Those disasters are almost always the obvious result of code being duct-taped together by programmers who didn't really know how to program. So what would happen if candidates boycott interviews that include programming tests? Companies that actually care about code quality would see a higher number of applicants who can pass the tests due to programming skill. Because those of us who don't find programming problems difficult wouldn't join the boycott, because we never saw programming tests as a problem to be protested. Given that, I highly encourage anyone who feels that programming tests are unfair to senior developers to join the boycott against companies that require such tests. Yes, join the boycott. I've seen dozens of posts indicating that developers already boycott such companies. Which is honestly good for everyone involved. So go for it! No more programming tests for you! And the rest of us will keep applying to companies with programming challenges, and their stack of resumes won't be quite so high and they'll get to ours sooner. Win-win!

Question: Why is coding not easy?
Answer: Coding is easy. Learning to think like a programmer is hard. Once you can think like a programmer, coding is a matter of knowing the syntax of the language you're using. If you're stuck at the point where even learning to code is hard, and you've given it months of good effort, you might want to try a new career direction. That said, some problems are harder to solve with programming than others. Even when you know how to write code, and know how to think like a programmer, there are problems that require that you visualize the interactions between more moving parts than your brain can track at once. So even when you attempt to solve the problem, there's a process of trial and error that you need to work through to find the code that solves the problem in a way that's robust and reliable. Coding is the easy part. Design is hard. Figuring out what exactly the user needs can be hard. Once you have the requirements and design, there are few hard parts to actually coding it up. Debugging and fixing any emergent behavior can be hard, but again, that's not the coding part. (This assumes the design doesn't include AI to accomplish part of the task, which can be an R&D element with unknowable difficulty. And that's also not coding.)

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Who agrees if you are a guy and you have no skills associated with masculinity, it is humiliating to admit you are not a real man? As a man, there are certain skills you should know how to do such as hunting and fishing, am I right?
Answer: Who defines this “real man” crap? Is it the same person who claims we don't eat quiche?! I love quiche! And no, I'm not even slightly humiliated by this fact. Nor by lacking hunting and fishing skills. Nor by lacking any interest in bars, or watching sports, or engaging in other worthless pissing contests. Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How do I transition away from a bad developer?
Answer: If they're bad enough, drop them immediately, within the constraints of the contract you have with them. Don't be a jerk about it, but letting them know you don't have any more work for them as soon as possible is likely to be your best bet. Caveat: Make sure you have access to the source control, or at least the latest source code, before even hinting that you might fire them. If you don't have it already, tell them you need it because you're hiring someone else to work on some other feature while they're busy with whatever they're working on, and the other developer needs to see the code to give an accurate bid. Also, if there are server credentials, make sure you have control over those as well. And if you don't own your own domain names, make sure you do before you fire them. All of the above is very important, unless they haven't been working for very long and the code they've created is worthless. In which case just make sure you own your domain names. The harder part is finding a developer who is good. The best advice I have for that is to hit up your most technical friends to see if you can talk them into helping you find a good developer. Or contract with a highly reviewed team on a site like Upwork. Beware of fake reviews on Upwork, or any site, really. I'm pretty sure groups of the same people end up reviewing each other's work, paying each other back and forth (where Upwork just keeps the commissions) in order to lure in real customers. I've had multiple people approach me on LinkedIn, asking me to create an Upwork account in my name, where they would promise to do all the work and give me a percentage. Meaning that their account likely got bad reviews or banned, and so they can't create a new account themselves since Upwork does some identity verification to prevent people from creating unlimited sock-puppet accounts. If only Quora would use the same techniques to prevent unlimited sock-puppet accounts… So yes, it's hard to find good developers, and bad developers are nearly indistinguishable from scammers in the methods they use. Be careful out there. (I would offer my own services, but I'm probably too expensive for whatever you need done; I specialize in really hard problems, and most sites and apps aren't that hard, so my rates don't make sense for them.) Good luck!

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: It's clear to me that AI won't completely replace software engineers anytime soon, as the job is too complex for current AI, but will it reduce demand for so many devs? Couldn't AI increase developer productivity so much that many devs aren't needed?
Answer: You can divide professional software developers into two categories. The kind that can program competently without help Googling every single thing from the internet, and the kind that can't. There's a huge range of skill even in the first category, but for the most part the highest demand vs supply ratio is on developers in that category. And the thing is, AI is only marginally, if at all, useful in helping programmers in that category. The second category, though? AI can be a lot of help for. That said, the second category was already hitting saturation with thousands (millions?) of bootcamp graduates being cranked out, and that level of job is also the easiest to outsource overseas to developers who are paid $10/hour, so that category was already hard to get jobs in. So the question to ask yourself is, which category of developer are you? If you're good enough that easy-difficulty Leetcode problems are barely a challenge, then you're in the first category and shouldn't have any problem continuing to get jobs moving forward. If instead you think Leetcode problems have nothing to do with the work we do day to day, and that they should be banished from the hiring process and replaced by interviews that, at most, ask you to accomplish a simple task like adding a button to a page? Or you struggle to do anything at all without looking up how to do it on the internet? Then you might be in the second category, and regardless of AI, you may have trouble finding jobs in the future.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Do experienced programmers also look up solutions for their code?
Answer: Yes. But also, no. Do I look up complex or optimized algorithms when I need them? Absolutely! This happens…maybe a few times a year. Do I look up how to use specific library calls that I don't remember the details for? Sure! That happens several times a week, and occasionally multiple times in a day. Do I look up obscure error conditions to try to figure out why something isn't working? Yup! Happens a few times a month or so, depending on what I'm working on. Do I use documentation and examples when working on a completely new domain? Sure! No need to reinvent the wheel entirely. But day to day, as I'm solving the same general category of problems that I have been solving for the last several years? I've learned and completely understand the solutions to those problems, so there's no need for me to look anything up. And when confronted with a really unusual customer requirement, I sometimes do need to develop a solution from scratch from first principles. Doing research is good. Saving time is good. Memorizing tons of trivia solely to avoid needing to use the internet is bad. But actually learning to program is good. Getting every solution from the internet to every task you're given means you're not actually learning to program. And that means you're not fully understanding what you're doing. And if you don't fully understand, you can't intentionally design solutions; all you can do is pile up Lego pieces without regard to architecture. And that's bad.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How can people leverage their programming or software development skills for remote work to reach a $500 income goal?
Answer: That's a really, really low income goal for a programmer. And is that a total amount of money, or do you mean $500 per hour, day, week, or month? $500 per hour is a challenge. Per day is not hard, but you need to be reasonably good and have experience you can point to. Per week or month…is a very low bar. You could go onto Upwork and post a $25/hour rate, and then you'd make your $500 after only a bit more than 20 hours of work (the extra to cover Upwork’s cut). Or post a gig on Fiverr. Or you could, I don't know, apply to a remote job? If you're a kid looking to buy a PS5 or similar, then it gets more complicated, since many work sites require you to be 18 to sign up. In that case you probably need a parent or guardian to assist. Good luck.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is it true that programmers usually leave programming and change their career after 5 to 6 years because it’s difficult, or is it just a myth?
Answer: Many don't make it through a CS degree. Some who do make it through the degree, probably shouldn't have. They study harder and put in many more hours in the lab than their peers only to barely squeak by with a degree, thinking that it's the piece of paper that guarantees them a good job. They're wrong. Being good at programming, and in general, software engineering, is what gets you the good jobs. Making yourself miserable to get a degree that will qualify you for a job that will then make you miserable is a questionable life strategy to begin with. But the industry will eventually reject candidates that perform at a level of junior developer despite having a few years of experience. So those developers leave the industry after they find it harder and harder to get a job. But others leave simply because they're miserable and can't take it any more. They might describe it as too difficult. But then there are those of us who are good at it and love it. I've been programming professionally for over 35 years now, and I'm still going strong. It's not difficult for me. I don't know any hard numbers, so I can't say whether new programmers “usually” leave. But I wouldn't be at all surprised.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: A military contractor claimed that many developers at FAANG and similar companies are like construction workers since the software they create is equal to "shanty towns ". Do you disagree, and if so, why?
Answer: Glass houses… It was predominantly military contractors who took on—and famously failed at—the ObamaCare web site. Fifty separate government contractors (!!!) with who knows how many developers working at each, but if it was fewer than 5-10 I'd be amazed. So these 250-500 or more developers couldn't make a web site over the course of multiple months that could handle even a few dozen users, much less thousands. They were rescued by a small group (fewer than 20, IIRC) of FAANG-level developers in a few weeks. If the FAANG developers were building shanty towns, the military contractors were piling up mud and wondering why it was sliding back down again. Government software engineers are famously ignorant of current best practices in software development. I've worked with government software developers who had near zero skill or knowledge of anything that had become standard in the industry in the last 20-25 years. Who still, today, don't know how to use source control. Not everyone. The org I'm dealing with has a great set of best practices that they're trying to get developers to follow. But many, many developers are ignoring those recommendations and to some degree haven't even yet entered the 21st century in terms of dev practices. So yeah. Glass houses indeed.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Are tiny homes a passing trend or a long-term shift in real estate preferences?
Answer: Tiny homes are cheaper, and allow for higher density of housing, which are both compelling reasons they'll likely continue to be popular for the foreseeable future. They have additional benefits as well: Less space to clean and maintain. Less space to heat or cool (though more surface area and less heat mass work against that advantage unless we're talking about attached tiny homes). I'm attracted to them in concept myself, but in practice I have too many big hobbies for tiny homes to work for me as my primary residence. I also work from home and need additional space to have privacy while I work. Since I can afford a larger home, it makes sense for me to own one. So there will likely be multiple kinds of homes sold to people with different budget, needs, and preferences. Zoning rules will likely be changed to allow more building of tiny homes as backfill in existing single family home neighborhoods to help increase the housing density in cities, so the tiny home supply will increase, but existing large homes aren't likely to be bulldozed en masse to be replaced with tiny homes.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Do Embedded software engineers earn more or less than software engineers?
Answer: In my experience, embedded development isn't particularly well paid in general. But then again, software engineers have a huge salary range depending on skill and aptitude required for the job. And I've had at least one job offer at FAANG-level salaries to work on embedded/firmware development at a company that actually valued their engineers. So in my experience the best salaries go to the developers with the highest skills. That said, in a particular location there may not be companies willing to pay top salaries in every domain. And despite the move toward working from home, some jobs, embedded development included, really require you to be in the office. I mean, if you're programming hardware that's being developed in the office, and there may be times when you need to take that hardware to the hardware engineers for diagnostics or to use the expensive in-circuit-emulator or digital oscilloscope that you don't have at home. So while most of the embedded jobs I've seen have pretty average salaries, at least one in Denver paid really well, but they were looking for specific kinds of experts who could work in their office. There are undoubtedly high paying embedded jobs in the Bay Area as well, but if you live anywhere else, or if you can't compete with top developers, then don't assume that the best pay in your area will be available for embedded developers.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Will AI kill most of the tech jobs in the next 5-10 years? And which jobs will be least impacted?
Answer: No. Not even close Any jobs requiring human reason and judgment will still need humans. It's only the unskilled or lower skill jobs that are being phased out. And that's just normal automation; AI is really only effective at replacing a small minority of jobs, and even then it at best makes humans more productive rather than replacing them entirely. The hype about AI elimination of jobs is extremely overblown.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Im in grade 12 and did poorly all through high school. Is my dream of becoming a software engineer basically 0 at this point?
Answer: No. Not zero, but at the same time, not high. I had undiagnosed ADHD and my high school record was, at best, mediocre, especially if my goal was to get into a top college. I didn't even try to get into a four year college out of high school. I just went to the local community college and started on classes that would qualify me to transfer to a four year school. I got my act together in college enough that I was accepted to both UC Berkeley and UC San Diego as a transfer, got my degree at UCSD, and have been a software engineer ever since. That said, one of the things distracting me in high school was programming. I was writing games. I started at 13. I didn't have a dream of becoming a software engineer as much as I considered it an inevitability. So if your dream is based on being obsessed with programming and already being pretty good at it, the odds are actually good you can turn it around, get a degree, and succeed. But if your dream is more of a fantasy based strictly on reading about famous software engineers who got rich, and you've done no actual work to learn software development at all? Odds are much, much lower. Even if you didn't do great in high school, if you want a desk job instead of working in the trades, go to college. Nothing wrong with working as a plumber or electrician or similar, in that they can make quite a lot of money, but it's not for everyone. Even a college that will accept lower grades from high school, or a community college that won't care about your grades at all, can be a stepping stone to your goals. But programming isn't for everyone either. If you haven't even tried it yet, then you don't know if you have the aptitude. Without the aptitude, it can be a miserable job. So give it a try if you haven't already, and see how far you get. Good luck.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: What are the different types of computer software?
Answer: You probably needed to pay attention more in class and do the homework to know what answer the teacher is expecting. There are probably dozens of ways to categorize computer software. I could invent categories, like “applications, servers, operating systems, and hybrid.” It's not really useful distinctions, but it is one way to categorize all types of software. Your teacher is expecting a particular answer based on what you were taught, though. Which actually kind of sucks. If they're going to make you memorize things, it would be nice if the things you memorize were actually, you know, useful things to know. But such is how mass education works; they make you spew out answers to make sure you at least read the material or taken notes in class. Which you clearly haven't. Shame.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: As a software engineer, how can you craft code that reveals your intent without resorting to writing explicit comments?
Answer: You can… For some things. Naming is hard. They say it's one of the two hardest parts of programming, along with caching and off-by-one errors. 😂 But with good names you can communicate much of the intent of the function or method you're writing. Names of variables and constants as well as the method and function names. But not everything is so simple, and sometimes you are best served by writing comments. APIs, including public methods, should almost always be documented, and that documentation generally also belongs in comments, though often that documentation can be mostly redundant. And if there's something you have to do that's at all surprising, it should always be documented. You don't always have control over the libraries you use or the behavior of the OS, and if you need to set some flag before a particular method call, explain why you're setting the flag, especially if it's not obvious you would need to do it. Related: If you ever feel like you should warn the user of a function or method about some pitfall that might surprise them, think carefully about whether you can simply fix that design flaw rather than just documenting it. I've lost count of how many times I've started to write WARNING in all caps to explain how a user needed to use a method, only to realize that I could remove that restriction or limitation by writing appropriate code. My guideline is “It Should Just Work.” Which is extra important if you realize that users never bother to read the docs anyway. So anything surprising will be a perpetual support nightmare.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How does a software developer code his/her app to manage the communication with the internet/server, etc.?
Answer: This is one of those, “If you have to ask…” questions. In particular, if you have to ask, you don't have the context to understand the answer in a useful way. I mean, the short answer is that the communication is handled based on how it needs to be handled. For a single request, you just…make the request. For a real time or continuous feed, you make a connection and assign a callback or notification queue or similar to handle the messages you get from the server. And then there's the management of the data itself, which effectively requires a couple of years of CS classes or equivalent, plus a few more years working in industry, to learn how to do effectively. There is no answer for laymen that would communicate anything more than which particular jargon is appropriate to the domain. Once you understand how the calls work and have a sufficient background, you simply don't need to ask. I recommend you focus on the basics if you want to learn. You'll get there, or you won't, but answers to questions like this one won't help.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: All software that is written today ultimately turns out into a big ball of mud. Does software design even matter in the longer run or has it become irrelevant today?
Answer: I challenge the assertion. Let me rephrase the question: “All software that is written today by teams that lack direction from strong software engineers with a solid design sense turns into a big ball of mud. Does software design even matter when no one on the team has any design sense?” I think the answer to my new question is a no: If no one knows what good design looks like, then what's the point in trying to apply design patterns arbitrarily? Design is hard; you can't apply arbitrary structure to a program an expect it to be the “right” design. I've seen just about every design guideline be tortured nearly beyond recognition. “DRY” code that became so convoluted that a little duplication (or a completely new design) would vastly simplify the code. “YAGNI” code that ended up lacking the ability to do something it did eventually need to do. Every aspect of SOLID used to justify horrendous design, and many design patterns applied in ways that increased complexity and decreased readability without improving the design at all. Another possible rephrase is: “All software that is written today by teams that are constantly overworked and understaffed turns into a big ball of mud. Does software design even matter when no one on the team has any time to do more than the bare minimum to get features to ship?” In this question, at least someone on the team might be good at design, but they aren't given time and resources to push back against the glacier of mud that's slowly overwhelming the project. They can only do so much, and maybe aren't given the authority to tell others to fix their code before it hurts the design. In this case? Yes, any design they can enforce and improve is a step in the right direction, but they can't save the project alone. Odds are good, though, that those on the project with good design sense will eventually leave for jobs where the team appreciates their skills, and the team will devolve to my first variant of the question. Design is hard. Some developers clearly don't have the knack. That doesn't mean it's not worthwhile. It just means some teams are incapable of it.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Which programmer do you hire: the one who programs a messy program in three hours or the other who does a well-structured program in twelve?
Answer: I find this be a false dichotomy. I've met programmers who are meticulous. They may take twelve hours to do something I'd complete in three or less. And the code is clean and carefully structured. But it's not always what I would call well structured. And if a programmer can create a program in three hours, and the program is messy but competent? There is potential for teaching this developer better design and clean coding practices. In my experience, however, there's no real potential for teaching a methodical developer that takes 4x as long how to be more efficient. Edit to add: Due to my writing being (apparently) unclear, there's a lot of confusion in the comments as to what I mean. Let me be blunt. A fast programmer might be a great programmer. One that can write robust code accurately, quickly, and with good design. That code might also be able to be characterized as messy because they have bad habits. A slow programmer is, at best, an average programmer. There is zero chance you can take an average programmer and make them great. There's at least a chance you can take a messy but great programmer and teach them better habits. If the fast programmer produces crap code, then I hire neither. I work in small teams with strong developers. Period. Hiring a meticulous, average developer would be a net negative to team productivity. I've seen it before, where they slowly and carefully produce well crafted code that's subtly wrong, and needs to be rewritten. Again and again. And each revision takes forever, to the point where if I'd written the code myself, it would have taken less time than the time I spent code reviewing and giving feedback and arguing about the need for changes. It's never worth it. “Messy” can mean poor naming conventions, inconsistent indent, using less than optimal language features because they don't know a better way, or any of a hundred other things, many of which can be easily improved if the programmer is willing. Many can be fixed with a linter and code formatter. But many comments seem to assume I'd hire a crap programmer because they were faster. I wouldn't. Good program quality is important. I just don't believe that the slow developer would produce the best code if it takes them 4x as long to get a result. If you're good, it just doesn't take that much longer to do things well. It doesn't. My code is cleaner than most, and I would certainly be on the faster end of the spectrum. When you can code really quickly, the cost to change an approach is very low, so if I think of a better way to do something, I just rewrite or refactor. Someone who takes 4–20x longer to achieve the same result will not want to start over and write the same code twice or three times. If it only takes ten minutes, it's just not a big deal.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Why are IQ tests so useful everywhere but criticised? The average IQ is 100, and half will have an IQ of above 100 and half below 100. Why are IQ test so useful?
Answer: The average IQ is 100 by definition. The curve of scores is even normalized to be a standard distribution. So you can't look at the IQ results of a thousand tests and say, for instance, that the intelligence measured by the test follows a particular distribution. The test results are forced into a standard distribution curve. Before you ask why the tests are useful, you need to ask whether they're useful. If you're claiming they're useful, maybe you should tell us what you believe they're useful for?

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Would you take a job for lower pay at a company just to meet a celebrity or reputable insider working at or with the company? If so, who would you do this for and which company?
Answer: It seems like most answers to this are some variant of “hell no.” But I almost did once. Now, “lower pay” is relative. I wouldn't take enough of a pay cut to hurt my cash flow or quality of life. But at one point I was working with a FAANG for a very healthy total compensation, and a recruiter called with a very unique selling point for a job. “Work with John Carmack.” Would I have taken a pay cut to work with Carmack for several years? Absolutely. First, some people have enough recognition that if you name drop, it opens doors. Carmack is that big of a name. Getting a recommendation from Carmack would have been even better. Second, it looked like a fun project. I mean, working with Carmack would have been awesome on its own, but I also really enjoy working in game development. Third, it wasn't much of a pay cut. So why did I decline the interview? The job required that I move to Texas for at least three years. I had a kid that was already in elementary school at the time and I didn't want to uproot my kids if I didn't really have to. I also really didn't want to tie myself to Texas for the long term.
