But it was very tempting. If the job hadn't required a move to Texas, I would have at least interviewed. But I couldn't handle the idea of moving to Texas and possibly getting stuck there. It's not all about money, after all.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: What fields in technology/CS don’t require a lot of coding and pay 6 figures?
Answer: Being a startup founder. Oh, and succeeding. Aside from that… Management of various flavors. Agile consulting. Data science.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is it a common thing in software development to be threatened of firing if you do not want to work uncompensated overtime?
Answer: I honestly don't know how common it is. Yes, software engineers, in the US at least, are generally considered salaried/exempt workers. So technically they can ask for more than 40 hours without offering additional pay. And there are well known companies that seem to expect extreme hours. I would guess it's the minority that explicitly demand high hours as opposed to high productivity. But regardless of how common it is, it's unacceptable. If you're a skilled programmer, under no circumstances should you continue to work for a company that tries to motivate you with threats. If they're actually hinting that you're not getting enough done, though? That's not as clear from the information that you provided. I don't work overtime any more. I have in the past, but no one has demanded I work overtime directly. Instead there were explicit expectations as to when things would be done, and I would put in extra time to meet the deadlines. Now I am much more likely to be skeptical about deadlines. They're often artificial and externally imposed. Even if they're based on my own estimates, I always make clear that my estimates are exactly that, and that sometimes things come up that are unexpected. But really what it comes down to is that I do freelance work now, and no one watches the number of hours I work. So I can tell my clients how long time something will probably take, and it generally takes that long—but in the rare case that something takes longer than I estimate, I explain to them that it will take longer. There is mutual trust and no demands or threats being thrown.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: In 5 years, AI may replace programmers. Who can you learn from then?
Answer: AI is not on track to replace programmers any time in the foreseeable future. Like really. Not even close. We still don't even know what we don't know about how to make a computer understand and reason about a problem. AI is great at regurgitating the answers to problems that are easy to Google (because there were so many training examples!), and mediocre to terrible at everything else. Hint: All of the interesting parts of programming? The parts you get paid for? Are the parts that aren't already demonstrated on the internet a million times. Can AI allow non-programmers to hobble together code? Sure. And they will soon discover that there's a reason we went to school and studied computer science. Heck, there have been no-code solutions for decades that have been way easier to use than AI to create apps, if you just need something simple. And yet, programmers have remained in high demand the entire time. I'm not even sure how your question relates to that assertion (learn what? Programming? If computers are doing it, why would you need to learn it?), but since the assertion is false, the question is irrelevant. Whoever you're learning from now, I guess? Learning to think like a programmer is something you need to do yourself anyway rather than learning it from someone. You can get help along the way, but you need to do the work to train your brain to think in the right way. And you do that by practicing and reading other people's code. Or better, typing it in. Copying and pasting doesn't get you the brain-muscle memory. So don't expect a major change in the next five years. Nothing to see here. Move along.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: What would you do with $1 million cash and coding skills?
Answer: Well, I have coding (and software architectural) skills, so I've thought about this a lot. I'd likely invest most of it and use the income from the investment to reduce my burn rate enough so that I could spend my time finishing up one of several app ideas I've been fiddling with. If any of those ideas get any traction, then maybe I spend some of the cash to promote and expand the successful ideas. If I had $10M, though? There's a game I've been working on, off and on, for years. I'd hire a team that could dedicate their time to it and manage it to completion. That would likely only cost about a half million or less, so the rest of the money also gets invested and I'd live off of the interest. If it only costs a half million, why wouldn't I spend the million on it? Because game development is a hit driven business. Odds are good that, even if I think it's awesome when it's done, it won't make back its money. So I'd rather spend my time and money on several better bets, make that $10M on one that's a winner, and then blow a half million on a vanity project. If I can have my vanity project and still live off the interest of what's left, then I'm much better off over the long term than if I blow half of my million on a project that may not even break even. And then I can keep doing whatever projects strike my fancy.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: John Johnson, the principal engineer at SpaceX with optics industry experience, was replaced by a group of junior developers. Can elites like Musk do the same with software developers? Can a few junior developers replace an experienced senior?
Answer: Can they? Sure! Will the project eventually go off the rails and crash and burn? Sure! “A few” junior developers costs nearly as much as or more than a senior developer anyway. If it's three junior developers, they have increased communication overhead and diffusion of responsibility compared to the senior developer. Something that's missing from the question, though, is skill. One highly skilled junior developer might quickly outperform all the other developers combined. That junior developer won't be paid like a junior for long, though. Not if they play their cards right. But assuming similar levels of skill and aptitude? The senior developer will be able to perform better than the full set of junior developers, and almost certainly will cost less. Especially if you count how much more quickly your product makes it to market. Will the SpaceX project suffer as a result of the new less experienced engineers? Only time will tell for sure, but I'd be willing to put money on it.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Some authors, including John Grisham and George R.R. Martin, are suing ChatGPT. Do you think they have a legitimate case?
Answer: It's complicated. Copyright law recognizes “fair use” as an exception. There are several categories of fair use, but the relevant one in this case is called a “transformative use.” In other words, is the new use different than the original use? Google creating thumbnails of images for its image search pages was considered transformative, for example, because the way an index is used is sufficiently different from how a full sized image can be used. Another key concept from copyright is a “derivative work.” Roughly, it's a work that's based on, or derived from, another work. It doesn't matter how much you change the work; if the new derived work was based in any way on the original, then it's legally a derivative work. For instance, blurring a copyrighted image doesn't suddenly make it OK to copy. In novels, using characters from another work that you don't own is also considered derivative. From a technical standpoint, I'm pretty sure that the resulting model that OpenAI generated, the model that runs behind the scenes to power ChatGPT, would, and should, be considered a transformative use. I mean, it is the epitome of transformative: The original novels are for humans to read. The data embedded in ChatGPT is not human readable. So the model itself should be clear of copyright claims. But the output of ChatGPT is very human readable. That's pretty much the point. And when someone asks for text “in the style of X”, ChatGPT is using what it learned from being trained on those novels to generate similar novels. That data was encoded in non-obvious ways into the model, yes. And the model itself is fair use. But when you use the model to create a work that isn't transformative as compared to the original, you're using the data from the copyrighted works to create derivative works. Here's the tricky part: How do you know what original works the new work is derivative of? You don't. No one knows. No one can know. So effectively, every single phrase created by ChatGPT is arguably a derivative work of all of the text it was trained on. If anything, all authors with currently valid copyrights should be represented by a class action lawsuit against OpenAI. Individual authors suing OpenAI is a waste when really OpenAI is infringing on all the authors; they are training from all works they can find and scrape from the web, so the only authors they aren't infringing are those who either have no digital versions of their books available, or those digital books haven't been found by OpenAI. And no, GPT is not “learning like a human.” We still don't know how humans (or mammals, or birds, or even insects!) learn. Like, at all. But what we do know for absolutely certain is that training a neural net is not like training a human. I mean, how many billions of times did you need to repeat your studies of millions of texts before you could barely understand what you were reading? Do you have memories of spending decades listening to repeated sound samples before you could (barely) understand English? I hope not. And these models understand nothing. So even after all of that training, they still really only have complex encoded patterns. That's it. And those encoded patterns are effectively a blending of the various training material. A derivative work of all of the training data. There is no question in my mind. And it's only fair use until they use that derivative work to create output that competes with the original, that is no longer transformative—which is the main reason ChatGPT exists. And so, like Napster and various torrent trackers before, ChatGPT is helping people commit copyright infringement. And as Napster and its later kin have been shut down hard, I suspect we'll see the same thing happen with ChatGPT. But who knows. Maybe the judge will believe the BS about it “learning like a human” and consider it to be sufficiently different that it's not a derivative work. But is it a legitimate case? Absolutely.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How do you write an algorithm and draw a flowchart to find the average of all odd numbers from 1-100?
Answer: I don't write flowcharts. Almost ever. So I write the algorithm by sitting down and… Writing the code. Big shocker, I know. Here's the tricky part: I use skills that I obtained from sitting down and writing code. By myself. Without asking strangers on the internet to do my homework for me. If you're in a class, ask the teacher or a TA. They can help you without giving you the answer. It's literally their job to help you. Cheating by copying answers from the internet is completely useless. If you can't do the work after getting help, drop the class and switch majors to something that doesn't require programming. Getting the degree without the skills is a waste of time.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Do programmers, after 10 mins of browsing for a solution to their problem, ever slap their foreheads and mutter to themselves, "I'm an idiot"?
Answer: It happens…sometimes? There was an old programming book that was one of the first I read that had a cartoon. It showed someone working really hard to unlock a car with a coat hanger. Yes, this was a thing a long time ago. Don't make me feel old. 😛 In any case, the guy in the cartoon is focused entirely on unlocking the door, but as you look at the cartoon, you can see that the door on the other side of the car is hanging open. The caption: “Intent on a complicated problem.” Early in my programming career, I would think of this cartoon frequently. Because I would get overly focused on one aspect of a problem all the time, missing that there was an easier way. Today, with Google available, the solution is often found by searching. When I was younger, it was generally your own blood, sweat, and tears that eventually resulted in a revelation, but the feeling of “why didn't I see that sooner!” is similar. But over time that feeling gets more and more rare. Now when I find a solution after ten minutes or more of Googling it's more likely that I'll sigh and curse someone else for not fixing some bug or non-intuitive behavior. It still happens that I miss something obvious. But it's blessedly rare at this point.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is the tech industry's obsession for hiring high-paid superstars creating unemployment in society? Can't we have many average paid jobs with good work-life balance?
Answer: Unemployment of… Whom, exactly? Because the last time I checked, there were still lots of programming jobs available. Not just for superstars, but for those who are “just” reasonably strong developers. And, sorry to say, but the industry isn't a charity. Nor do they not hire good candidates who they interview just because they're waiting for “superstars.” They don't owe you a job; if you want to be hired, you need to convince them that you can provide them more value than your salary will cost them. I've known a ton of ”tech industry” developers, from those at FAANG companies to those working for large but boring companies. Of those who were strong developers, a common complaint is how many “average or below” developers they have to work with. Even at FAANG companies. And some non-tech companies aren't even that picky. That's where many of the below average developers end up. But with the glut of below average bootcamp graduates on the market, the demand from that segment may not be enough to keep up with the large supply. So maybe you haven't proven your skills enough to compete with the high skill developers? Or you simply don't have those skills. There's no way for me to know. Also remember that hiring in the industry is often cyclical, and there are times when layoffs temporarily increase the supply. That can mean your job search takes longer than the couple of weeks to a month a typical strong developer takes to get a new job offer. But the core of your idea has merit. If software development were better managed, we could probably do better work with fewer overall developers. Giant teams cause their own problems and are responsible for extremely bad code and architecture, and yet they are the go-to for many big companies. But suggesting that companies should use large teams of average developers to increase the number of jobs available is effectively suggesting that these companies should operate like charities. You may as well argue that modern manufacturing techniques should be abandoned so that we can have 50 lower-skill jobs for every one higher skill employee they need to monitor the machines now. The results would be better, projects would be produced more quickly, and the overall cost would be lower, if smaller teams run by higher skill developers were the norm. What would the motivation be to use larger number of lower skill developers, when the costs would be higher and the chance of project failure would be higher?

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How do I deal with Python issues?
Answer: Issues with the language? I generally deal with them by avoiding Python. If I'm working on ML code, then I just suck it up and work around the various idiosyncrasies of Python that are so annoying. Given that we don't know what issues you are having, I can't really say how you should deal with them. But whatever the issues are, using a different language would be guaranteed to prevent you having more Python issues. If you're a beginner, though, you're probably just having learning to program at all issues and blaming them on Python. In which case you need to put in the time to learn and stop whining about how hard it is—or you need to decide it's too hard and pivot your career goals. Asking unanswerable questions will get you nowhere.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Which one to use for web development: Python or Go?
Answer: Neither? There exist reasons to use Go. It's better than Python for most uses. Go’s static types are better than Python's type hints. Go is much faster. Go has a generally cleaner library. But if you're talking general web development, there's little motivation to use either. Probably the best of the popular approaches today is to use TypeScript and Node.js. Then your backend (which is all you can really create with Python and Go) can be written in the same language as, and share type declarations with, your frontend. Performance is good enough for most purposes. Support libraries are available for just about anything you can need. And the community is large. It's arguable that Blazor and C# is a better approach in some ways. I prefer the flexibility of TypeScript to the strictness of C#, as well as the breadth of the Node.js ecosystem, but for some web development of might be arguable that Blazor would be better. Flexibility can get you in trouble if you're not careful. The world is much larger than just Python and Go. Learn about more languages before making your decision.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is it correct that FAANG or FAANG-like companies have designed the interview system in a way to keep the median age of the workforce below 35? Do layoffs serve the same purpose? If not, why not? No company openly admits this to prevent lawsuits.
Answer: It's said that the number of programmers has been doubling every five years. If you accept that, and if the median developer starts out in the industry at 22 years old (when a typical college student will graduate), then based solely on that, you would expect half of all developers to be 27 years old or younger: Over those five years, as many new people must have entered the industry as were already in the industry, after all, and most new developers are those coming straight from college. So the median developer being 35 seems to imply the opposite of what you're claiming, since the natural conclusion would be that the median would be closer to 27 years old. Now the truth is that we're probably not really seeing a doubling every five years any more. And it's also true that many of the younger developers who get junior positions when they graduate never progress to full developers, and as such typically drop out of the industry in less than five years. So a median of about 35 (assuming that number is real) seems just about right. But wait, there's more. 35 years ago was 1988. I was already programming and in college in 1988, but I was in the serious minority of kids who had access to computers from a young age. By the time those 1988 babies were teens, computers were ubiquitous. By that fact alone, most developers would likely be younger than 35 years old. So again, I don't see 35 as an unreasonable median. I also know developers (myself included!) who were hired by a FAANG after they were 40. So I think your premise is faulty. Do companies sometimes lay off older workers? Sure. They often make more than younger workers, and yeah, that sucks, but the time of companies being loyal to their workers as a matter of ethics is long past. So the older developers who have higher salaries need no actually be providing correspondingly (and visibly) increased value for their companies, or they're at risk of losing their jobs. I'm not justifying this practice. I'm just naming it as a fact of life in the industry. Does ageism exist? Yes. Do teams of younger developers tend to prefer younger hires? Yes. Do older developers ask for more money? Often. Will companies prefer the younger, cheaper developers? Also often. Is the interview process designed to hire only younger developers? No, I don't see it. In some cases the process could be redesigned to minimize unintentional ageism. Ironically, some of the FAANG companies have specifically implemented those strategies, which is further evidence that the process isn't designed to do the exact opposite. The odds are stacked against us in some ways as we get older. That's why there are laws against discrimination by age, after all. But there's no reason to ascribe malice when incompetence (or ignorance) is sufficient to explain the behavior.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Does it make it too difficult for devs if I decide that I will create my own software and programs myself, then get a few professional developers to bug check and make sure my code is working efficiently before others can begin using it?
Answer: It… Depends? I can imagine a project simple enough where your work would be useful enough that a professional developer could just clean it up. But it's a pretty narrow set of requirements that a non-expert wouldn't make a mess of. And a mess is not something that a professional will want to clean up rather than rewrite it from scratch. For the simple reason that “fixing” the code you write will take more time and effort than just creating completely clean, well-designed code to begin with. So how can you tell the difference between a project you can meaningfully contribute to and one you can't? You pretty much need to ask an expert. 🤷🏻‍♂️

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Do you believe that senior developers who can't pass coding interviews are incompetent? What is your argument for or against coding interviews?
Answer: It depends on the coding interviews. Some interviewers are better than others. There are some pretty terrible interviewers who think that they should choose coding problems that can only be solved using obscure tricks. Or they have you write in a language you're not familiar with. Or they have you write code on a white board and mark you down for missing a semicolon. Failing interviews like that is no shame, and is no indication of skill. But a well chosen coding problem, where the test is really to see if you can program and think creatively about the problem you're presented with? Or where they give you a harder problem, but expect you to talk through your reasoning and give you hints, to see if you're willing to think on your feet and take suggestions? Those are legit tests that any competent software engineer should be able to pass. My fundamental belief is that a senior software engineer should know how to program. If they want to only make architectural decisions, they should update their title.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: If some IT companies hire software engineers with the test of world-class programming questions, do those companies' daily operations really have to encounter the challenge of that world-class level?
Answer: Daily? Maybe not. It only takes a few key decisions per year, and more general design choices several times per month for a world class developer to make a huge difference in a project. And then there's the fact that every single thing they do is done faster, and with fewer flaws, and the resulting code is more optimized. I know there's a tendency for those who have trouble with programming problems to look for reasons to denigrate the process. And sometimes interviewers suck, choosing problems with an obscure trick or algorithm that they expect you to memorize, or they want you to write on a whiteboard and mark you down for syntax errors. I'm not defending bad interviews. But a well designed interview will test a candidate's ability to think and their ability to program. And yes, as a programmer, a candidate should know how to program. And it's absolutely reasonable for IT companies to want their new programmers to…know how to program.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: In software development, some say that you have to work without asking anyone even if you deliver late, others say that after 4 or 5 hours, you have to ask someone who knows to be efficient, what do you think?
Answer: Whoever says you should never ask questions is an idiot. I would put the threshold at 2-3 hours, or less if the answer is likely to be simple and unique to your existing project but hard to determine on your own. The only problem with asking questions is if you don't learn from the answers. No software developer should complain if you're asking about the code base for a company you just joined, unless it's the third time you have asked that exact same question. It shouldn't even take you longer to complete if you don't ask the question yet again, because really you should have learned it the first or second time.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Should I still pursue a tech-related career in data science, programming, etc., when there are tools such as ChatGPT Code Interpreter that can do anything 10+ times better and faster than me?
Answer: It depends? If you've been programming seriously for years and you're still having trouble, then with or without the existence of ChatGPT, you should probably pivot to a new career goal. If you've not even started to learn to program? Well, all of the predictions about ChatGPT being better than actual skilled programmers are somewhere between delusional and outright fabrications. Can ChatGPT spit out code when given a prompt? Sure. Can ChatGPT replace an actual skilled programmer? Not in the slightest. Can ChatGPT assist a skilled programmer? Sometimes. Mostly when looking for high level ideas or details about how to do some common thing in a language they aren't that familiar with. Software development is much more than typing code. It involves understanding. ChatGPT doesn't understand what it's doing. At all. I used it for a while as a fast documentation lookup, and it was so bad at hallucinating new APIs and keywords, I've given up on using it even that much. The few experiments I've done with having it generate code have been abysmal. Even trying to get it to convert code between programming languages was a compete failure, generating naive code that looked similar but that didn't actually do the same thing. Not even close. It's (almost) all hype. There are uses for generative models, but replacing programmers isn't one of those uses. But frankly, if you're asking this question? Odds are high that you probably should switch to another career. When I was starting out, I was told that I shouldn't try to become a programmer because it was no better than being a plumber. I couldn't help it; programming was too compelling to ignore. It was fun. The act of creation at my fingertips. Puzzle solving for a living. And more than 30 years later, it's all still just as fun! Was it hard work to learn? Sure. Are there parts that aren't fun? Absolutely. But overall, it's a joy. If it's going to be a job you hate? If you resent being forced into it because of someone else's expectations? You've really given it a serious try and it still doesn't catch your interest? Then I encourage you to try other careers. We'll need good programmers for the foreseeable future. We have a glut of “I only learned this to make money” programmers who do the absolute minimum to make a paycheck and complain about how companies want them to learn things in their spare time. I get that we all work for money. It's not bad to do a job for money. But doing a job poorly for money isn't a winning long term strategy. I've lost count of the number of posts I've seen by people who chose CS and software development “because it's lucrative and easier than becoming a doctor or lawyer,” not realizing that it really is just about as much work to become good. And worse, that becoming good requires the correct aptitude. If you don't have the right aptitude to become a doctor or lawyer, you'll find out because you'll fail out of too many classes to finish your studies, or you'll never complete your residency or get promoted from associate. In software there's no one to tell you you're incompetent. But it can become increasingly hard to get jobs when you don't have the skills, along with the drive and desire to keep those skills fresh. So you see claims that no software developers are employable after they're 30-35 years old, which is nonsense. So if you're enthusiastic about programming but afraid because of some garbage article that claimed AI would take all the jobs? By all means, stay in software. But if you're really just looking for an excuse to change careers? Why wait? Better to literally be a plumber than to try to suffer through a career you hate. Plumbers make a lot of money, after all. 🤷🏻‍♂️ .

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Why do software developers age over 40 leave the industry?
Answer: We certainly don't all leave the industry. There does exist ageism in the industry. And there is a pattern of firing older, more expensive developers, that's more common than it should be, despite being extremely shortsighted. But in general, demand for good developers is strong enough that we can continue to get good gigs well past 40. But. Lots of developers aren't really that good. Some may manage to keep their jobs into their 30s, but when developers aren't that strong it takes tons of extra effort to accomplish their jobs. I hear about constant overtime, constant stress, and low pay. If that's your life, then hitting your 40s is likely to make you realize you're miserable. Hitting that age milestone is enough to convince them to either switch to management or something completely different. Honestly, many give up or pivot by 30. But some of us love programming and are good at it. No extra stress. No extreme overtime. And when you're good, you can usually demand a good salary. So none of the downsides, and plenty of upside. So that's why some leave the industry, but many of us stay for the long haul.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Can I actually become a software engineer/programmer from home and without high math knowledge?
Answer: Technically? Yes. From a practical standpoint? Depends on what you mean by “high math knowledge.” You don't need to be fresh on all of calculus to program. I happen to remember more calculus than average, but I basically never use the knowledge. But that feeds into my point: To be good at software development requires an overlapping skill and aptitude set to math. So if you're asking the question because you were terrible at all of your math courses after basic arithmetic, there's a very high chance you will also be terrible at programming. Not because you don't know the math, but because the same things that make it hard for you to learn math will make it hard for you to learn programming. There's one exception I'd like to call out, though: If you're “bad at math” because you lack attention to detail, or more to the point, lack attention to detail when you're forced to sit down and solve arbitrary equations by hand for hours at a time, that may mean you're at least partially ADHD. It's all about whether you understood the concepts, not about whether you can repeat them by rote. So I'm not saying you need to have gotten all A's. Because in programming, it's the understanding that's key. The computer will happily tell you if you've made a stupid mistake; if you understand what you're doing and why, then being a little sloppy isn't a deal breaker. There are even defensive programming patterns you can use to help prevent stupid mistakes from slipping past in the first place. As programmers, one of the first things we (should!) do is to eliminate, as much as possible any rote tasks. That way we don't end up with human error breaking our product nearly as often. So cranking out rote code over and over isn't the job of a software engineer. There are (apparently) coder jobs that are like that, but those jobs are at risk of being replaced by AI or $10/hour workers in Southeast Asia. I don't recommend competing with them.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Which is preferred and who will you hire: a team of collaborative, high-morale, and intuitively managed normal developers, or a team of arrogant rockstar x10 engineers facing morale, confusion, and management challenges?
Answer: I second the answer by Christopher F Clark. The entire meme of “arrogant rockstar 10x engineer” is a gross exaggeration at best, and a complete lie at worst. It's true that the very best engineers are more of a challenge to manage. But the very best engineers don't actually require much management, if any, and most of the “problems” reported by managers are the engineers objecting to stupid directions and rules. But morale problems? Really strong developers usually work well with each other. If there's a toxic developer or two in the group, then ditch them and your (slightly smaller) rockstar team will still likely outperform your team of normal developers. But why hire only one team? There are problems in most projects that can really benefit from a 10x developer, and there are more routine tasks that a 10x developer is kind of wasted on. The advantage of a strong developer is that they can solve the hard problems faster; on more routine tasks, they're probably not any faster at all. The book “The Mythical Man Month” is often credited as having popularized the idea of the 10x developer. But people seem to not know the entire story, which is that the book recommends a single strong developer per team as the team's “surgeon,” guiding the entire team, with supporting developers to handle the tasks that don't need a surgeon. So the right answer might be to break up the rockstars into several collaborating teams, spreading the “normal” developers around to each team. Not because the rockstars will have personality conflicts, but because the teams will be more efficient that way. All of this “rockstar” bashing gets old. Strong developers exist, and they can improve the entire trajectory of a project. Denying that they exist, or accusing them all of being arrogant assholes, says more about the bruised egos of the accusers than it says about actual 10x developers.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes better at writing code than humans, will coding become less important in the future?
Answer: Premise false. In no way is AI better at writing code than humans. Nor is there any trajectory in that direction at the moment. Right now AI is only able to regurgitate code that was already written by humans. When being asked to accomplish very simple tasks, it can even regurgitate code that's correct. But it's atrociously bad at writing novel code, for the simple reason that no current technology embodies any understanding into the AI models. And since it periodically spits out code that's laughably bad, the code is only useful to a programmer who knows how to fix it or rewrite it. Programming isn't just specialized typing. It's not simply memorizing syntax and translating the English description of a project into code. It requires that the programmer understand the goal of the code they're writing. It requires the programmer be able to design the overall architecture of the application. AI can do none of this. Zero. Zilch. Null-pointer-exception, reference-not-found level of nothing when searching for any actual understanding in the current models. But that's all ignoring the elephant in the room: Coding is not, nor has it ever been, the hard part. Only beginners who are trying to avoid actually learning to code think it's hard. I suspect the same people who used to ask questions about programming “in plain English” are now hoping that AI will prevent them from needing to learn the syntax of a language. A bit later in the beginner's journey, they often end up asking “I've learned [Python/JavaScript/Ruby/Java/etc.] completely, but I still don't know how to make X. What am I doing wrong?” These beginners have had their first real insight into programming: Learning the syntax of a language doesn't magically make them a programmer. Conversely, once you do learn to think like a programmer, you can transition to another language quickly. Using AI can, in fact, speed up this process. But given that there are only on the order of a half dozen popular languages you might be required to use at any one time, and the AI will only cut a week or so off of the learning process, there's only about six weeks of potential time savings for any one developer—and that's mostly across their whole career, so not even six weeks per year. My point is that “learning to think like a programmer” is the hard part, and AI can't do that at all. Learning to code will be required as a part of programming for the foreseeable future, and it's actually the easier part of learning to program. If learning to code is so hard that you're desperate to figure out ways around doing the learning, I might recommend a career/major change to a domain that is more compatible with your brain. Programming isn't for everyone.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is PHP still a goto language for web programming?
Answer: No. Pretty much not at all. WordPress is a go-to for low skill web developers to create cheap sites for clients. They will use PHP to customize the sites. So it's still used in a tremendous number of sites (with questionable security and typically awful performance). Even new sites. But it's not because PHP is a go-to language. It's because WordPress is the de facto cheap approach to creating sites. Are there developers who use PHP for things like Laravel? Sure. But they're in a pretty small minority compared to those who use Node, Java, C#, Python, Go, and even Ruby to create their sites. So in no way is PHP a go-to for anyone except those who have never bothered to transition to a better ecosystem. And all the ones I listed have better ecosystems today. Edit to add: No more PHP apologists please. Read the existing comments to this and my other answers if you want to see that a) I'm not just spouting outdated beliefs, and b) whatever your arguments are, I've already addressed them. Violators will have their comments deleted and will be blocked with prejudice. If you like PHP, by all means, use it and write your own answer about how great it is. Don't argue with me to try to convince me it doesn't suck, because I've heard all the arguments and they all fall flat when faced with the reality, which is that you're defending PHP because it's what you know, not because it's better. Of the dozens of people who have tried to come up with any reason it's better, exactly zero have succeeded. Zero. Any reasons you think you have are weak justifications for not spending the time to learn another ecosystem, and I'm sick of needing to address them again and again. Better to ask yourself why you feel so strongly that you need to defend the language? Is it because you're insecure about your beliefs? Edit2: Hateful trolls, or one with several sockpuppet accounts, have ruined it for everyone. Comments closed. This is why we can't have good things. Funny how emotional and ad hominem the attacks get. This is a programming language. For computers. The desperation in these comments pretty much prove what I said above: That the apologists are driven by insecurities. If I saw someone slamming a language I liked, I might make an attempt to correct their blatant errors or add a counterpoint if no one else had, but if there's already a wall of such, I'd downvote and move on. I certainly wouldn't stop to post insults about the author. Because that would undermine any point I thought I was making.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Should a software engineering interview be geared towards ensuring that a poor developer isn’t hired even if it means losing 10 good developers?
Answer: This is one of those Things That Never Happen. It's commonly brought up as a justification as to why someone who just failed an interview…failed the interview. Because clearly they are a good developer, despite the fact that they couldn't even barely understand how one might solve the simple programming problem the interviewer asked them to compete. I mean, real work never looks like those programming problems! Instead there's a request for a button that does something specific, or to display a list of elements! Not something weird like reversing a string! And the interview didn't let them Google the code for the answer! How unrealistic! The truth is that developers who really understand computer science fundamentals are faster, better developers and designers of code. Everything they create is completed sooner, with fewer major flaws, and with reasonable performance. And the developers who need to Google everything often don't fully understand all of the consequences and interactions of the code they write. This has profound consequences to the security, design, and implementation. Every aspect of the code is affected, and will be inferior to that of the CS expert. Are good developers overlooked by the interview process? Undoubtedly. But not ten rejects for every good developer hire.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: I fear that AI in the next 20 years will replace programmers/software developers. Not now now it's not that good, but in 20 years it's definitely replacing us. Should I be worried about AI or not?
Answer: The prediction that I've seen is that in 20 years, computers will be able to fully think like humans. Thing is, that prediction was made in the 1950s. It is still just as good of a prediction today. It might be just as good of a prediction in a hundred years. And let me be clear: Until a computer can fully and completely think like a human, we will still need software engineers. Not only is any prediction complete garbage, we don't even know what we don't know about what we need to invent to create the first Artificial General Intelligence. All you're seeing today is hype and magic tricks. But you can take comfort in the fact that, of the jobs available to humanity, they very last job to go to AGI will be software engineering. Because the first step is to make it think like a human. And then you need to teach it how to program—and not all humans can learn how to program, so there's no guarantee the first AGI will be good at it.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Why do programmers deserve to make ten times what an average worker makes?
Answer: It's not really about ”deserve.” It's true that everyone deserves to make a living wage. Beyond that, we're a capitalism. Wages follow the same supply and demand curve as everything else. Honestly, the average worker deserves to make more money right now. Wages have been flat since the 70s (!!), while productivity has been going through the roof. C-level and VP level executives have been pocketing the difference, and the average person has been screwed. Programmers, though, have been in enough demand that they could continue to negotiate for higher wages. The work that programming produces is also extremely valuable; at the right company, a single programmer can create millions of dollars in profits—or cause millions in losses if they're not good enough. So to some degree it's what people are willing to pay, and it's also because programmers can force companies to compete to hire them. And the best developers are the only ones who command the 10x larger salary, largely because they will create new value and be less likely to make a mistake that costs the company millions.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Can I update my website content after it is developed?
Answer: That completely depends on what you've paid for and what company develops the site for you. It will be much more likely to be true if you're sure to include “ability to update the site” as a part of the specifications you request for your website. Ask for what you want. Novel idea, I know.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Did pair programming ever catch on?
Answer: I've encountered a few companies that religiously pair program. They're almost universally consulting companies that charge by the programmer hour. Is quality higher? Than those two programmers working separately, probably. Is productivity higher? Only if one or both of those programmers were so slow that they'd take more than two hours to do the work the pair can do in an hour, or one is sloppy and inaccurate that it would take the full time work of more than a second programmer to clean up their mess. Full time pair programming can only at all be productive for very junior developers, or very low skill developers. When I see other answers talking about how much more productive it is, well, there's only one implication I get from that, and it's not pretty. My conclusion is that those consulting companies I mentioned can use pair programming to allow them to hire less skilled developers who aren't as expensive, have them pair so that they don't do as much damage, and then bill the client four times as much as if they'd hired a single skilled developer who could have done the work in half the time of the pair. A skilled developer who would have had a higher salary. It's a scam. Edit to add: I've said this many times in the comments already, but occasional pairing is fine. I thought I was clear above that I was talking about 100% pairing, as advocated by the early agile methodology “Extreme Programming.” I've paired to train a coworker on a particular bit of code. I've paired to learn about code. And I've paired to work on a particularly challenging problem. None of those would be described as “religiously pairing.” It's likely less than 5% of my programming time. And yes, I used “religiously” in the very first sentence of this post. And no, you're not going to be able to convince me that 100% pairing is productive. I've occasionally saved time while pairing, and I even enjoy it, but there's absolutely no possibility that it's even close to double my productivity. If I got a 10% boost, I'd be amazed. The other benefits can make occasional pairing worth it. But 100% pairing is only useful to compensate for lower developer skill, in my experience.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: What is a no-code software platform?
Answer: A no-code software platform is primarily a method of extracting money from business people who have been shocked by how much custom programming costs by lying to them about how easy it will be to create any app with their product. The idea is that users will be able to create their software much cheaper if they can do it themselves, or alternatively, if they hire a non-programmer to do the work. What could possibly go wrong? 🙄 Proponents (mostly those selling a no-code solution or writing sensationalized articles to attract eyeballs) will imply that no-code solutions can do anything. “The age of the programmer is over! The future of software doesn't need programmers! Buy our product and you'll never need to pay a programmer again!” Ignoring the fact that no-code platforms need to be written by programmers, and that most no-code platforms fail profoundly to live up to their promises. In order for it to truly be no-code, users of the platform will only be able to achieve exactly what the designers of the platform have created the functionality to support. And there are a near infinite number of things someone might want their app to do. You see the problem? For extremely basic apps, this can sometimes even work. Example: Restaurants don't need a huge amount of unique custom functionality, in general, so creating an app or web site for a restaurant should be totally doable. In a no-code solution designed to support restaurants, at least. A general no-code solution might not have an interface to a printer that can create order tickets in real time, for instance. And that's the crux of the lie. In practice, the people buying no-code solutions aren't programmers, and as such they are completely unqualified to judge whether or not a particular platform can achieve their goals. Much of the time the platform is purchased and dozens to hundreds of hours are sunk into it before the user realizes that the no-code platform is missing a key feature their app absolutely requires. And most of the time that means starting from scratch. Some of these platforms are “low code.” That gives them a bit more flexibility, but really, the same limitations apply. There are successful no-code platforms that aren't scams. Excel is one. People with zero programming skill can use Excel to create a smart spreadsheet “app” that can be quite sophisticated. Simple web-site builders also exist that are quite capable; if all you need is a blog or a site with a number of static pages, they will generally do the job. But you'll note that Excel and web site builders don't generally refer to their products as “no code.” That's because they aren't lying to you. When someone tries to to sell you on “no-code”, be skeptical. Be very skeptical.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Why is Xcode so unfriendly to users, but Apple's software is extremely designed to be user-friendly, why is Xcode the only exception? Are programmers not Apple's main revenue group, so Apple doesn't want to care about them?
Answer: Apple's software is designed to be idiot proof and pretty. That's not the same thing as user friendly. The iTunes user interface, in fact, is often considered the absolute worst UI of any popular consumer software package. And I mean any—not just among music related software. The Apple “image” (also known as their “reality distortion field”) fools people into thinking their products are better than they actually are. In fact, most of their software products aren't as good as the alternatives. Just don't say that to an Apple fanboy. They do have nice hardware. So do other manufacturers. But most of their software is dumbed down, with minimal features, and as such it's more accessible to the average user. I find that I'm not happy with any of their software, from OS to flagship applications. Power users generally prefer having more control. Creating software for power users simply isn't their strength. And who is more often going to be a power user than a programmer?

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Why can’t I understand or code simplest LeetCode questions, not even talking about hard or medium ones? I feel like I have 0 logical skills and I can never be good at coding.
Answer: How much learning have you done already? Have you already spent a year or more in learning how to program? Because it does take time to really learn to think like a programmer. If you have been spending a solid year on learning, and you're still feeling like you can't understand any programming logic? Even any of the Leetcode easy problems? Well, the truth is that not everyone has the right aptitude to learn how to program. People who lack the aptitude do frequently try to succeed anyway, and some do for a time. They're generally miserable, and frequently suffer from impostor syndrome because they perpetually lack any real understanding of what they're doing. And they seem to have a hard time keeping their job past about 30 years old. So if you lack the aptitude, the sooner you change to a new career path, the better. If you're still young, it will be easier to break into a new field. Good luck.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is anyone good with Delphi/Pascal coding? I need help, like a lot of help. like fr. Can someone like tutor me or something. I'm dying. I don't mind zoom calls or MS Teams. I honestly just wanna pass😭 Note: I can't pay you, I'm broke asf 🙂
Answer: You don't learn to program by having someone give you a couple of hours of tutoring. So it seems like you want someone to walk you through exactly what you need to do. And passing a programming class by having someone do the work for you helps no one. If you're in a class, there are almost certainly resources connected to the class. A TA, or the teacher, or at least other students in the class. This is just about the worst possible forum to ask for personal help on, by the way. No, StackOverflow isn't a forum for beginners either. Finding a Slack or Discord that's full of people who are willing to help beginners would really be the only reasonable choice, and even then it sounds like you're so lost that in-person teaching is the only reasonable answer. But you're in a class where that teaching has allegedly already happened, right? And you've already looked for YouTube tutorials prior to asking strangers to help you for free, right? If you've tried all of those resources and none help, then the best choice is to drop the class and either change your major so that the class isn't required, or do some independent learning before you attempt to retake the class. Software development isn't for everyone, and some people seem to profoundly lack the aptitude. You'd be doing yourself a favor to recognize that, if that's your issue, and change your goals. Good luck.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Which programming language is best to design a program that can host a minimum of 250,000 clients everyday at the same time online without crashing?
Answer: OK, that's nowhere near enough information to give you a single answer as a “best language.” The correct answer might actually be two or more languages for different parts of the server, in fact. What are those clients doing? There are some tasks that I would only recommend highly performant C++ code for, say, and others that would be fine using, say, Node.js. The load per client, the nature of any transactions, and the bandwidth per client all matter. But there are some bits of advice I can give you. First, don't choose a language with dynamic types. No Python. No Ruby. No PHP. No JavaScript. Yes, I'm aware of the “let's duct tape on static types” extensions available for each of those languages (TypeScript excepted; TypeScript is great). It's too little, too late; pick a language with all of the static type features, including full library and external module support, or you don't get all the software engineering benefits. * Why static types? They eliminate entire categories of errors from your code. Proper types make it easier to write correct code, so your developers can spend more time adding features and less time getting things working. Less technical debt accumulates, in part because refactoring is easier, in part because static types force better habits. And static types separate mediocre developers from good developers: Really learning how to use static types seems to be a barrier to entry to the “copy and paste and pray” crowd, so the developer pool is higher quality when you're asking for languages with static types. It's not enough to make them all good developers, unfortunately, so you still need to interview them as usual. If you don't want your site to crash, you need a good design and solid code. Design is hard, so you need at least one or more really strong developers on the project to keep both the overall design and the code clean. Second, don't choose a language (or framework) that's going to hamper your performance so much that your server costs will explode. You can't support 250,000 concurrent users if the server cost per user exceeds what those users are willing to pay—or their advertising revenue. I've actually seen a project canceled that had over $500k of developer time invested; they figured out that their Python server could support so few users that each would need to be paying an unreasonably high monthly fee to use the system. A better server design in a faster language could have handled 100x as many users per server, and the project would have been profitable. So that again excludes Python and Ruby. PHP used to be slow, but recent versions are much faster. On the other hand, PHP has about the worst developer pool of any language today, and developer skill will trump every other aspect of this project. Beyond that… My advice would be to hire a highly skilled consultant to put together recommendations for your specific project requirements. This advice is, if course, self serving, since I offer that kind of consultation, but you don't need to talk to me. Sites like Upwork have many highly skilled developers available for consultations, for instance. You just won't find them in the sub-$75/hour price range. Look for developers with experience using many languages. Ideally that would include several of C++, Java, C#, TypeScript, and Go. You want your architecture to be designed based on the best language for each part, not just one developer's pet language. Good luck. * I'm not interested in debating static type features of dynamic languages Yet Again. I've done this ad nauseum in other answers’ comments. Fanboy posts defending one of the languages I mentioned above will be summarily deleted. You've been warned. Write your own answer if you disagree. Search my other answers if you're curious how those debates go.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Why do software engineers tend to consistently underestimate how much work a given effort takes?
Answer: Actually… We don't. Speak for yourself. 😜 Over the course of a huge project, though? What often happens is that some small number of tasks will take much longer than expected. Either you'll come across a previously unidentified requirement, or maybe something that you thought would be easy turns out to be much harder. Maybe an API doesn't work the way you expect. Or the code that works great on one system fails on others, requiring much more work to get it running smoothly everywhere. This is true for all engineering projects, by the way. I think I've seen a quoted average that construction projects tend to go over time and budget by something like 30%. And that's for projects that are generally well understood. In any event, when building something new, sometimes your assumptions are incorrect. So even if 98% of your estimates are spot on, that remaining 2% can take up 50% or more of the project time and cause extreme overruns.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Which job should a person who’s focused on the money choose? Aerospace engineering (which interests me) pilotage (also interests me) architecture, computer or software engineering? I am into sky and space.
Answer: You should first adjust your goals. Being “focused on money” is a mistake. It's the wrong goal. I'm not going to say to follow your heart and the money will magically come. There certainly are a lot of domains where people barely survive, professionally. But completely ignoring your interests and talents is also a mistake. The best approach is to look at what you're good at, cross reference that to what you're interested in, and only then look at salaries. And don't look at salaries to see what's highest. Look for what makes enough money and has sufficient demand that getting a job won't be near impossible. Chasing top dollar is a fool's errand. Don't fall into that trap. Enough money will make you happy. More than that doesn't equate to more happiness, and can actually lead to more misery. So there's not enough information in your question. Talk to a career counselor. Only then can someone give you advice that fits your situation.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: As a great programmer, how would you appropriately express your dissatisfaction to your team members and managers, conveying the message that their performance falls below average and they need to enhance their pace and efficiency?
Answer: You just… Can't. If you want to work with top developers, you need to interview the team you'll be working with before you join a company. If the company performs peer reviews, you can include your opinions then. But don't expect change. If you're really good, finding a new job shouldn't be hard. Start looking until you find a team where you're not the best developer, and switch jobs. No one likes a whiner, especially not when they're brag-whining. Companies hire developers who they can both find and afford, and odds are good that they're doing the best they can. But even worse, what good will it do to tell them to “work harder”? If you are actually a great developer, then you know that people are usually doing their best. That there really isn't much they can do to “improve their efficiency,” or they would have already done it. Now if you have identified specific practices you think they should change to improve their performance, then that's an excellent opportunity to mentor your coworkers, if they're amenable.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: I want to be a software developer but I cannot learn JavaScript. Does it mean that I will not be able to learn other programming languages and this universe is not designed for me?
Answer: Of current popular languages, JavaScript is one of the easiest to learn. But it's never really about learning a language. It's about learning to think like a programmer. And making that leap takes work. Some people suggest that learning a static type language might be easier. But really the hard part is learning to program at all. And some people never seem to get good at programming. Not sure if some just give up too early and that they'd succeed if they tried harder—but giving up early guarantees you won't learn. Only you can decide whether you're ready to give up.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Will AI kill engineering as a career?
Answer: This seems to be a difficult to kill meme. No. Not even close. I think there are at least three categories of people who are asking this question over and over. AI has positive applications. Don't get me wrong. But all of the hype that claims AI will replace engineers of any flavor is effectively a fabrication that isn't based on reality. In my own domain of software engineering, I've played with the tools. Yes, I've used GPT-4. Yes, it can be useful as a “smart documentation lookup.” But no, it won't replace any engineers. It can't even perform an absolutely brain-dead simple conversion of a trivial script from one language to another without writing code that could not possibly have worked under any circumstances—and that's the easy part of the challenge. Current AI tech understands nothing. When stringing together words, it often sounds decent. But it's only spewing words that seem to fit well together. Words that are effectively stolen from actual humans, but that are used with zero understanding. One of the brain dead Quora Prompt Generator (an AI they use to write questions) questions was about how to travel to Quebec from Canada. In case your geography is rusty, Quebec is in Canada. So the question makes no sense. But for fun, I dropped it into ChatGPT, and it happily told me about several ways someone might travel from Canada to Quebec. Zero. Understanding. It's a magic trick. A very good one, in some cases. But it's all an illusion. What shocks me is how persistent the doomsayers are. How they'll throw code at me that was generated by so much question text, you would have been better off writing the code rather than the English, and then point at it to say that AI will replace programmers. When only a programmer could have written that English to begin with. 🙄 And when every experiment I've done the code generated has been awful, or wrong, or entirely inappropriate. They natter on about my lack of skill at ”prompt engineering” being why my experiments fail, without even recognizing the irony of the situation: If they have to write in highly specific language to produce the correct result, then they've simply created a new, poorly defined and sometimes inaccurate, programming language, and are claiming that it's somehow better than the well defined languages we've been using for years. And more importantly, the code generation that it only barely gets right is the easy part of being a software engineer. Creating an architectural design and knowing what code needs to be written are also necessary skills. Not to mention requirements gathering and interviewing the client to gain an actual understanding of their needs. Which, as I've said, current AI cannot have. Please, if you comment to disagree and tell me that AI will, in fact, take over the world any day now, let me know which category you're in. It will influence my reaction to your comment.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: I am stuck in a situation where I have to choose between studying what I want to (psychology) or study artificial intelligence because it brings more money. What should I choose? Plus I hate- absolutely despise mathematics.
Answer: Psychology can be a good basis for training as a therapist. Therapists absolutely make good money. Likely more than a mediocre AI/machine learning engineer who doesn't really like the math. If you want to go for even more money, go the full medical school route and become a psychiatrist. Or switch directions and look into UI/UX design. Use aspects of psychology and cognitive science to learn how to design human/computer interactions. “More money” is overrated, in any case. The goal should be “enough money.” I know therapists that charge $300/hour and who are booked out for weeks. Even at 20 hours per week, that can be $300k/year. Isn't that enough? But don't go that direction if you hate it either. Pick a direction that resonates with you, or you'll be miserable. And no one wants to work with a miserable therapist. Or a miserable AI researcher, for that matter. A degree isn't a golden ticket. You also have to have the talent to do the work. And that talent is much easier to develop when you don't hate the work.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: If you had to choose between an arrogant but brilliant programmer with weak collaboration abilities and an average programmer with strong cooperative skills, whom would you hire, and why?
Answer: There's no hesitation here. The brilliant programmer, hands down, no question. Brilliant software development is something that can't be taught. You either have or you don't. It's a rare enough aptitude that, when you find a developer who is genuinely good, you hire them. More than that, if you find a brilliant developer who is willing to work for you, you create a position for them so you can hire them now. Do not wait until you have a position available. Do not wait for the budget to be available. Hire them and figure out how the budget will work later. Make it happen. A brilliant developer can make the difference between barely getting a product done on time and finishing a product with enough time to spare while adding more features and fixing more bugs. About a developer having enough insight that they can anticipate and correct for potential problems. About being able to solve some problems that the average developer would never be able to overcome. So what if they don't have existing collaboration skills. You can teach people to collaborate. You can't teach them to be brilliant. Arrogance can be somewhat justified, but more to the point, brilliant developers are often accused of being arrogant when they're simply confident. But I'd put up with an arrogant, even abrasive, programmer, if they were willing to do what we asked. That said… I simply don't hire average developers. If I'm on a team, an average developer is likely not going to be good enough to keep up. So there really wasn't a choice from my point of view. Certainly, average developers do get hired, and from what I can tell, most of the places that hire average developers do select against brilliant developers. Larger companies especially have a hard time with developers who are several standard deviations above the mean, preferring to hire developers who are interchangeable instead of irreplaceable. So I'm really answering for only myself, and other answers that express preference for the personable developer aren't wrong. We just work at different kinds of companies.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is it okay for a software engineer to say that they don’t want to do a specific job (e.g., training doc, manual regression testing, etc.) when assigned by their manager?
Answer: So… Finding myself shocked at the number of “only if you want to be fired” answers. I mean, if I've been hired as a backend engineer, with the understanding that I'd be working on the new architecture, and instead they started assigning me to fixing frontend bugs, I'd absolutely push back. I can do the work, but I'm always clear in my negotiations what I want to be working on. So to all of the people who have been warning us that we'll be fired if we said no to a request, I have a simple response: Well before they got around to firing me, I'd have resigned my position if they kept insisting. I mean, I've almost never had trouble getting a new gig, and odds are good that I'd have one lined up well before the HR machine could have worked it's way through the mandatory PIP and warnings and so forth. In practice, though? I've refused manager requests that I didn't find to be reasonable many times. The consequence is… They ask again the next week. Using stronger language, sometimes. And I'd ignore the new requests in a loop until they gave up asking or I quit. A good software engineer has a golden ticket. They aren't completely proof against being let go, as recent FAANG layoffs demonstrate, but in general, if they're actually a good engineer, they have job security. If the reason they're asking you to do manual regression testing of writing documentation is that the team has requested that you stop writing code, though? Because the code you write causes them more work than if they'd written the code themselves from scratch? Then you're not a software engineer, title notwithstanding, and they're trying to be nice by giving you something productive to work on rather than just firing you. In that situation, it's agree with the other answers: If you're being asked to stop programming, then that means your days at the job are numbered if you don't comply—and odds are good you won't be able to easily walk into another job if your skills are weak. To me, it's about respect. You don't hire me as a programmer and then expect me to spend all of my time doing manual regression testing. Now should I test to see if the code I wrote broke something? Well, yes, duh, that's part of the programming job. You don't write code but then never test it! But if they're asking you to sit around testing instead of programming? Then you're not performing the duties of a software engineer.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Do you think engineers, especially software developers, are overpaid?
Answer: Kurt Guntheroth points out that supply and demand puts software developer compensation at exactly the point the market will bear. Which is 100% correct. What confuses me about this question, though, is how the asker could even wonder if we're “overpaid.” What would the criteria be? More money than they want to spend to create their billion dollar app, presumably? But there it is. “Billion dollar.” A software developer has the potential to create software that makes a potentially unlimited amount of money. How can even a half million dollars per year be “too much” when the potential profits from a single developer can be into the millions per year? Why would someone consider a 500% profit on the software developer's services to be overpaid? Either extreme wishful thinking, in the case of person who actually wants a developer to create their million dollar idea for peanuts since they don't have the funding they need to pay for development…or simply raw greed, in the case of the person who is running a company that is making millions, and they resent the need to pay a developer a fair wage for their work. Back to Kurt's point: Not everyone can be a competent software engineer. I suspect that the percentage of the population who has the right aptitude may not be more than a percent. Maybe a tenth of a percent. Probably half or more professional developers don't hit the minimum threshold, are struggling to get by, and will transition to a management role before they're 30. So when someone is genuinely good at software engineering? The supply of such developers is limited by the number of developers with that aptitude, and demand is high because billion dollar apps are a thing, so compensation keeps going up. And from the other side, an engineer's potential for profits for the company hiring them is limited only by the business plan (and savvy) of the company management, and so there is no inherent limit of “value per hour of work” that you'd see in other industries. So no, there's really no such thing as “overpaid” in software engineering. “Underpaid,” however, is endemic.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: As a software engineer do you feel there is a strong argument to go back from micro services to monolithic architecture given that Amazon prime was able to save cost and be more performant by doing the same?
Answer: I was hired to help out with a project once. The team was enthusiastic about something called Domain-Driven Design, and had designed their backend with nearly 20 microservices as a result of believing DDD was the right way to design a system. DDD, it turns out, advocated for isolation between units of your app before microservices were a thing. It outlines how the various units should be isolated from each other, and how each should have a sole motivating principle. And a lot more; I only remember the highlights. The team in charge of this project had reinterpreted DDD as appropriate guidance for how to split the app into microservices. And then they very liberally split up the system, even though I don't even think DDD would justify some of their services. If they had a hundred developers spread over 20 teams, I could see this approach making some sense. Maybe. At least it would be arguable. Each team could have full ownership of a microservice, and adding new functionality could be done in each silo without breaking anyone else's code. But their team consisted of two developers. Yup. Two. They were sure their team would eventually be much larger, but… It wasn't larger. Worse, their whole backend could have comfortably been a single monolith. There was zero reason to have that many microservices. Knowing what it know of their actual service, I could see having two microservices to support a monolith. That's really it. And the microservices meant that everything was harder. In fact, it was so complex to work on, every developer they'd tried to hire before me had failed to learn enough to get anything done. So their plan to expand the team was hampered by the fact that onboarding people was near impossible. But they had drunk the kool-aid and believed, heart and soul, that their interpretation of DDD was The Way, and they did what they could to stay true to that path. How is this at all relevant to the question? I'm glad you asked! Design is hard. Good design is worth its weight in gold. Good design is not, nor does it even remotely resemble, following the latest trend. Or believing any blog entry or book has The Answer. There are as many answers as there are problems. More than there are problems, in fact. Domain Driven Design was never “The Answer.” Neither were microservices in general. Neither are monoliths. Nor are server functions. Or containers. Or crypto, for that matter.* (* Crypto/blockchain turns out to not be the answer to any question, in fact, unless the question has to do with scamming people. But I digress…) So should you have converted everything to microservices because books and blogs were singing the praises of microservices? No. And should you convert everything to a monolith because everyone is talking about microservice disasters? Also no. Instead of blindly following architectural design advice from popular blogs, you should learn the pros and cons of all the architectural decisions. If you can't carefully consider the implications of a design, then you shouldn't be in charge of the design. Our industry, far too often, is vulnerable to design trends. There is no silver bullet. Think about that phrase. Say it to yourself ever time you consider trying a new technology. Don't be sucked in by the hype; evaluate options based on actual context and experience. And apply that to every architectural and technology decision you make. Don't switch to a monolith because the guys at Amazon Prime did. Don't switch to microservices because some other blog has a rebuttal that sounds convincing. Make changes because, after you carefully consider the pros and cons, you project that the benefits of making those changes will likely more than offset the costs. There are absolutely situations where microservices might result in higher throughput and lower overall costs. Amazon has shown the reverse to also be true. Sometimes the cost difference will be nearly irrelevant, making the cost to convert a waste of resources. Do the work to figure out what's best for your application. The answer for one service doesn't necessarily apply to any other service, and you have homework to do before you can arrive at any conclusions. And no part of that homework is done for you by asking Quora a generic question about architecture.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: I want to get hired as a software developer but they won't hire me because I'm self-taught. Do I have to lie to get my foot in the door?
Answer: Lying is just about the worst idea possible. If you get caught, you'll likely lose your job and the industry isn't so big that it won't come back to bite you later. On every future job rejection, you will need to wonder if it was because someone told them you lied in a previous job application. It could haunt you for years. And as I allude to above, being “self taught” can range from “Learn Python in 24 hours!” to a deep dive into writing apps that spans years and includes the study of CS concepts. Honestly, my guess is that you're much closer to the first than the second, simply because most developers are. If you want to compete, you need to stand out.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: I was told by people that software engineers right out of college usually get $120k~300k. However, the median salaries listed on schools’ websites rarely go over $100k. Why is this?
Answer: There are a couple potential reasons I can think of: What they don't tell you is that, in order to get the really high salaries early in your career (or at all for the most part) you need to be good at software engineering. Even if your school isn't the best, that doesn't really matter. What matters is how good you are at the fundamentals. And unfortunately, not everyone can get to that level of skill. Developers who can't pass the programming tests and interviews of the top employers end up in a different kind of programming job. One that doesn't pay as well. I've seen jobs posted at $30/hour that were asking for a set of skills that should have demanded $80/hour, and when I dropped them a note to tell them how far off their salary offer was, they wrote back to tell me the role was filled. So at least one person willing to claim those skills was willing to accept $60k/year for them. Given how easy it is for a skilled developer to get a job paying twice that, I have to assume that employer doesn't care at all about any actual skill. And they're not alone in that—but there are a lot more lower skill developers out there competing for those lower skill jobs. I hear from people about year long job searches, when the high skill developers I know complain if it takes them three months to find a gig. So ask yourself whether you're on the lower or higher end of skill. You're in college, yes? How do you compare to your peers? Do you blaze through programming assignments without much help?
