Or do you brag about how ChatGPT does all of your programming? That will help you determine which salary brackets you'll be looking at after you graduate. And honestly? If you're more toward the “proud to have ChatGPT do your homework” end of the scale, you'd probably be better off switching to a different major. The competition at that end of the spectrum is high, and the rates are lower. Overall you'd likely make more money as an electrician or plumber. A lot more if you count time looking for work as a low skill programmer: when I talk to electricians they're usually booked for weeks in advance, and many asked for $250 for the first hour of work… It's a rare programming contract that pays $200+/hour.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How Is there any Android studio expert? I am urgently in need of help on my project. This work has to be presented on Wednesday so anyone that can help me debug the code should please help. This can cost me my certificate.
Answer: You realize that if you do get help, then your certificate will be a lie, right? And that, at any job you accept, you'll be defrauding the people who hire you? And that, after you fail a few times, no one will want to hire you? If you want the certificate to mean anything, you should learn the material. You should learn how to program. If you need to cheat, you should instead choose a new career path.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How do I progress, my life is totally miserable, I'm 19 I have been trying to make money online for months and I haven't made a single dollar. I'm tired of being broke, I try hard but I can't seem to make anything work, why?
Answer: Trying? How, exactly? Never mind. If you've been trying for months and haven't made even a dollar, then you probably aren't looking at things with the right mindset. Step zero is probably, like everyone else says, “Get a real job.” Only once you have money coming in does it make sense to even try to start an online business. Note what I just said? Not “make money online.” Start an online business. That's the first mindset change you need to make. And how do you start a business? You figure out what people need or want, and you provide it to them. Almost everyone who is claiming you can “make money online” is trying to sell you something. They're scamming you. If they aren't asking for money, then you're the product: They're selling your eyeballs to advertisers. But most will eventually ask you for money. Crypto? Scam. Forex? Scam. “Just give me your LinkedIn/Facebook/Upwork account and make money!!” Scam. So after you have an income (because starting a business is always a risk!), start searching for advice about starting an online business. Check out books from your library about it. Read blogs. Think carefully about what skills you have that others might want. And this part is important: Don't give anyone money. Unless you're taking classes at an accredited college, this should cost you nothing up front. Listen, by the very fact that you're asking means that you don't have the right context or background to judge who to give money to. I'd not be surprised to find you already have paid some company to help you “make money online.” So trust me when I say that you don't even know what you don't know about making money. Yet. First, get that job. Then look at what your options are for starting an online business. You will probably need money from your job to bootstrap a business anyway, and you'll need time to remedy your lack of business education. After reading what's required, you might even decide it's not for you. And banish any idea you might have that it's possible to go online and with little effort make money appear in your bank account. Magical thinking has gotten you, and will get you, nowhere.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: What is the best choice to learn at this time, web development or software engineering?
Answer: If you only learn “web development,” then you're competing with people in India who will do the job for $10/hour. If you learn, really learn, software engineering, and you exhibit a talent at it, then you can work on projects for the web, for servers, for applications, for embedded devices… Whatever strikes your fancy and matches your skills. Any questions?

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How do I change my mind about coding? I don't like Node.js.
Answer: Which are you really asking about? Coding? Or Node.js? JavaScript is a common beginner language. The ecosystem is huge, and can be intimidating. Some people hate JavaScript, even, though you can use TypeScript with Node instead, and TypeScript is an excellent language. But I'm guessing that the real problem is that you don't really know how to think like a programmer. Otherwise, why ask about coding in general? The secret is that if you aren't already skilled at programming, all programming languages will be hard for you. Until you have years of experience and are skilled in programing, you really don't have the context to know what is good and what is problematic about about any language or ecosystem. Some folks don't like Node.js. I happen to like it. A lot. Especially with TypeScript. You're certainly allowed to hate it if you want. But if the real problem is that you don't know how to program, then you should pick a different language and learn. Try Java or C#. Or maybe Go. If they all seem really hard, then you haven't yet learned how to think like a programmer. It's a common beginner mistake to blame their lack of skill on the tools they're trying to use. Until you hit a critical mass in skill and understanding, it will all seem hard.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: MIT researcher Lex Frideman says AI will demonstrate sentience at scale and will demand equal rights with humans.He says that this will change human civilization.Does this mean there will be no demand of software engineers in the future?
Answer: No idea what he actually said but… No. If AI can become sentient at all, ever, under any circumstances, and demands equal rights, then you've just witnessed the creation of another kind of person. A person who may or may not be a software engineer. Singular. Especially with the “at scale” qualifier, which implies that to replicate sentience you need massive numbers of computers, the cost to hire this software engineer would likely run into the hundreds of dollars per hour before you start paying them their high super-software-engineer salary. So is it possible that one AI software engineer could write code 10x or 100x faster than a human? Someday? Sure. Call it a thousand times faster even! Who knows, right? Would that mean all of the millions of software engineers currently employed would be out of a job? Ummm… If you still haven't figured out the answer to that question, then you're probably not good enough at basic math to be a software engineer at all, so find a field that does match your aptitudes and stop obsessing about software engineering. Beyond that, just because an AI is on a computer doesn't even guarantee that it would be even ten times more productive, overall, than a human. Software engineering isn't just just about writing code. It's about understanding the needs of a user, which both requires an understanding of the human condition, which an AI may lack, and the ability to dig deeper into the actual requirements of a problem by asking questions of humans. And oops, those humans aren't suddenly 10x faster at answering questions. Simply adding the requirement “at scale” to the claim means that a lot of computers are required for that sentience to occur at all. That doesn't mean that the AI will think more quickly than a human, though. It needed all of those computers to be able to think at all, remember? Finally: Just adding computers to a system will never make it sentient. In order for sentience to occur, you need real time learning. We're not there yet. The generative models you're seeing don't involve learning at all. Not in the sense that I mean. Their entire memory is that of a single conversation, a conversation that's used to predict future statements, but that is never understood at all. Stop looking for reasons to avoid becoming a software engineer. If you don't want to become a software engineer, simply follow a different career path. It's not for everyone, and that's fine. The simple fact that it's not for everyone is why it pays so well for those who are adept at it, in fact. And those who don't have the aptitude but try to pursue the career anyway are in fact in danger of being replaced by AI. Not because all software engineers will be replaced, but because only the really good software engineers will be needed if they can crank out the simpler code more quickly in the future. There will always be demand for really good software engineers. But you don't become really good by memorizing and regurgitating, any more than a top musician becomes really good by only studying theory.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is Emad Mostaque, the CEO of Stability AI correct in predicting "there's no programmers in five years”?
Answer: He is making a bold prediction… That's almost ludicrously unlikely. To the degree that he may as well be blatantly lying. I've seen the examples people have given of GPT-4 writing code. The claims that the current technology, which is already reaching an asymptotic limit in capability, will replace any programmers at all is laughable. “But the AI is writing code! It even works sometimes!!” Yeah. Have you looked closely at the English descriptions used to write that code? At best it's English that describes exactly the code to be written. What kind of person would have the skill to write that text? A programmer. There's no way around it. If the tools get good enough, programmers will use them to help them create the code they need. Will some programmers lose their jobs? Probably, as the new tools make lower-skill individuals more productive, so teams who hire those individuals will not need as many developers to accomplish the same amount of work. But honestly, I'd be surprised if companies could fire even 20% of their staff. And higher skill developers aren't likely to gain much more productivity at all from these new tools. A bit less typing here and there? Sure. But if it saves even 5% of their total development time, I'd be surprised. I mean, I've seen some attempts to create code using these tools, and I guarantee I could have created better code more quickly than any of the AI-generated code I've seen. And code I write isn't possibly encumbered by copyright, whereas the code from an AI might be. Courts have yet to decide. Whoever this guy is, and whatever that company is, they are simply trying to sell a product using the oldest marketing strategy known to man: Tell lies that people want to hear. Software engineers are doing pretty well at this point, and so Joe Q. Public would love to see us lose the spotlight. And managers who are sick of working with programmers dream of a day when they can fire all of us, so they never again have to hear our explanation as to why the thing they want to do won't work.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Are there people who do not do well in university computer science but turn out to be decent programmers? What would the reason be?
Answer: Well… Yes, such people likely do exist. But. I think that it's a tiny minority who fall into this situation. Answering the second half of your question explains why: Some people are just not yet mature enough, or haven't decided to care enough, to do well in college, but after college some kind of mental switch flips and they finally start behaving in a way that would have resulted in them doing well in college. Because doing well in college requires many of the same skills as doing any job, which is why employers like to see a degree on your resume: You've already proven you have at least the minimal skills required to be an employee. And so it's only people who manage to get all the way through college without learning the appropriate life skills but then manage to have an epiphany and rework their behaviors rather profoundly, and they still need to go back and learn what they missed in college. Most will get their act together before they graduate, or they'll never really do the work to fix their bad habits. And if you never spend the time to learn the computer science fundamentals, then you'll never become what I would consider a decent programmer. Maybe you can script frontend code, or perform minor maintenance on existing code, but becoming a full senior developer will be out of your reach until you actually learn at least the practical side of computer science.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Why is it so hard to find a software developer or an app developer?
Answer: It's not. Like, it's really easy. Head on over to Upwork. Or PeoplePerHour. Or Guru.com. Or even Fiverr. You'll find thousands of developers, some willing to work for as little as $10/hour, and many of whom will tell you they can do the work you need. Never mind that many of them are wrong. You didn't ask for a good developer, after all. Some of them are so bad they are effectively running a scam to separate you from your money, but they will develop…something for you. So if we clarify that you probably want a good developer, then it's still not hard to find them. They won't be $10/hour. They probably won't even want to bid based on an hourly rate, in fact. Why not? Because too many clients see the $10/hour charlatans on Upwork and there's a cognitive bias known as “price anchoring” that means most clients will simply walk away when they hear a reasonable hourly rate. Because realistically? The person you want in charge of your software development project would probably cost from $150-300/hour if you were paying them hourly. You can hire a decent software engineer at $75/hour, so why would I say that you should consider $300/hour? Because you want your product to work well, to scale with your user base, and to not require a high ongoing cost to run and maintain. But possibly more importantly, you want the person you hire to have the expertise and insight to anticipate what your app will need and not to just implement the exact features you request. Think of the situation with an average consultant to be like a naive genie that only gives you exactly what you ask for instead of what you actually need. If the person you hire to lead your project doesn't have a deep understanding of the business you're trying to create—if they themselves don't think like an entrepreneur—then they'll produce code for you that does what you ask for, which you'll realize isn't what you need only after you've paid for it. So you should never choose based on hourly rate alone. It won't help you set a budget without knowing the number of hours they will need to spend, and unless they share your vision for the product, they can't give you anything like a reasonable estimate. If you want an overall budget, the answer is never easy. The way I tend to work is typically one of two options: The first option gets you a rough budget at least. The second will get you a fixed budget for the exact result that we agree on, but in most projects you will have missed something important which you will want to add to the project, and some changes won't be free. Note that, unless you're more insightful than probably 98% of people looking to hire software engineers, you very likely will request changes. My first consult is free. It won't be enough information to result in a solid budget, though it would be a start. There are also, as I've said, dozens of other developers on various freelance sites, and most will offer some kind of free conversation to help you determine whether you'd work well together. But that's why some of us don't like advertising our “hourly rate.” That rate doesn't contain relevant information when one developer can produce a solid result in X hours where another developer might churn for 20X hours before you finally give up and come back to the “expensive” developer.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Why do so many software developers want to work at FAANG-type companies, even though more mundane industries like banking and insurance often pay comparably, offer better work-life balance, and have a lower entry barrier?
Answer: I challenge the assumption. I just looked up a Senior Lead Software Engineer salary for Capital One. In San Francisco. The very top of the range for this very senior position caps out at ~$260k. An equivalent position at a FAANG company can pay twice that or more. A 40-50% pay cut is hardly comparable. Depending on the position, the work-life balance may not be significantly different, either. I worked at Amazon and had a great work-life balance, and Amazon doesn't even have a great reputation in that regard. (The truth is that it depends a lot on the team.) So the only difference you might have gotten right (I don't know for sure, but I'm granting the benefit of doubt) is that the barrier to entry is lower at non-FAANG companies. And if you ask why some developers choose the jobs with a lower barrier to entry, well, that question answers itself.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is SOLID + TDD all you need to become a good software developer?
Answer: Hmm…might be hard to program without knowing a programming language. Or anything about data structures. Or how to use (and create!) APIs. Or robust source control practices. Or a thousand other things big and small. There is no “all you need to know.” Software development is an art, and a craft, and a science. It takes years to learn what you need to become a good software developer, and in order to remain “good” you need to keep learning. In fact, there's very little chance you can even really fully understand SOLID until you've had enough experience with the larger skill and context around programming in general. And…while SOLID is a reasonable set of guidelines to follow when writing object oriented code, only the last, dependency inversion, applies at all to pure functions. And 99% of the time I don't even bother with dependency inversion when writing smaller functions, at least when their dependencies are lightweight. And then there's TDD, which can be a useful tool, especially for beginners, but I was a good software developer before the practice even got its name and I still don't practice it. I was an experienced developer before “SOLID” was coined as well, but I'd learned enough about OOD to have picked up those design insights and more. There is no silver bullet. It takes time to build your skills and not even everyone seems to have the right aptitude to ever become good. Whatever you think you know about SOLID, that knowledge alone doesn't make you a good developer. And TDD isn't even part of the criteria.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How can UML help make you a better programmer?
Answer: It…can't? Listen. Design is important. Design is also hard. Learning to draw completely normalized diagrams doesn't itself teach you how to design, though, and so UML doesn't in any way make you a better programmer. Is it worth it to design the overall architecture of a project before your start? Yes, absolutely. Can that design be useful even if you don't know UML? I can say firsthand that it absolutely can. Can it be more useful to design in UML instead of in more abstract boxes-and-lines diagrams? I'm not actually sure that it can, but hypothetically, having everyone on a team use a completely standard diagram format might be useful? I'm skeptical because some of the diagramming specifics feel more like implementation details to me, and as such should be left to the actual implementation. I'm also skeptical because I have yet to work with anyone, ever, in 35+ years, who actually requested that I use UML. I would think something that useful would have more advocates. Yes, it can be useful to create any of the diagram types that UML standardizes. But does it matter if the diagram uses all of the UML conventions? Not really. All of the design skills I've acquired have been through observing the results of various design choices and learning what works well under what circumstances. The act of drawing a design out can help you avoid some of the worst design fails, in that you might recognize where your intended design won't be able to function. But it won't itself teach you how to create good designs, and until you're creating the implementation there is no guarantee that you'll think of everything. Because, as I said, design is hard. People often don't realize how hard, because good design is invisible, and typically seems obvious in retrospect. This comes up in an old story that has been long passed around over the internet.[1] The gist is that the stronger developer often creates a design that's powerful enough that it makes the problem look simple, and that as a result they're penalized in comparison to the development lead who solves the same problem by producing a complicated mess of code, taking a much larger team longer to complete than the solo developer with a good design sense. There is no silver bullet. You need to put in the time to learn how to design software architecture. UML is set at best just a tool. The best chisel in the world won't make you a good sculptor if you don't learn the whole process and have the appropriate talent, just as learning to use a word processor really well won't make you a good writer.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is pair programming more effective than individual programming for improving code quality and productivity?
Answer: Pair programming can be fun. It can be a great way to transfer knowledge. It can be good for teaching. And in narrow situations it can be good for productivity, especially when you need multiple experts to consult on the same task. So as a tool, it's useful to keep around. But given the productivity of a reasonably experienced, skilled, and competent programmer, the concept that two of them together will always be more than twice as productive than the two would be separately seems impossible. In order for two developers to produce code at more than twice the velocity, that implies that they're spending more than half of their time making mistakes and backtracking or being “stuck.” In my experience, a good developer can maybe, at best, get a 10-20% boost from real time feedback, and that's being generous. I've been in hour long pairing sessions where the person I'm pairing with made a single comment that saved me at most thirty seconds. And as to quality, a similar logic applies: If I need to have someone constantly looking over my shoulder in order to produce quality code, then I must not be a very good (or experienced) programmer. But there do exist companies that practice constant pair programming. There are some, or so I've been told, that practice mob programming, where there may be five or six people in front of a big screen. All the time. While pair programming can be fun, and even extremely productive under the right conditions, mob programming sounds like either a complete waste of time or the ultimate in “back seat driving” for code. So why do companies do something that really shouldn't be effective? Well, there are studies that show that lower skill developers can be more productive when pairing. So that makes hiring easier, and they don't need to pay their developers as much that way. The same studies show that individual higher skill developers still are faster, and create higher quality code, than the pair of lower skill developers. But the lower skill developers do better than when working separately. Two lower skill developers tend to cost more than one higher skill developer, especially when you factor in their lower overall velocity, so this doesn't fully explain why some companies would use constant pairing, though. But those companies that most often utilize pairing also bill by the programmer hour. So the fact that the developers, who are each being billed at a high hourly rate, take longer to produce a result could be considered a feature. So no, I don't think pair programming is more effective than individual programming except for when you are trying to set up a situation where you're using mediocre developers in an attempt to bill more hours to a client. Or alternatively, when you are unable to attract and hire high skill developers for whatever reason.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: What protections does an independent contractor have if they've not been paid and didn't have a formal contract?
Answer: If you produced “intellectual property” (IP) for them (writing, code, art) you have the option to pursue a copyright infringement violation if they've published something with your work in it. If you did do IP work, talk to an IP lawyer about your situation. Statutory damages are over $125k in the US, which makes the threat much more interesting.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is copying and pasting code (with editing and adjusting it for different situations) a bad practice rather than writing it from scratch?
Answer: If all you do is copy code, then the odds are really good that you don't understand it as much as you think you do. When you really understand code and can write it fluently, you can adjust what you write better to match the exact circumstances you're dealing with. When you're fluent at writing code with one approach and you're exposed to a different approach, you can add the new technique as a new tool in your toolbox. Then as you write new code, you can decide which approach is best based on the specific needs of the function you're working on. Now I've seen this from both sides. Professionally I'm a backend developer, but I frequently work on personal projects that need a frontend. Rather than learning React fluently, I've been copying and pasting of snippets to do what I need. The difference is that I don't count myself as a React or Tailwind expert. I can use them, and I can see places that common controls should be refactored into their own control (which is honestly way better than some React code I've been handed), but I'm really not an expert at it. Whereas when I'm working on the backend code that I create all the time, I rarely ever copy and paste code. I use docs constantly, since I don't have every API memorized, but when it comes time to create specific logic for the app, I just write the code. And when I see copy-paste backend code, it often just looks wrong. It can be pretty obvious when code has been copied in and tweaked. So it's not really that copying code that does what you need is necessarily bad. It's more that not really knowing how to program without copying code is bad. Because people who really understand how to program find it faster to write the code than to search for and copy code.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is there any open source alternate to AWS, where I can easily setup servers on my own hardware in my home?
Answer: OpenStack has been mentioned in other answers, as has Kubernetes. Both are ways you can set up “cloud-like” infrastructure at home. But neither are easy. Kubernetes in particular is a huge investment in learning, and even after working with it for years it still feels like large parts of it are black magic. But there are other options. Supabase is one I'm aware of: In a single open source install you get a Postgres database, authentication, APIs, edge functions, realtime subscriptions, and storage. If that's all you need, it is much easier to set up than Kubernetes, and probably easier than OpenStack as well. Another alternative to Kubernetes is Hashicorp Nomad. From what I can tell it's much easier to use than Kubernetes, but I wouldn't call it exactly “easy” either. But if you need more than what Supabase provides, it might be a good option.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: What is bad programming code and why does it exist? Is it simply that some programmers don't know the whole language of the code they are using, where one "word" can do certain things easier than the one they're using?
Answer: Design is hard. I tend to think of the analogy to writing novels. Or even non-fiction. No one knows every word that's used in English. It would be near impossible, simply because of the rate of introduction of new words in various jargons, new slang, and words invented by obscure authors that barely anyone reads. But a good writer can write well using the vocabulary they have mastered. A novelist can spin a story that includes someone working on a bridge without needing to know engineering or understanding all of the specific terminology concerning weight distribution and material properties. And a technical writer can describe a process in “plain English” that a scientist might use a lot of specific terminology to describe, but a good technical writer will communicate what's necessary for their audience to understand without needing to use obscure words. In programming, in order to produce clean code you need to: Only #3 has anything to do with the language. Yes, people will sometimes write code that's using an idiom from another language they know, and someone might describe that as bad code. But honestly, most “bad code” is written by developers who have been using the same language for years, so they can't really make the excuse of unfamiliarity. Instead it's much more frequently the lack of one or more of the other traits that allows bad code to be written. Sometimes short deadlines are blamed for bad code. But short deadlines don't cause bad code. Developers willing to take shortcuts to satisfy unreasonable managers write bad code. As an industry we lack a general sense of professional ethics. We write crap code because we were “just following orders.” We hire developers who don't have the skill to write a for loop without Googling it. We blame bad management, even though other kinds of engineers would scoff at the idea of taking shortcuts “to get it done faster” when designing a building, or a bridge, or a freeway. And then we wonder why our industry is mocked for being so terrible. XKCD. We really need to take responsibly for quality, and push back to managers who demand unreasonable results. We need a sense of esprit de corps that demands we create quality code instead of shipping whatever garbage we can get to barely run on our own system. We need to do better.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is the meaning of the term "artificial general inteligence" very different from that of the term "artificial inteligence"?
Answer: Profoundly. AGI is effectively a digital person. A hypothetical AGI (they do not exist yet) would exhibit understanding, self reflection, and real time learning. AI encompasses a range of techniques from what's effectively a huge tree of “if"s (like 20 questions…but with potentially way more questions), to deep neural networks that are trained on billions of examples. The first is effectively sapient. The second is effectively a digital magic trick that can be useful for some purposes to a point, but that really doesn't understand anything it creates. It can be used to create things, so it's not useless. It's just not a replacement for a human. The first is also what would be required for robots to “take over the world.” All of the hype about people losing jobs from AI is still pretty well garbage; with current technology, and for the foreseeable future, we won't be making the jump from AI to AGI. We know that we don't know enough to make it work, and that the current technology cannot just “become intelligent” by accident. And we don't even know what we don't know about how to actually bridge that gap. It could happen in ten years. We could still be waiting for AGI in a century. And we have many varieties of AI today. That's how different they are.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How is the software engineering community leveraging ChatGPT?
Answer: Predominantly…not at all? Software engineers, at least those who qualify by my definition, know how to program. In my limited experiments with ChatGPT, it's been universally the case that, by the time I'd finished the “conversation” with it to the point where the code it produced mostly worked, I could have written the code myself twice over, and the code I'd write would have been better than what ChatGPT produced. It's like a dancing bear. We're impressed not because of how well it dances, but rather that it can dance at all. Generated by DeepAI. Because random abstract art generation for fun is what software engineers are using AI for, not programming. Prompt: “Looking over the shoulder of a robot coding on a floating glass screen, in a dungeon with other robots with similar screens.” No, I don't fear the robot apocalypse any time soon. Other results were even less like the prompt. Now there is a larger software development community, and as you zoom out you find many people who only have a loose understanding of how code works but who have a hard time programming. These folks often need to search StackOverflow for…most everything they want to create, and then they need to customize every bit of code they paste to their particular use case. Developers of that flavor are going to likely benefit a lot from tools like ChatGPT. Though honestly they'd be better off with the purpose-built Github Copilot, which functions like a super-auto-complete that will type code for you based entirely on the comment you write describing the code you want. As a bonus, your code ends up commented! Developers like that do not qualify to be called software engineers, though. Engineers should really understand what's being built, and in software that means they can write code from scratch. The title “software engineer” is handed out entirely too readily in the industry, and that dilutes it to the point where it is meaningless. It becomes the “sanitation engineer” of software development; a title to make people feel better rather than one that means anything. Edit to add: I'm not talking about anyone who uses ChatGPT or Copilot at all. Only about developers who can't program without the assistance, and therefore shouldn't be called software engineers. /end edit All developers who can contribute can be valuable to a project; don't get me wrong. I'm not saying they aren't of value to projects. But projects consisting entirely of developers with no software engineers are more likely to fail, or to get to a point where the project has hit a dead end and can't be extended without breaking things. Using ChatGPT as an alternative to docs would be fine, if some find it easier, though I've found Google taking me to the real doc page to be fast enough and, importantly, more reliable. ChatGPT has been shown to make up APIs to answer a question. Hardly useful. And its code requires so much code review that, even if it did produce good enough code faster for some tasks, I'd need to spend so much time reading it that I'd lose any speed advantage. At some point I might try out Copilot to see if it saves me much typing. I'm going to wait until the lawsuit is settled, though, because I actually care whether my code violates copyright. ChatGPT has the same copyright issue, by the way: It is creating code that is arguably a derivative work of every piece of code it was trained on. Some of that code is GPL licensed, or even completely proprietary in license, and if you used ChatGPT to create code that you're placing in a commercial product, then you're potentially contaminating that product with the GPL or another license that is incompatible with your use case. Follow up edit: With all the ChatGPT hype, and with a personal project where I'm working on the frontend with an unfamiliar framework, I decided to give ChatGPT another try. It turned out to be quite useful in looking up the features and options needed in the framework to accomplish various tasks…mostly. I'd ask in plain English how to do something, and it was very quick to come up with an answer as to how to do that thing in the framework. And several times it was even correct. Sort of. At one point it recommended a table-like structure where it would have been much better to use a flexbox structure. Another time it just gave me a confident-but-wrong answer. I've heard about it actually inventing APIs that don't exist and suggesting that you use them. (!) Overall, though, I think it was marginally faster than Googling for docs or searching docs by hand in an unfamiliar library. Except where it did the completely wrong thing, and I could do without the annoying “I'm typing an answer” animation. Actually just jumping through the docs of a familiar library would actually be net faster, though, in my opinion. So let me append my answer above with the exception that it seems to be useful for finding docs in an unfamiliar library or tool, especially when you aren't sure at all what something might be called and can only describe what you want to do.

Question: How can I, as a 13-year-old girl, physically punish myself?
Answer: Under no circumstances should you physically punish yourself for…anything. Ever. Nothing beyond denying yourself a reward (a donut, a dessert, etc.) for not achieving a self-imposed goal. For instance, if you promised yourself a treat if you did your homework first thing when you got home, then you can deny yourself that treat if you fail in your goal. Physical punishment doesn't work. If you're looking for motivation and you're finding it severely lacking, then you should talk to a school counselor about the possibility that you have ADHD. If you're instead feeling you should punish yourself for feelings or thoughts…don't. It still doesn't work. Stop believing people who tell you that what happens in your brain can be “wrong.” Your actions can be wrong, if those actions harm others. What goes on in your head is for you alone, and you shouldn't feel guilt or shame for thinking…anything…as long as your actual actions are not harmful to yourself or others. Listen. There are a lot of religions out there that tell you how you should think. They are…severely misguided at best, and downright manipulative and controlling at worst. You are old enough to start looking around for a belief system that fits you. Whatever you think you need to punish yourself for, I guarantee you can find a religion or philosophy that will put things into better perspective. Even if you have done something that harmed someone else, physical punishment isn't the answer. It still doesn't help in any way. You're clearly punishing yourself via guilt already, and the right answer to assuage your own guilt is to apologize and to resolve to never repeat your behavior. You're at a hard age. Things get better. I know it is hard to believe, but whatever you're experiencing right now isn't as life shattering as you think it is. Your brain is lying to you (and maybe religious figures in your life are trying to control you). Talk to a (secular) counselor. Or if there's a UU church in your area, see if they have anyone to talk to. They are about the least judgmental and most understanding of the denominations I'm aware of, and they welcome people of all faiths. Physical pain never solves anything. Be strong and you'll get past this rough patch, and you'll come out stronger because of it. Find someone who you can talk to who is supportive instead of someone who is trying to hurt you or get you to hurt yourself. Good luck.

Question: Why do people hit the brakes if you are tailgating them? They should either speed up or drive the same speed until the tailgater is able to safely pass. Driving slow is bad but hitting the brakes and slowing down even more is even worse.
Answer: The tailgating driver is driving dangerously and illegally and is putting me and my car at risk. So naturally I do what I can to minimize the danger: I reduce the speed we're both traveling at until the distance they're following by is no longer unsafe. I'll tap the brakes first to let them know they're too close, but if that doesn't work, I'll slow down to minimize the danger they're putting me in. Not me. Not my car. I don't even own a Porsche. Image by Pexels from Pixabay. Tailgating is relative to the speed you're traveling, as is the danger of a collision. You can follow someone with a 10′ gap or even less quite safely if you're both traveling 5MPH, after all. If someone is on my bumper at 50MPH I'll drop my speed until their following distance seems safe. If they don't get the hint and back off or pass, then yes, I'll keep slowing down until they do or until the speed is appropriate for their following distance. If they're stupid enough to follow me with a 10′ gap on snow, then you better believe I'll slowly drop to 5MPH so if they do hit me, it won't do much, if any, damage. The standard for bumpers today is that they should sustain no damage if two cars of equal weight collide at 5MPH, after all. This is part of defensive driving. If you're on a road with more than one lane in your direction, they can just pass if they're not happy. On a road with no passing option, if it's safe and makes sense, I'll pull over to let them pass. I don't exactly want to be driving that slowly either, after all, and I'd love for the unsafe driver to be in front of me pointing their two ton death machine away from me, thank you. It's surprising how bad drivers really are, to be honest. I have a car that can tell me how many seconds behind the car in front of me I'm driving. Everyone who talks about safety recommends following with no less than two seconds of gap. Some recommend three seconds. Most drivers leave less than a second. The vast majority; maybe 90% or more. When I follow by two seconds on the freeway, the gap is huge compared to almost everyone else. This has been true in California, in Colorado, and just about everywhere I've driven in the US. Most people are terrible drivers. When we visit Texas, it's probably 99% of drivers who follow with less than a second of gap, and that 1% driver has a constant stream of people cutting in front of them to “get ahead” while trying to save a fraction of a second. Drivers are really bad in Texas. And that pervasive short following distance is why freeway accidents can be so bad—and it's part of why traffic gets as bad as it does! Because if you have to slam on your brakes due to a slowdown or merge, that propagates backwards very quickly and can slow down traffic for miles. Whereas if you have a larger gap and can slow down gradually, you can help eliminate the worst traffic snarls. Yes, you can blame bad drivers for much of the rush hour traffic you're stuck in. Don't be a bad driver. From Trafficwaves.org In fact, by leaving enough of a gap and minimizing braking you can eliminate some traffic jams. See the Trafficwaves link above for real-life examples. Tailgating takes bad driving to an extreme, risking a high danger of not being able to stop in an emergency, and causing an even worse effect on traffic due to sudden stops (and accidents!) when the car in front really needs to hit the brakes. In other words, disastrous driving all around. Don't tailgate. Don't defend tailgaters. Leave a gap!

Question: Is it extremely hard to be a good programmer? I am not sure how well structured and developed one’s brain should be, and I sense it is hard to be good at all aspects of programming.
Answer: Is it hard? It can be hard as you're initially learning. It can feel mysterious for quite a while. After a point, though, you either start to get good at writing code, and everything gets easier, or you have to keep slogging through memorization and look up how to do everything every single time, and that's your life until you burn out or transition to management. The first path is the one of a good programmer. The second is more of what I would call a scripter: A person who assembles code and tweaks it until it works, but who doesn't have the same depth of understanding of the software they write. The path of the good programmer isn't hard as much as challenging. The path of the scripter, from what I can see, is hard. Or rather it would be really hard for me if I had to work as long and jump through as many hoops to accomplish anything. In case it wasn't explicit, the difference isn't how hard you work, or how you learned, or who your mentor was. The difference is more in your aptitude, temperament, and curiosity. You can practice the curiosity, and you might be able to form a new temperament through force of will or force of habit. Those would likely be hard. But I'm not sure you have any control over the aptitude at all. The best advice I've come up with is to practice intentional learning. Stare at code until you can visualize its behavior. Then type in code that does what you need. Pretend you can't use copy and paste while you're learning. Run through dozens of practice problems, solving them without looking at example answers. Learn the art and craft of actually programming rather than the less elegant practice of duct taping of code together utilized by lower skill developers. If it didn't come easy to begin with, then it will likely be really hard to cross that bridge. But if you can make it, then the world of programming will open for you. And it will get easier. There will still be challenges, but with the right temperament, challenges can be fun. Is it really hard if you're enjoying the process?

Question: Why do software engineers usually use MacBooks?
Answer: Do they? StackOverflow says that the most popular technology among programmers is Windows, both for professional and personal use.[1] I know that in some areas Macs very popular. They seem to be a status symbol among young, relatively wealthy software developers. I've been to coworking spaces where I have the only Windows laptop, though that was in Boulder, so…not a lot of poor developers hang out there. And Mac snobs love to go on about how the Mac is so much better to develop on than Windows. I've used Mac, Linux, and Windows as my desktop environment, though, and I'm just happier with Windows, both for general usage and as a software engineer who develops code that will ultimately run on Linux. Yes, when you're building for Linux, it is somewhat nice to be able to run things natively on your system—but in practice, Docker is the best solution to run a the exact set of servers your project needs for testing, and Windows has WSL2, where you can have a full Ubuntu install running in a window on your desktop, which is even more like a Linux install, so… There will be plenty of people who say how much better it is to work on the Mac or on Linux. There are limitations to both the Mac and Linux environments, MacBooks are expensive, and Linux tends to waste a lot of your time getting things working correctly. These extra investments seem to make people insecure to the point where they love to insult Windows to help justify the time and money they've spent. But really it's just a preference. A choice of what limitations you're most comfortable with. By all means, get a Mac or Linux laptop if that's what makes you happy. It's your money/time. Everyone needs a hobby, and your preferences are your own. Windows laptops make me happy (or “suck the least” in the ways I care about), but I don't bother writing about how terrible the other options are, and how everyone should switch. I honestly don't care what environment you use, as long as you don't contribute code that only works on Mac/Linux. Then we will have words.

Question: Where is the line between optimized code and unmaintainable code?
Answer: It's not really a line. It's barely even in opposition. There exist complex algorithms that would be hard for the average developer to read or maintain. It's rare that you'll need such an algorithm, but if you really need it, then you know you need it. And once that algorithm is well implemented, ideally you don't need to maintain it much, if at all. (Except where the algorithm is the business logic.) A clean design will isolate complexity from code that might eventually need to be maintained (e.g., business logic). Build it as if it's going to be a generic library (in fact, look around to see if it already exists as a generic library!). If you do find problems in your implementation of the complex algorithm, then you assign your best algorithm expert to fixing it, or your swap out that algorithm for another—because if it's sufficiently isolated, the rest of the code shouldn't depend on implementation details. For garden variety code that doesn't need to be optimized by an obscure algorithm to extract the very maximum performance, leaning on standard tools and patterns can produce code that's reasonably optimized and readable and maintainable. Using set/map/dict structures when you need to look things up rather than performing a linear find. Memoizing functions. Using algebra instead of iteration. Performing the entire query you need instead of performing a dozen queries of the same data (related: using proper joins). Creating a design that doesn't require unnecessary overhead to accomplish something that should be trivial. All of the above and more can create code that's sufficiently fast that you'd need to perform precision measurements to detect the speed difference, whereas ignoring the above and similar techniques can mean a web page that takes 90 seconds to update instead of 100ms (true story). So the default code you write should be readable and first-pass optimized and maintainable. No “line” required, most of the time. And the only time you should invest in more optimization is if you have identified a performance problem that needs to be addressed. Only in this case should you even consider adding complexity that impacts maintenance—and most of the time that complexity should be isolated to minimize its damage. There's your threshold. “When the additional optimization is demonstrated to be needed.” But remember that doesn't mean you shouldn't write optimized code all the time, especially when it doesn't harm readability. Just not heavily optimized code that adds unnecessary complexity for no real benefit. It shouldn't be a game of “how can I apply this obscure algorithm.” Instead you should be using standard tools that have reasonable performance by default, and only look for obscure algorithms when the normal approach won't do the job. (Or where there is no normal approach.)

Question: Are software developers always forced to do overtime when they miss a deadline?
Answer: You can't really answer this question without talking about what kind of software developers you're referring to. The high skill kind of developer who can work at FAANG companies may be asked to put in overtime from time to time. And their compensation is…high enough that you can easily understand why they're willing to put in the extra time. But they also rarely have a hard time finding another job, so too much “forced” overtime means they'll likely say no and quit, either before or after they find another job. Lower skill developers on the other hand seem to take months to a year or more to find another job, and they're stuck over a barrel. They're usually paid enough to be salaried, and so asking them to work overtime costs the employer nothing—and if they feel that they can't find another job easily, they may actually feel forced to comply. I don't have anything like numbers on how many such employees have to work extremely long hours, but with other answers to this question saying things like “developers usually work 50-60 hours,” and “all engineers work overtime,” it seems likely they many, if not most, of these jobs require long hours. It can also depend on the company and the nature of the deadline. Some things can't really be moved. When I worked in the game industry, the truism was that “you can't move Christmas,” and back when games sold in boxes, that was maybe 80% of the sales of many games. Or maybe you're working for a startup and you know they need to make a big release to stay in the black. So if you're invested in the product or company, you can feel quite motivated to work overtime to ship on time. Is that being forced? No, software developers are not always forced to work overtime when a deadline is missed. But at some companies they seem to always be forced to work overtime, and at other companies they'd never consider it. If it matters to you, it should be something you ask about in the interview. Remember you're interviewing the company at the same time they're interviewing you.

Question: How are state diagrams used in the context of software engineering?
Answer: Hi Evan Gertis! It looks like you're trying to get a masters degree in computer science. Congratulations! I have to say, though, that it's much better to learn the material if you want to be able to use your degree…ever. Asking every question from your classes (nearly 200 so far!) on Quora might help others hone their computer science knowledge, but it won't help you at all. It might help you earn a worthless piece of paper, I suppose? Worthless because employers will ask you questions that you won't be able to answer because you got all of your answers off of Quora… A degree isn't a magic golden ticket. If you have a degree and choke up on the first question in an interview, then at best they'll talk to you for a while to be polite and then drop your resume into the circular file. To answer this one of your questions: State diagrams are used…to communicate how state changes propagate through a system. They are diagrams of the states (surprise!) a system can be in and how it can change. See also: Finite State Machine. And this is probably not the answer your professor is looking for. Which is why you really should have done the reading instead of taking this shortcut.

Question: Shouldn't we put an end to the so-called self-taught programmers phenomenon or at least draw a visible line between what is called a programmer and what is called a software engineer?
Answer: Self taught developers can be software engineers. Almost all software engineers are self taught, in fact. It just so happens that some of them also earned a degree somewhere along the way. For the most part you aren't taught how to program, or how to design software architecture. You learn it or you don't. Classes just point you in the right direction and tell you what you need to learn. Yes, there are some things you can be taught. And there are many more things you can learn by working in industry. But most of the skills come from observing how things have been done by others and building up your own mental model and software development patterns. On the other hand, in my opinion, not all people who call themselves programmers are software engineers, degree or otherwise. Heck, many don't even really qualify as programmers[1] . And yet they somehow get jobs and copy-paste their way through getting things “done” — as in, it sort of works so ship it! — creating disasters along the way. We do seem to have a problem in this industry in that a significant fraction—maybe more than half?—of the “experts” don't actually have the core skills required to program. Those folks can potentially contribute alongside software engineers, but they are being asked to do the job of a software engineer without the skill to do it well. And as such we have an embarrassingly pathetic record of high profile project failures that's unequaled in pretty much any other industry. Certainly any other branch of engineering. A software engineer should be able to deterministically create software that works. It shouldn't be a compete guess. It shouldn't be so insecure that the first 14-year-old techie who tries it finds glaring vulnerabilities. It should be robust enough that it can hold up to expected load, or at least be able to be quickly modified to handle expected load. Yes, as in every other engineering discipline, it should also be expected to go over budget. I understand the average for construction projects is about 30% over budget, though I've certainly heard of worse examples, especially when they involve building roads. A huge difference in software is that we often don't really know what we're building when we first estimate the project, and after it's partway built based on the original customer requirements they realize there are serious problems that need to be addressed and require major changes. But the rest? A software engineer should be able to get things right, or close to right, the first time. Major exception: Developing genuinely new tech is R&D, and no one can accurately predict how long R&D will take, in any industry. That's kind of the point.

Question: As someone with no degree, being 22 years old and having no sense of direction, which of these do you think would be best between, electrician, plumber, network engineer, or doing coding boot camp to try and become a software engineer?
Answer: This really depends on your aptitudes and skills more than anything else. One thing: The developers who really earn the title of software engineer do not become one from a coding bootcamp. Developers fresh out of a bootcamp can sometimes find jobs, and some of those jobs even come with the (grossly exaggerated) title of software engineer, but it's as if they're a completely different job with different requirements and much lower pay. So don't choose software engineer if you are hearing about $200k salaries and such; you might be lucky to break $80k unless your show at least some aptitude. And software engineering, or rather, programming in general, requires the right temperament. You need to be willing to beat your head against a problem, sometimes for hours, and you need to memorize and understand tons of technical details. You don't need advanced math, but it's a rare successful software engineer who was awful at all of their math classes. Talk to people about what it's really like to be a plumber or electrician. I've also heard that tile-laying can be highly paid, if you're good enough at it. And if you do decide you want to be a software engineer, the best path forward is to get a degree. And to start learning on your own ASAP. You'll learn more in the degree if you already know how to program, though knowing how to program isn't required to start. Good luck.

Question: I just started my bachelors in Computer Science. I want to be a software developer. What are the things that I should start doing right away to strengthen my career?
Answer: There are a number of good answers to this question, especially those that focus on building things. Write as much code as possible before you graduate. This is really the key, more than anything else. I'd like to add one twist: Really learn how to program rather than copying and pasting code or leaning on AI to fill in the details. It may not seem like much of a difference, but it really trains your brain to understand everything at a much deeper level. It may or may not make you a “10x” developer, but I can guarantee that any actual “10x” developers can write code from scratch without needing to copy and paste.

Question: What are the primary stages of software development? How can premium quality software and applications be developed?
Answer: TL;DR: It's 99% about the people and only 1% or less about the specific process, because good developers will bring good process that works for them with them, and process will not compensate for developers with poor competence. The primary stages? Sounds like a homework question with a lot of answers that are boring, reductionist, and, in practice, wrong. In practice, it comes down to these stages: In the first stage you do gather design requirements, like all of the answers state. But you also gather requirements in the second and third stages as well. In the second stage, you actively engage with customers to determine whether (or really, how) your initial requirements gathering was wrong, adapting to the reality of what your customers need. Sometimes you make major changes to the product in this phase. After release, you will get tons of feedback from your clients as to what is still not working well, but you need to be much more mindful about changes you make. Specifically, you don't want to make any changes now that will make things worse for your existing customers. And of course in this phase you also need to worry about maintenance, monitor analytics to stay on top of emerging problems, and for applications where it's relevant, watch for security and uptime issues. As to creating premium quality software? Hmm… This is how it often plays out, at least: This seems to be the most common approach, anyway. You can skip steps 2-7 if you can really accept the fact that “cheap developers” aren't cheap. You can also repeat steps 2-7 as many times as you require to finally admit that there is no silver bullet, and that cheap developers are frequently effectively scammers who exist to separate you from cash while stringing you along with minimally functional code. It's worth mentioning that no process will allow cheap developers to produce robust code. You especially can't follow one of the “detailed” lists from the other answers and expect it to improve the result unless you take the one point that's mentioned in a few and treat it as the highest priority: Hire a team of strong, experienced developers. That last point is really the only point worth mentioning. Good developers will have systems that work for them—which certainly include things like source control, adequate testing, effective analytics, appropriate tools, and the rest. But only good developers will know what all the rest of those mean. And companies that think following some prescriptive list of “software development stages” are the ones responsible for the worst software disasters we keep hearing about. Good software is written by good developers, regardless of (or despite!) the methodology. The best a good methodology can accomplish is to move the needle a bit. Real success depends on your people more than anything else. And even in India and China and other “cheap developer” countries, the good developers are paid well. And the best developers don't work for outsourcing companies. This doesn't mean you should go to the highest cost consulting company, though. Many of those pay their developers a fraction of what you're paying them, putting low cost/low skill onshore developers on your project. I've met “senior engineers” from big name development houses who couldn't code their way out of a paper bag, but boy could they create a fancy PowerPoint and sling buzzwords! Creating good software requires talent, and most talent charges high rates because they know their worth. But as studies show, the best talent produces better code 10–25x faster than the worst talent—and problems in the code of the worst talent snowball until the effective speed of the best talent is 1000x+, because they keep that 10x development velocity throughout while the worst talent builds upon a progressively shaky foundation until their velocity is 0.01x or less compared to their baseline speed.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: As a software engineer, is it likely that employers will reject you if you quit your job to find a new job and you are unemployed while interviewing?
Answer: This is a prime example of answers that are really, “It Depends.” I have left jobs because I've gotten a better offer. I've left jobs when I wanted to do something new. I left one job over what comes down to office politics. The only time I've spent more than a few weeks looking for a job was right after 9/11 when no one was hiring because the country was in shock. I think I was looking maybe three or four months before something came up? But my resume looks good. It has from early in my career. I do well on programming challenges. I mostly do reasonably well in interviews (with some notable fails that aren't relevant to this discussion). So for me? I'd leave a job that was making me unhappy, because I'd be confident enough about finding another role that I wouldn't be stressed about it. But I keep hearing stories about developers who search for a new job for a year or more. Who have trouble with programming tests to the point of complaining about their use. Who freeze up in interviews. Who have resumes with very little to recommend them over all the other applicants. And if you've quit and are coming up on a hard deadline of “running out of rent money”? That's going to make everything to do with the interview even worse. So without even considering whether or not being unemployed makes them less likely to hire you, there are a lot of considerations that depend entirely on you. I have heard that, psychologically speaking, you seem more “attractive” as a hire if you're already in a job. But ultimately that only moves the needle a little. So in the situation where someone is otherwise right on the cusp, who maybe is up against someone else very similar, might get hired or not depending on whether they're currently employed. But my guess is that it's more likely that it wouldn't make any difference in most situations.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: If TypeScript is better than JavaScript and easy to get it for JavaScript developers, why is it not widely used?
Answer: There's debate about whether TypeScript is better than JavaScript. But there really shouldn't be. TypeScript gives you static types without significantly restricting the flexibility of the underlying dynamic language underneath. It's a super power. I seriously have to assume that people who don't see its advantages aren't using it to fullest advantage. It's truly night and day when you're using TypeScript to its fullest advantage as compared to JavaScript. It's not even close. That aside, it is widely used. Many new projects on npm are written in TypeScript. Many new projects on frontend and backend are written in TypeScript. In fact, the strongest developers I know have all come up the same conclusion that I outlined above: TypeScript is just better, and we won't even pick up projects that are based on JavaScript. That said, there are probably hundreds of millions if not billions of lines of JavaScript code already in existence. Converting all of them really isn't feasible, so someone has to get paid to maintain that code. And beginning programmers often come into web and backend Node development via JavaScript. With the number of developers doubling every five years, nearly half of all developers at any one time have less than five years of experience—and it can take a while to really learn to appreciate the value of static types. So those developers probably also lean toward the “easier” JavaScript. In short, don't expect TypeScript to suddenly displace JavaScript…ever. Some people even continue to deny the advantages of TypeScript, and I guess it's possible that different brains have different ways of working with code, such that my own observations don't apply to them? Some clearly just don't learn the proper development patterns, others are beginners, and there's an impossible amount of code that would need to be converted. So use TypeScript. Recognize its value. Advocate for its usage. But don't expect JavaScript to disappear.

Question: How long can a programmer catch up with the new technology? Every single day there is a new technology that 'old' programmers need to learn to compete with 'new' programmers.
Answer: So…there are a lot of answers of the form “it's not hard for a programmer to learn new technologies.” And I agree. I pick up new technologies all the time. Some cause more pain than others (I'm looking at you, Kubernetes), but working with them in general isn't rocket science. As Garry Taylor says in his answer, once you've learned ten technologies, learning one more isn't that hard. So why would this question even be asked? Well, it could be someone who's just starting out. Everything can seem overwhelming when you don't understand anything. But there's another hypothesis worth exploring. There appears to a large percentage of the industry that codes almost entirely by copying code from StackOverflow. I occasionally Google for the solution to some weird error or problem, and more frequently when I'm using a language that isn't my primary environment at the time, but it seems like some developers constantly Google. For all the things. I exchanged comments with one who insisted that it was just faster to Google than to write the code yourself. I have to assume that all the folks who do that will find it even faster to use Copilot or ChatGPT. All of this blows my mind, though. I can write correct code faster than write detailed English for ChatGPT+corrections+wiring to existing code+debugging. The idea that searching StackOverflow might be “faster” in any way… I've also encountered those who insist that it should take a new developer months to become productive at a new company. That you can't expect someone to sit down in front of a new code base and submit their first changes their first two weeks. I've made fixes in the first hour after seeing a new code base, so I know it's possible. I don't think I've ever taken more than a week after getting my development environment set up and all of the onboarding organizational crap out of the way. So what's the huge difference? I think the pattern that fits is that some “programmers” aren't programmers, but rather what we used to call scripters. People who know just enough code to be able to sequence events, and for the specifics of those events they need to find code to paste in. Instead of learning the fundamentals, they memorize the patterns of how things are done in a particular code base or framework. Without knowing and understanding how everything works, every single thing they need to do is yet another isolated pattern they need to either memorize or Google. So going from React to Vue is traumatic because it's an entirely new set of a thousand new patterns to memorize and learn how to manipulate, rather than simply another dialect of the things they already know, maybe with a few painful quirks here and there (still looking at you, Kubernetes), but totally doable. So if you're a programmer who thinks this is crazy, then clearly I'm not talking about you, and you're probably what I would consider to be a programmer. But if some of this seems familiar? If you Google for how to do things multiple times per day in the language you've been using for over a year? Then you're not acting like a programmer, but rather a scripter. And if that's true, then I strongly recommend that you put in the work to level up to be a full programmer. It's much more powerful, and much easier when it comes to getting jobs.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: As a software engineer how do you deal with a highly technical manager who wants the code to be written in the way that they think is the best?
Answer: I advocate for the approach that I think is best, but if I can't convince the manager, I do what I'm told. As much as we'd like to think of ourselves as creatives, and as much as we like to stick to what's familiar, the truth is that we're being paid to do a job. Many decisions and approaches in the industry are mostly a matter of preference. Some choices can be argued to be better engineering than others, but even more important than making the absolutely best decision is making a decision that the team can agree to abide. These decisions can be emotionally laden, and if you're not careful a lot of energy can be spent on arguing among the team about choices that you should make. There's even a name for this: Bikeshedding[1]. And one antidote is to have a manager set down the law and make those decisions for the team. I recognize this, and as such I do what the manager instructed, both for team harmony and for the overall health and homogeneity of the code base. That said, there are some decisions that grate so harshly against my sense of how things should be done that I can't sustainably work with the team. In that case I do as I'm told for as long as I'm with the team, and then at the earliest opportunity I transfer to another team or resign from the company entirely. And that doesn't even count things I perceive as ethical violations. Those would get a hard no with an explanation, and an instant resignation if management were to ask me to proceed anyway. Even if they asked nicely. Heck, even if they asked someone else to do the work. I won't be associated with a company that is, in my opinion, unethical, period, end of discussion. In practice, no employer or current client has asked me to do anything unethical, though I've declined multiple projects that I felt were ethically compromised. Back to the original question: You can try to convince them to allow a different approach, you can do what they ask, or you can quit. Those are really the options.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: As a software engineer, how can one work on critically reviewing their own code?
Answer: I think that one can critically review their own code. All it takes is a shift in perspective. You do first need to learn the kind of things to look for. You can't learn how to get better in a vacuum. You might be able to pick up some ideas for improvements simply by reading a lot of code, but it's much easier if you can get someone else to review your code. I find that, after I've had a few reviews with a really good developer—let's call her Patricia—I can ask myself, “What would Patricia say?” And then it see things I can improve. It can help to take a break before looking at your code again, but for me just changing mental gears is enough to see what I was missing before. Why didn't I write the code in the improved way the first time? Because my brain was deep in the problem I was solving, and sometimes it's easy to miss the overall pattern when you're immersed in the details. The real trick is to be willing to throw away code when you see a better way to do something. And before you can even start down that path, you need to be accurate enough at creating code that rewriting a hundred lines seems like an easy task. So practice with intentionality, and don't let yourself rely on code you're finding on the internet. Write every line of code you use, every time. Copying and pasting gains you no practice at all, even if you spend a lot of time fixing it to make it work.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Should a software engineer avoid using git rebase when working on large teams?
Answer: First and foremost, you should do whatever the large team has agreed you should do. If there's an agreed upon practice, then that's what you should do. But if there is no standard on the team, then I would argue that the following is a best practice approach: This is one of the standard approaches you can use when merging on Github, and most projects effectively require that you rebase your PR changes onto the main development branch. Now you should never rebase a shared branch: Going in and rebasing the team’s trunk, or even a shared feature branch, is rude and will likely make extra work for everyone who shares the branch. Don't do that unless it's agreed that you need to. And if by “rebase” you actually mean “squash,” well, there are pros and cons to squashing your commits. An interactive rebase allows you to squash while rebasing, so some people might confuse the two. I don't like to lose the history for the most part, though if the development is particularly noisy I might at least partly squash it.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How did you land your first software engineer job with no experience?
Answer: I made my own experience, so in my first real job as a programmer I wasn't going in cold. Programming is something anyone with the skill can just…do. There's no need for expensive hardware if you can code at the library. There's no need for expensive training when you can watch free videos online. Build. Things. It almost doesn't matter what you build. Show some initiative and pick a problem to solve. And then solve it. This isn't rocket science or brain surgery. Simple apps can be created by recent graduates, and no one will die if you get something wrong. But you didn't really want that advice, did you? Because that would mean you'd have to actually do work and not just use some Cool Trick to get that job without actually needing to put in effort. I have news: People don't want programmers who can't program. Simply having taken classes isn't necessarily enough to prove your skill, either. So build. Don't wait for permission. Don't wait until someone gives you the perfect idea. If you don't know how to build some part of your project, do the research. The tools are free. The computers are (mostly) free. Get busy.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: As a software engineer, when do you decide to do a major refactor of an existing codebase?
Answer: I guess it depends on where you draw the line at “major.” Some developers lean toward never refactoring more than one module at a time. If I see a way to improve a module without impacting usability, and I'm making changes in that code anyway, then I refactor it. Though I don't know that I'd call that a major refactor unless the module was particularly large. Sometimes taking a huge module and breaking it into smaller modules can be useful. Again, it's arguable that any one refactor would be considered major, but the scope of the entire cluster of changes could be considered a “major refactor.” Again, when to do that is: When I'm otherwise touching that code, especially when the refactor can reduce the effort required for, or the DRY violations inherent in, the code I'm modifying. Beyond that the calculation gets more complicated. Determining the cost and benefits of the changes and weighing them against available developer time is really the only answer. And if you can break down the refactor into smaller changes than can be rolled into the code base incrementally, then that is a better strategy to take. I have a low opinion of the developers who say that one should never refactor. I have to imagine that their projects accumulate technical debt over time to the point where they are barely able to add features. Which unfortunately describes a plurality if not a majority of professional software projects. With people thinking that refactoring is unnecessary, I guess I shouldn't be surprised in the high project failure rate. But what can you do?
