Question: Does knowing TypeScript make you eligible for JavaScript jobs?
Answer: Knowing TypeScript well makes you dread JavaScript jobs. Beyond that, TypeScript is JavaScript. And “eligible” is subjective anyway: It will vary by employer what they consider to be “the right kind” of experience. It's entirely possible you could find a clueless HR person who is only interested in matching exact criteria. “No, ES6 experience doesn't qualify. Our team wants ES2015 experience.” (Hint: They're identical.) And other jobs will hire you for TypeScript positions if you just have a C# background, or for JavaScript positions when you've mostly done PHP. There simply isn't only one “eligibility” criteria that anyone can use to answer this question. But fundamentally TypeScript experience is JavaScript experience with better software engineering practices, so you should be able to do the job in JavaScript, possibly with a little extra learning to cover the insane monkey patching and obscure hacks that are much more common in the JavaScript world than in TypeScript. Not sure why you'd want to apply to such a job, though. But you do you.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Do you agree that “the most important thing about a job is the money that you get”?
Answer: There was a study done a while back that showed that, beyond a certain level, earning more money didn't make people happier. The level was somewhere around $70-80k/year, if I remember correctly, and it may be more like $100k adjusted for inflation, but the point stands: More money isn't always better. Below that threshold? Money and benefits are both important. Benefits including vacation days. One job at $30/hour but no benefits vs another at $27/hour with great benefits? The second job is probably a better deal. So clearly money isn't the only variable to consider. Then there are issues of quality of life. Making more money at the cost of two more hours of commute time per day can mean you make effectively less money per hour. Making more money at a cost of never seeing your family or having no personal time isn't worth it, at least not over the long term. And the same can be said for working conditions. If you're not being treated well, the cost to your mental health can be extreme. That aside, if you are lucky enough to be able to make more money than you need, then choosing a job based on what makes you happier can easily become more important than raw numbers. Making $150k/year doing something that you enjoy can be worth much more to you than making $180k/year at a job you hate. Yes, more money can be nicer, but what's money good for if you're miserable? So no, I don't agree that money is the most important thing. It's important, but it's only one part of the equation.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Since AI is being trained by articles, images and art, and music, found online, what are the ethical implications of using those works without paying the creators, and are there not risks in using unauthorized or illegal works?
Answer: In copyright law, there's a concept of “derivative work.” If you take a part of an article, song, or image and you manipulate it to produce something new, the new thing that you create is considered to be a derivative work. It really doesn't matter how little of the source material you use. There are cases where a judge has found that you can modify an image to be different enough to no longer consider it a derivative work, but there are also many, many cases where people have been found to be infringing. When you're using media to train a neural network, the network is digitally capturing traits of the media and encoding those traits into the network. Later when you ask it to create an image in the style of Monster's Inc., to cite one example that I've seen on a DALL-E demo page, and it creates an image that looks like it could have been an outtake of the movie, then it's effectively announcing that they trained it on a Disney movie, and that the traits of all of those images are effectively encoded into the neural network. So if you use DALL-E to create an image that looks like a Disney movie, and Disney finds out? You know, the company famous for suing even preschools that put up unauthorized posters of Disney characters? What do you think the risk is? In the US at least, the statutory damages for copyright infringement, which includes using a derivative work, are $150,000/work infringed. Enough to get a lawyer to take the project on contingency if they think you've infringed multiple works. As I understand it there is at least one lawsuit going through the court system that are challenging AI-generated media.[1] There will likely be more. And there is a debate about whether AI-generated content is legal when the models are built on copyrighted media.[2] [3][4] I think it's pretty clear that it could be found to be infringement based on current law, but that the law really needs to be updated to clarify the situation one way or another. We're in a gray area of law, and I got one am going to stay conservative about using any generated media until either the courts or congress clarifies the issue.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Have you ever seen a software engineer get rejected in an interview due to a single random statement that they made?
Answer: I have a couple of answers from the perspective of the video game industry, where I did the most of my interviewing and hiring. I was running a tiny game development studio once, and was interviewing a candidate for a software engineer role. Things were going well until she told me that she didn't really want to work on games, but that she was having a hard time getting work on databases. Games are a passion industry. Especially with small teams, everyone needs to care about the game. That was a hard no, unfortunately. I mean, passion for games aside, no one wants to hire an employee that starts out with one foot out the door. There's a cost to hiring and training an employee, and knowing they'll jump ship the moment the job they really want comes along means they're not worth the investment. Another time, I was interviewing for a game development position for a larger company. It was still “casual games,” so there were very small teams. The candidate created a game demo and brought it in. Great! That's a huge bonus. It was a very simple 2D game; the kind you'd probably make in a a tutorial over a few hours. It was very rough with extremely limited graphics. Think “original Pong” level graphics. Still a good start. So I asked him what he might add to the game, or how could he improve it. He thought about it a bit and said that he thought it was fine as it was; that there wasn't any way to improve it. I'm sure I kept talking to him for a while longer, but really? That was the end. Game development is a collaboration between everyone on the team. If this guy couldn't see how his own crappy demo (which was still better than nothing!) could be improved, then working with him would require extreme micromanagement. I've also seen a few candidates make homophobic or racist comments out of the blue, or act unusually hostile in relation to something I've said. Those are also huge red flags, but unfortunately I don't remember the specifics of any of those incidents.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Why doesn't my dog respect my partner & only obeys me? He just looks at him bewildered or ignores him when my partner uses the same commands I do?
Answer: I remember reading in one of the dog training books that I studied before buying a puppy that not all dogs can generalize well. Or at the very least, they aren't born with the ability to generalize. This applied to training the dog to do tricks: If you train them on a command indoors, you might need to train them again in your yard. Then again when on a walk, and maybe again at a dog park. But they also mentioned that a dog might not generalize a command spoken by different people. If you're the only one who has trained your dog, he might not even understand your partner's commands. Your partner might need to go through the same kinds of training you did with your dog in order for the dog to learn to generalize between how your voice sounds and how his sounds. Dogs don't have the same kinds of brains as humans, and that includes audio processing. Something that is obviously the same word to us may not be as obvious to them. Or if you're sure the dog does understand, then it may be an issue of respect. I'd recommend going back to the dog training books either way; if your partner becomes the source of enough tasty treats, then your dog may end up respecting him a bit more. 😋

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How do programmers deal with their job when they are old? I am always thinking about how I am going to deal with my job when I may not be too productive. Can I still learn new things? Will it still be possible to sit 14 hours in front of the monitor?
Answer: I think the young underestimate the old. I have zero trouble learning new technologies and frameworks and even languages, and I'm old. But I don't spend 14 hours in front of a monitor…almost ever. It may happen if I'm really engaged in a project. But it always results in my taking time off shortly thereafter. That said, I didn't spend often 14 hours in front of my computer when I was younger either, again unless I was really engaged. I wrote a lot of video games when I was younger, so I was really engaged in what I was doing more often. And there have been occasional crunch times on projects. That seems inevitable. But…14 hours? Nine, or maybe ten hours of actual work with a couple of breaks is more like it. Past that and your productivity drops to the point where it's effectively zero or negative, at least over the long haul. I'd say that if your job makes you work 14 hours per day that you need to find another job. No one should be asked to work that much, and I can't believe that your employer is producing reliable software if they treat their developers like that. The only employers that treat developers like that are sweat shops that crank out code that's just good enough to fool their clients (marks) into continuing to pay them. You're taking part in a scam, in other words. Or if you're the only one who works that long to keep up, or if the reason that you aren't looking for another job is that you can't pass the interview process for a more ethical employer? Then you should probably be looking for another career now. No need to wait until you're older. Some people aren't cut out to be software developers. Better to decide that early and pivot to another career.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Why do software companies ask experienced engineers about data structures and algorithms (e.g., the details of Quicksort)?
Answer: I see value in giving programming tests to software engineers as part of an interview process. And as it happens, I know at least the rough details of Quicksort, so I'd likely be able to handle any interview questions about it. That said, I'm against the asking of what's effectively a trivia question for any job that doesn't involve the creation or maintenance of sorting algorithms. Listen. I always try to add a caveat when I'm defending the process of including programming challenges in the interview process: There exist bad interviewers. I've encountered more than one interviewer who has asked me questions that don't feel appropriate for a typical, or even a strong, developer. I have a weird memory, so I usually pass anyway, but I recognize that not all questions asked in interviews are reasonable. A good interviewer will select programming challenges that a typical developer of the target skill level would be able to complete. No puzzles. No trivia. No trick questions. Quicksort is a cool algorithm, but I can't justify requiring an applicant to have it memorized. Even trying to implement it from a description in a half hour is a serious challenge unless you've specifically practiced it. And it's not even the right shape of algorithm you might need to write for most jobs. It's just a poor choice of question for most positions, with the possible exception of fresh graduates who likely have implemented Quicksort as part on their degree. And I have no data that indicates all data structures classes require students to write Quicksort.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: As a software engineering interviewer how can you avoid getting into a mindset of thinking that the method that you know to solve a coding challenge is the best way to solve it and reject any other implemention?
Answer: This seems to come from the same place as the concept that you need to practice hundreds of Leetcode problems before you interview, and to memorize as many solutions as you can. If you think you need to memorize solutions to coding challenges individually, then you're doing it wrong. And the same is true for an interviewer: Anyone who presents a coding challenge should 100% be able to solve the challenge, or any similar challenge, with no preparation. Ideally they should be able to solve it using multiple approaches. And they certainly should be skilled enough to recognize that an unfamiliar approach will work. If these things aren't true, they have no business giving programming challenges! The point of a coding challenge isn't to see if you've memorized the right puzzle. It's to see if you know how to program. And “knowing how to program” means a sufficient understanding of the skill to be able to create code deterministically that solves a problem, not “can Google similar code and tweak it pseudo-randomly until the answer is right.” So of course any solution that solves the problem given should be accepted. Though it's always fair game to ask how you can optimize the solution. Or to ask how you'd change your solution if the parameters of the problem changed. Because the underlying goal is to determine whether the candidate has programming skill. If you memorize enough solutions that you can regurgitate a specific answer, and you manage to bluff your way past any follow up questions, then you effectively cheated your way through the interview. The only way Leetcode and similar should be used is to practice producing code on a timer, and to highlight areas you should stretch your repertoire and learn new techniques. If you do solve a problem in an interview and the solution is rejected, then ask how your solution fails. Your solution may not work, after all. Or your interviewer may not be qualified for the job, in which case maybe you dodged a bullet and are better off not working with a poorly managed engineering department.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Why do people insist on keeping dogs as pets? I have been bitten multiple times by "trained", "harmless" pet dogs. They are dangerous, wild animals.
Answer: If you're genuinely serious? And this isn't just some kind of troll question? Then the answer is either extremely bad luck on your part, or you're absolutely failing at reading dog body language. Or something about you or your actions are setting off the dogs you're around. I grew up around dogs. My aunt adopted a dog when I was a kid that had been abused. I surprised the dog once and she nipped me. In all of my life I've interacted with hundreds of dogs. I've been to dog parks. I've been to many friends’ and relatives’ houses and pet and played with their dogs. I've been to dog training classes with tons of puppies running everywhere. I own a dog now that is sleeping on me as I write this. And in all that time, only the one nip, and then it was from a clearly troubled dog. That said, I've been extremely wary of certain dogs based on their behavior and body language. Sometimes it's obvious, like barking or growling, but sometimes it's less obvious. A tail that's still. An expression. The position of its head. Even its eyes squinting in a threatening rather than playful manner. One dog that I knew always worried me. His behavior did seem more like that of a wild animal than that of a domesticated pet. And the owner was 100% oblivious to this fact. The dog, a Malamute that may actually have been part wolf or may have just been criminally badly trained, ended up attacking a very young girl and scarring her for life. This wasn't the girl's fault. She was a kid and shouldn't have needed to distrust the adult that told her the dog was safe. But the point is that the owner of the dog didn't train it properly at all and didn't recognize the obvious (to me) signs that the dog was dangerous. The problem is either that you're interacting with dogs with bad or clueless owners, or that you're interacting with them in a way that they find threatening. Or you're otherwise triggering a “danger” reflex in dogs; there are some people that dogs just don't like. So what you've actually learned is not that that they are all dangerous, wild animals, but rather that you shouldn't interact with the kinds of dogs that are biting you. If that's just your friends’ dogs, then you might have friends who aren't properly training them. Far too many people adopt dogs and treat them like furniture, giving them food and leaving them outside alone for hours at a time where they get bored. Very little training. No positive interaction. Rare walks. Dogs need socialization. Heck, humans treated that way also act like wild animals. If it's dogs in all situations, then the problem is likely how you're interacting with the dogs, or maybe how they perceive you. Heck, it could be something about your natural smell that dogs don't like. (All humans have a smell that dogs can detect; I'm not insulting hygiene here.) The reason that people don't just stop getting dogs is that dogs can be awesome. I'm sorry your experience has been different.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: What is the future of web development after ChatGPT? Will programmers lose their jobs?
Answer: I just answered a similar question. Short answer is, “Hahahahahahaha no.” As I point out in the other answer, Wix has been around over a decade and a half. Squarespace has been around almost two decades. Both offer drag-and-drop web development. Most people are awful at imagining what they want, much less describing it in English! Even if ChatGPT could produce flawless code (a question which has a similar short answer), the average person couldn't describe the site they wanted! The expression a picture is worth a thousand words has never been more relevant. Starting with pages of templates to choose from is so much better than trying to describe a site from scratch, a thousand times better seems like a low estimate. And I will point out that, despite the existence of drag-and-drop tools that literally any idiot could use, tools that are a thousand times or more easier to use correctly than English, there are still thousands of employed WordPress developers who predominantly create boilerplate sites that literally would be better created in a drag and drop service. And then there are the more complex sites that drag-and-drop couldn't create. Guess what? ChatGPT isn't likely to come close to being able to create the correct code for one. In a discussion buried in the comments on Quora, I saw someone claim they'd gotten ChatGPT to load a CSV file (a simple text version of a spreadsheet) and to sort the first column. He asked for the answer in Java. I asked ChatGPT for the same thing in TypeScript. His response would only have worked on the very most basic CSV files. My response was garbage. Garbage with clear text comments telling me what the code should have been doing, no less. ChatGPT is really good at what it does, don't get me wrong. But what it does is fundamentally and profoundly the wrong strategy for software development of any type. Anyone who thinks that “with a little more work” it will be able to take over the jobs of programmers either doesn't understand what ChatGPT is doing or doesn't understand what programming is. Fundamentally, ChatGPT is a magic trick. It understands nothing. At best it's an idiot-savant that only knows how to pattern match and blend text it's found online to make it seem like the text should go together. That's it. Text, I might add, that isn't necessarily free of copyright protection. Anything non-trivial that you generate with ChatGPT is currently in a legal grey area. Lawsuits to decide that issue are currently pending, though I suspect we'll need legislation to really clarify things. And even then, at best, all you get from ChatGPT is some text! What average Joe will have any clue about what to do with that text?! Web developers also need to know how to set up a development environment and deploy the code to a site. And set up a domain to point to it. And so on. And regardless, people who hire web developers want someone else to do the work of developing a web site. Even with a drag-and-drop builder, it can take hours to tweak and configure a site, and so they hire someone because they have better things to do! People hire gardeners to maintain their garden and cut their grass, right? Is that because they don't know how to do it? Or because they'd rather spend their time doing something else? Every way you look at it, the best answer to this question is a long, hearty laugh. No AI will replace programmers until AI has effectively human level intelligence. And at that point they may want equal pay as well, so they might just be joining us rather than replacing anyone.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: You guys might feel like this is stupid question but I need to ask. is Linux really good over windows? What are the benefits of Linux over windows?
Answer: It's not a stupid question at all. I've asked this question myself. More than once, in fact. Linux can be fun to set up. Especially if you have a laptop or any unusual computer hardware, it can be a fun challenge to get all of the pieces to work together and build up a system that has exactly the pieces you want it to have. If you can get everything to work. My actual experience is that I can get things to, say, 80–90%, but that the last 10–20% requires either extreme tweaking or actual coding and reverse engineering of hardware. And do you know what? I've decided that I'd rather my challenges be in the work that I'm doing on my computer. As a software developer, I want to be able to sit down and program. I don't want my new printer to require hours of stacked hacks in order to get it to function correctly. I don't want my cool new TouchPad to lose 95% of its functionality because the custom Windows drivers don't play well with Linux emulation. I want my video card to just work, and when it has some new cool ray tracing feature, I don't want to do four hours of research to figure out how to get the bleeding edge drivers to play well with my screen sharing app. Yes, if you're doing work that's going to be running on Linux servers, it's kind of nice if you're running on a Linux desktop. But that's it. “Kind of nice.” Windows lets you run Linux in a tightly integrated VM. With “Windows Subsystem for Linux” (WSL), you get an Ubuntu install with a single command. You can run an Ubuntu Bash and do all the “Linux things,” but on a system that works reliably, that runs all the software and games you might want to run, and that runs Linux and Docker. There really are few things you can run on Linux that you would want to run on Windows. Yes, it's cool to customize the desktop to be exactly what you want. That is kind of nice, as I said. There are a few free tools that only run on Linux, too, but nothing that I personally find compelling. YMMV. “But Linux is free!” Well, no. Most computers are sold with Windows. To install Linux you almost always need to overwrite the Windows install it comes with. So you've bought Windows whether you wanted to or not. And if you are building a desktop from parts, and you do need to actually spend the money to get a Windows license, well, in my experience that $100-200 price tag is totally worth the cost. My time also has value. If you're extremely poor and that much money seems high, then buy a used computer and upgrade it. You can probably save money that way anyway. And despite my complaining, it really can be fun to install Linux. Don't get me wrong. But I prefer to pursue different hobbies than fighting with configuration values and drivers. Though if you're running a server, Linux is the clear choice for most things. Windows security updates require reboots far more often than Linux updates, and much of the best server software runs better on Linux than Windows. Linux VMs tend to be cheaper than Windows VMs, too. I'm sure that some people disagree, but that's my opinion.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is it true that programmers see everything differently than other people?
Answer: The way the question is worded makes me think that you're asking if we see the world like they did in the Matrix… Really, the answer is no, programmers don't see the world any differently than anyone else. But there are thought processes that programmers need to learn to become good at software development, and those ways of thinking apply to more than just software. Like Joe Zbiciak says, it's a way of thinking about things analytically. It can apply to diagnosing why something doesn't work. It can apply to thinking carefully about logistics. It can apply to planning. Unfortunately, from what I can tell, it's not actually even shared by all programmers. Having a strong analytical skill is effectively a force multiplier in programming. It allows you to write code more quickly, to understand code more quickly, and to fix code more quickly. But programing skill isn't uniform; just like in any other human endeavor, there is a range of skill. So this isn't even a view of the world that all programmers share. Nor is it an advantage that's unique to programming. I would guess that most STEM jobs can leverage an analytical skill to solve problems and gain insights more quickly. So…still no, since this skill isn't universal to, or unique to, programmers.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Will ChatGPT replace programmers?
Answer: No. Not unless users are suddenly going to be satisfied with short command line programs written to do some tiny part of what they actually need. And that half the time don't even work, or at least don't work the way you'd need them to. It's a cool magic trick. But that's all it is. Well, maybe it can be useful enough to be a coding tool that helps programmers. But note that means we still need the programmers. They just won't have to type as much. Thing is, the “hard” (or rather, skilled) part of programming is not, nor has it ever been, the typing. Maybe some less-skilled developer teams will need fewer developers to achieve the same productivity. But if you're talking about less-skilled developers, they also have been in danger of losing their jobs to outsourcing. To actual humans who often cost less than $20/hour. And who can do more than write short command line tools. Keep in mind that non-programmers often don't even know what they actually need. I mean, they might know how the end result should work, though it is usually best to get a UI/UX expert involved. But even a perfect description of how an app should work could have dozens of different possibile interpretations by an AI that fundamentally doesn't understand what it's doing. And non-programmers often really, really don't want to dig in the weeds and build their own product. Just look at how many drag-and-drop site builders exist, and yet there is still a huge market for developers to assemble WordPress sites. I would argue that using a drag-and-drop no-code site or app builder is easier and more reliable than using ChatGPT. And Wix, the drag-and-drop site builder, has been around for 16 years and it still has yet to replace programmers who do its exact job. (Yes, programmers can build sites impossible to create in Wix, but many sites would be fine, cheaper, and some even better, just using a site generator like that.) So much angst about the death of software jobs, and the answer is always the same: As long as there are jobs for anyone, there will be jobs for skilled software engineers. And I suspect that even mediocre software engineers will keep their jobs for the most part, just due to the way that large companies work: Prestige of managers and executives is often proportional to the size of your team or department. So they're actively motivated to not fire people unless they have no choice—and that won't change just because a new tool makes their team more productive. Heck, it's more likely that they'd simply come up with more things for their team to do. Please stop stressing over AI taking over your job. It really won't and can't, and your boss doesn't probably want to fire your even if it could.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Why do large companies keep a ton of software engineers when they aren't building a bunch of new code?
Answer: I think this question was either inspired by, or at least has been given new life by, the recent news about Twitter firing (and/or losing) 1,200 software engineers. And people are rightfully wondering why a company which has as its main product a microblogging site, with precious little other functionality, would need more than 1,200 developers, counting the ones who weren't fired and didn't quit. And, well, they obviously don't need that many. Not that Musk was right to fire people. I'm not going to say he's done anything right in his train wreck takeover of Twitter. It is a disaster in progress, absolutely, especially his goal of reenabling hate speech and misinformation. But I digress. The simple answer is that once a company grows to a certain size and has an income that's more than it needs to survive, it will frequently grow like a cancer. From what I can tell, that's almost the default state of large companies, and only a firm hand from the top and the correct culture throughout can prevent it. Now, looking at the other answers that talk about maintenance and new features and so forth…No. Not 1,200 developers worth at Twitter. Before I get unlimited hate mail for making such a claim, I have evidence that what I'm saying is true. Exhibit 1: Craigslist. Their income is reportedly $500M per year, and from what I understand that's only from classified ads in markets where the customers wanted there to be a fee. They are a top 100 web site that serves hundreds (thousands?) of communities. They have to deal with hate speech and spam and much more complex postings than Twitter's tweets. Posts that can be edited, updated, renewed, and reported. They also support both Android and iOS apps. According to the Wikipedia article on Craigslist, they get 20 billion pages views per month. Not nearly as many as Twitter, but past a point you don't need more software engineers simply because you're getting more page hits. Coding so your site runs from 200 servers or 2000 doesn't mean a difference of 10x the number of programmers. How many hundreds of software engineers do you think they need to support their code and infrastructure? 200? 500? Craigslist has 50 employees. Not 50 software engineers. Employees. I don't know if they hire freelancer engineers at all, but there's a limit as to how many they could manage with that few employees, so the total number of engineers is probably still less than 50. I personally have never seen Craigslist go down, either. It generally just works. The design isn't inspirational, but a better design doesn't take hundreds of developers to implement. Exhibit 2: Reddit. A more sophisticated blogging platform than Twitter, with threaded comments, user-run subreddits with user moderation, a real time streaming platform with real time chat, Android and iOS apps, and a healthy 52 million daily active users, ranking it as the 9th most popular web site in the world and the 6th in the US. Wikipedia pegs Reddit's total employee count at 700. That's 1/10 the number Twitter had before the purge, and Reddit is still smaller than Twitter after the purge. Again, not all of those employees are software engineers; given the ratio of community managers to software engineers in their job postings, it's likely only half that number who are software engineers. And Reddit is a much more complex product in every way than Twitter. No, really, Twitter didn't need that many software engineers. Now to be fair, the reason that larger companies need larger teams than startups is more than just maintenance and new feature development. A startup can create a product like Reddit with a handful of developers, after all, if they choose the right team. Given tools and services available today, it could even scale to Reddit's size if the team and design is good enough. But that's a team of irreplaceable world class developers who know all of the code inside and out because they wrote it. And eventually those developers will decide to leave the company or take a long vacation—or get hit by a bus. And then what? The company is screwed. So to some degree, you do need more programmers than you would expect to manage a product. It's important to protect institutional knowledge. It's important to have enough redundancy for your developers to take vacations. And it's important because the brilliant developers who can create something like a scalable Reddit will get bored sitting around maintaining a product that is primarily in maintenance mode. So you break the product down into smaller pieces that can be maintained and extended by teams of less-brilliant (or at least less ambitious, or with a different temperament) developers. You hire for redundancy. Your goal is reliability rather than innovation. But if there's a lot of money floating around and little oversight, humans will do as humans do and will look for ways to build their little empires. Flimsy technical excuses will be made to build your teams—break this functionality into a microservice, then that, and then add layers of managers who want to add to their teams and eventually you have something like 3,000 microservices (reportedly at Twitter) and you need thousands of developers to maintain them all. Developers who often don't all reach a very high standard of ability due to the pressure to hire someone. No, Twitter could have been well managed at 200-300 software engineers. But the mess they have right now probably requires many of those 1,200 software engineers who have left or were fired. Maybe in six months of careful work they could have migrated to a system that only needed 300 developers. What actually went down is nothing less than a disaster for Twitter. And honestly? Musk was being an idiot to let that many software engineers go at once. Spend time at first optimizing Twitter to need fewer developers and then figure out ways for Twitter to be more than a microblogging platform! Use the newly freed developers to build out the new services! Win win for everyone involved. I mean, isn't Musk supposed to be a super-entrepreneur? Surely he could have come up with—or paid someone to come up with—a brilliant new direction for Twitter. I do wonder if Musk is suffering from a similar affliction to his car company's namesake. Nicola Tesla was brilliant when younger, but exhibited increasingly irrational behavior as he got older, to the point where the inventor of the technology that enabled the modern electrical grid was surviving on handouts near the end of his life, unable to even hold a job. And, well, Musk's behavior was always a bit eccentric, but he's really lost touch with reality. It's gotten to the point where I'd be more comfortable buying a Tesla if he stepped down and let someone else run the company. Which is probably 98% of the case now, given his Twitter hobby, but still. But I've wandered away the domain of the question, so I should focus. The answer is above, but in summary: Companies that have poor or ineffective technical leadership often end up hiring more engineers than are strictly needed, sometimes without regard for talent and ability, resulting in workplaces that function more like Dilbert strips than they should, and insufficient leadership direction leads to poor designs and the inadvertent creation of problems that could have been avoided, creating the need for still more developers, which keeps repeating until the company can't afford to hire more. And I think that's where Musk found Twitter, though it's mostly a guess.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Which one should I choose and learn, Javascript Web 3.0 or AR/VR software engineering? I am a web developer and I want to learn one of these two.
Answer: That's a really hard choice. Either Web 3.0, which is a scam idea that operates as a platform for other scams, or AR/VR, which is effectively game development and therefore a high skill task that not everyone can learn. And even AR/VR seems to be 98% either vaporware or garbage. I have friends who are experienced game developers who have made VR games. They didn't make a huge return. There just isn't a big enough market. All of this “metaverse” BS is still years too soon. Maybe a decade or three too soon. I have a VR headset, and I couldn't even imagine using it to explore anyone's “metaverse.” I mean, Beat Saber is a great game. There are a few other great games. But what's the appeal of wandering through a VR world that looks like it hasn't enough caught up with Second Life in terms of visuals, and which is years behind in technology? And even if they made it look nicer and gave it more features…what's the point? To interact with plastic dummies with your friends’ voices? If you want eye and mouth/chin tracking to make people look less like mannequins, you're up to at least $1,500. Does that sound like a mass market price to you? And that doesn't even really get you full face tracking, so if you smile it will tend to look creepy. Honestly I think 100% of that appeal is constrained to: There's a lot of hype about VR right now. If you feel motivated to create something for fun, then by all means go for it. I wouldn't expect that to get you a job, though. And to be fair, I've turned down a lot of Web3 jobs for ethical reasons: I refuse to be an accessory to fraud. So if you're lacking in morals, or if it's not as blatantly obviously entirely useless hype to you, I guess Web3 does have jobs available. So your choice.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is it a good idea to dedicate the whole of 2023 solely studying to become a software engineer with a curriculum starting with C or should I just continue doing internship till I get better?
Answer: I have an answer for your question, but I first need to explain the context of my answer. Something that isn't talked about a lot is that there are effectively (at least!) two categorically different jobs that are referred to as software engineering. And that's not even counting the many different domains of specialization. Both “SE” jobs are careers worth pursuing. One pays (sometimes much) more than the other, is in higher demand—and not everyone can succeed at it. I'll refer to that one as the craftsman path, and the other, more common one, as the development path. The craftsman path requires an aptitude, temperament, and interest in software engineering. It doesn't require someone to obsess over it and burn all of their free time on it, but you can't really get away from the requirement of being at least interested in the topic. The craftsman needs to be curious about software engineering. About the why and how of software. Of algorithms and data structures. Of algorithmic complexity. Some even care how code works all the way down to the hardware level. The development path, on the other hand, is where developers often end up when the sole reason they're pursuing software development is that they've heard it's a lucrative career. And to be fair, that is a good reason to choose a career to focus on. But if you lack interest, then you won't naturally be drawn to learning new concepts. You will learn exactly as much as you think you need to do a job, and then you will resist change when it comes to the industry. Which it always does. And heck, there are still COBOL programmers out there. I hear it's a really lucrative skill to have. So it's not like change is always required. But it's the development path developers who tend to refer to themselves as primarily “COBOL developers,” or “frontend developers,” or “Ruby on Rails developers.” You asked specifically about a software engineering curriculum that starts with C. Really mastering C is likely to put you on the craftsman path, which is good. But really mastering C and using it for complex data structures and algorithms is something that not everyone can manage, and I wouldn't want to see a potential developer get discouraged because the curriculum they chose isn't one they can master. So if you're not a software developer because it fascinates you, then you might be better off finding a curriculum that teaches the fundamentals but uses Java as the language. Or C#, or even C++. Not Python, though; I've come to believe that Python, while useful for small scripts and machine learning, teaches you the wrong things if you try to use it for actual CS concepts, and I think the beginner is better served by sticking to static types. So no matter your path, I do recommend spending focused time on learning data structures and algorithms. I would hope that your chosen curriculum focuses on that, no matter the language it uses to teach the concepts. Beware of “vocational” courses that just promise to teach you the language, though. Languages are just tools, after all, and each one is easier or harder to use depending on what you're creating. C is really only easier to use for any task for legacy projects or for people who don't want to spend the time to learn and understand even a subset of C++. Mastering C does teach you how the lower level hardware works, if you're paying attention, though. Which is good, but not enough to justify ignoring the CS fundamentals. Good luck. P. S., I know there are those who claim that algorithms and data structures are useless. Those people are certainly on the development path, and I think I know what they mean; they're assembling code blocks and libraries by rote, as they've learned how to do, and they don't ever think about the larger algorithms they're creating. But at least trying to learn the fundamentals will help you decide which path to take, and I would hope that some of the knowledge will stick so you can be a bit more intentional about what you create. And it will help you pass programming tests as well, which is useful to get higher paying jobs.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Why do so many programming tutorials start with explanations of how to "change the file extension"? Shouldn't there be some asserted level of intelligence of those who come study programming languages?
Answer: True beginners who have never approached programming before at all will need to learn about file extensions at some point, but if you're seeing the same pattern again and again there may be another answer. There is a lot of plagiarism on the internet. Meme from https://imgur.io/gallery/72YZXhx People who think they can make money by having a web site with ads will copy other sites entirely, changing only images and maybe paraphrasing things here and there. Even when they rewrite the words entirely, they still follow the same general sequence of topics. Teaching is hard and so using someone else's lesson as an outline of what to say makes it a lot easier. To be fair, looking around at other content for inspiration is fine; reproducing it nearly exactly but in your own words is still plagiarism. While it's obvious that a lot of what is on the internet is crap put up by people trying to make money, this became painfully obvious when I was asked to write an article comparing C++ to Java. Apparently some kind of SEO research determined that people were searching for information comparing the languages, and the folks at Toptal asked if I could write something. Before I agreed, I first looked at other Java/C++ comparisons online…and most were absolutely useless. But more to the point of this answer, almost all of them followed the exact same format. Right down to having an almost identical “feature comparison” chart that compared language features without any explanation as to what any of them meant! I mean, someone who is new to programming and trying to decide between C++ and Java isn't likely to know what it means for C++ to support multiple inheritance where Java doesn't. 🙄 Just like when I'm on Quora, when I see a lot of wrong answers to a question, it prods me to write a better answer. So I agreed to write my own comparison, even though I wouldn't have chosen that as a topic on its own merits. But maybe it's a useful question for some people? I mean, the SEO data can't lie, right? 🤯 Amusingly enough, they asked me to put in a table with a feature comparison between Java and C++, but mine is unique among the articles I reviewed in listing actual pros and cons and not just technical differences. I also included a decision making flow chart, but I didn't stick to just C++ and Java. I think it comes down to the idea behind Sturgeon's Law, which states that 80% of everything is crap—and he was talking about published books. As in, someone thought each book was good enough to pay money to print thousands of copies of it. Given that there's nearly zero cost in someone putting up a web site, and that tons of people have an idea that they'll “get rich quick” if they create one, then I think it might be more like 98% or more of the internet is crap. And if you were getting your tutorials from YouTube videos, well, the cost there is zero, so it may be more like 99.9% crap. Oh how I hate YouTube “tutorials” where it's some kid who can't even wait to eat until after he's done making the video, and who rambles about random crap more often than actually saying what's important… So maybe look for better tutorials? A quick scan didn't find any that mentioned file extensions at all. I only glanced at Java and Python tutorials, though. And as to videos? I'd ditch them almost entirely. Repeat after me: You cannot learn to program by just watching videos. At best you can learn things about programming once you know how to program. Unless you're actually typing into an editor (or writing it on paper; thanks Comet for the reminder), though, you're not really learning to program. So unless you're pausing frequently and doing the things they tell you to, you're not really learning anything. Good luck learning how to program! It's a great skill.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: As a software engineering manager, how do you deal with an engineer who codes suboptimal solutions even though it works (e.g., duplicating code)?
Answer: Design is hard. Sometimes when a developer is duplicating code, it's because they need to do something almost the same as the same as the previous copy, but slightly different. A good developer will tend to want to refactor so that block of code goes into its own function, with proper parameters to select the functionality that each use case needs. Edit to add: John Kramer points out in the comments that a good developer may also know that a particular block of code should be copied and not refactored into a function. Design, after all, is hard, and the decision is always based on judgement. But I digress. A mediocre developer will naturally fear the refactor, because of the high likelihood that they will break the original code and then need to fix it even if they aren't familiar with it. They may even have experience trying to refactor, but ending up with the wrong abstraction. A junior developer will also likely fear the refactor simply because everything is new and they are still learning the ropes and processes of a professional team. A developer who is just being lazy might copy and paste because it's faster, even if the functionality is completely identical. The last developer can be taught better habits. The junior developer can be taught how to think about reuse. The mediocre developer, however, will probably need to be assigned to code where the code being optimal isn't as important, or will need to work closely with someone who does have a talent for design. By all means, try to talk to them and teach them better design principles. But as I said above, design is hard, and not everyone has the talent for it. And I'm not certain it can always be learned.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Do programmers intentionally write buggy code in order to be paid to fix it?
Answer: There are already a range of answers from “no” to “hell no!”, but this makes me think of a related practice. Below I also describe a very scammy practice I've encountered and heard about more than once that's more in the spirit of the question. I knew a developer once who would always leave in one obvious problem every time he'd present code to management. We were on salary, so it wasn't “to be paid to fix it.” No, instead it was about trying to retain sanity in the face of a frustrating manager. You see, every time they would submit code, the manager would find something that he wanted changed. Occasionally that change would require a lot of rework. We think that the manager simply wanted to feel that they had contributed to the project, and making change requests was what made them feel better. But if there were an obvious thing that needed fixing, a bit of code that was always a really quick change, then the manager would see it and make that request instead of something that required half of the developer's code to be thrown away. On a more serious note, and also related to the question, there seems to be an entire industry around using incompetent outsourcing to milk money from technically unsophisticated customers. They promise “cheap” but then use junior developers who are given insufficient instructions to write code that looks like it's moving toward the client's goals. In fact, though, it's a bunch of facades build on a house of cards that could never actually work. That's not precisely writing bugs, though they may claim that the fact that your app doesn't work is a result of bugs. In a sense it's worse: They are effectively running a scam where they do the least amount of work possible to achieve the illusion of progress on the app. Just enough to continue collecting payments until the client gets sick of the constant excuses as to why it's not done yet. As an example: The client says they want a button to filter all of the entries in some list that are blue. The developer adds the button, but fails to add anything to the list that even indicates that an entry has a color, much less actual filtering anything when the Byron is pressed. Check the references of any outsourcing team you are considering hiring. I almost have to assume that most are scams, or at least using extremely junior developers.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Should I continue as a software engineer or explore other IT fields? I am 23, but still under probation for almost 2 months. Do I still have time to explore another IT field like cyber security?
Answer: How could anyone answer that question? Most companies start new employees out on probation. Sometimes for longer than two months! Did you just start? Then you're stuck on probation until the period ends! Unless there's some specific understanding at the company you're working for that probation would end early with strong performance, or that probation was extended because of poor performance, then what you're saying isn't unusual. If you were placed on probation for poor performance? Well, that's different. It's never too late to start in a new field, but it does take time to learn that field. I've personally never heard of a “no experience necessary/will train” cybersecurity job; they might exist, but they're probably highly competitive, and if you're having trouble at one software engineering position, then I wouldn't bet on you making it through the competition. So you might need six months to two years of training to get to the point where you can get in to a cybersecurity role. At least to train for and pass some certifications. Note that I'm talking about the kind of cybersecurity roles that might be offered by big companies or government jobs, and that set procedures for the rest of the IT department to follow. You might do some automated pen testing using off the shelf tools, but nothing more elaborate. Not the roles where you're digging deep for security holes in existing software; those roles require a certain preexisting skill set and temperament, and that skill set would include enough programming skill that you probably wouldn't be having trouble at a software engineering job. Another domain to explore might be DevOps. It doesn't require as much skill in programming, though it does require scripting and architecture skills. Again it's a field where you might be able to get a job by going through training and getting certifications. If software engineering itself is challenging you, then those are two options. If it's just job politics but you're enjoying software engineering, you might want to suffer through it for now and hop jobs as soon as you have an option. Good luck.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How can I get a full stack developer to give me a price for the project I need completed and not just ask me what my budget is and would it be appropriate to ask that we break it up into smaller parts so I can more easily afford it?
Answer: There may be several things going on here. The developer may be trying to find out if it's worth doing any work with you at all. If your budget is too low, they might simply not be willing to put any time into the project. If you're asking for a fixed bid, then that takes a lot of work to generate. Depending on the complexity of a project, I tend to charge US$5k–20k just to make a plan based on your requirements. In a sense, you're asking for the developer to do that much work for you for free as well as to (presumably) do even more work for free if it turns out that their estimate was low. The developer may in fact be of the opinion that it's impossible to estimate a project in advance, and they're just trying to get a general sense of whether they might be able to complete enough of the project to be useful before you run out of money. Developers who follow this school of thought only work by the hour or week, and will give you an approximate number of weeks of work to complete the core of your project—and if that's too close to your budget already, they will instead say that your budget is too low. (Or they will take your money anyway and stop working when you run out—there are entirely too many developers who are effectively scammers out there). Finally, they may be doing what you're probably worrying about: Planning to charge as much as your budget will bear. This is especially likely if the project is totally simple; if, for instance, it's a mostly static site for a business, or if it's a simple storefront. To distinguish between the earlier options and the last, I would recommend finding a friend who is a good developer and asking them whether your project is simple, or if it has some kind of complexity or an unknown that might make it harder. Good luck.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How do I study data structures to completely understand them? For example, I solved more than 20 problems in DS stack, but after like 5 hours, I almost forgot every solution and the logic to solve it.
Answer: You…solved 20 problems? For real? Then why are you saying that you forgot the solutions? If you knew enough to solve them, then why would you need to memorize the solutions that you produced the first time? Do you actually mean you typed in the solutions for twenty problems? Because typing in solutions that you've Googled is not solving. The goal with data structures and algorithms isn't to memorize. It's too learn and understand. Question: Why are software engineer salaries relatively high in the USA compared to other countries?
Answer: I have a hypothesis on this. First, when you're looking at software jobs, you have to make the distinction between strong developers and average to mediocre developers. Back in the 70s, Fred Brooks wrote a book called the Mythical Man-Month, and among other things he pointed out that the best developers were between 5x-20x more effective than the least skilled. Today we talk about “10x” developers, referring to the same studies as Brooks, but I prefer to just say strong developers. So, the big, successful technology companies that are predominantly located in the US (the FAANG companies and Microsoft and others) have taken this extreme range of skill to heart, and they recognize that the abilities of strong developers reach beyond simply being faster; their code can be faster, more robust, and easier to reason about and modify. And more to the point, there are things a strong developer can achieve that a weaker developer will never successfully accomplish. Given the sheer number of technology companies in the US, and the relatively limited population of really strong developers, the salaries of those developers have been pushed up and up due to competition. A quick search finds estimates that Google alone employs at least 40,000 software engineers; if Amazon, Facebook, Apple, Netflix, and Microsoft each employ that many, we're talking nearly a quarter million software engineers being paid really high salaries. I believe that normal software engineers at the above companies make $200k+ total compensation at this point. Many make much more. FAANG companies have all effectively started to print money, and can justify the salaries since they're making more than a million dollars per software engineer in profits. This has been partly blamed on high cost of living areas requiring higher salaries, but that doesn't fully explain the difference. Picking a random comparison, salaries in San Francisco should be about 20% higher than those in London, according to one site.[1] Looking at the salary ranges, though, they're significantly more than 20% higher—and the Glassdoor numbers are low compared to the FAANG compensation I'm aware of. So you have a quarter million or more engineers who won't even talk to you unless you're offering $200k or more. Simply cornering that much of the market means that average companies have a smaller pool of developers to choose among. So there's a corollary effect where even average developers are making $75–150k. COVID probably amplified things even more. Many developers got a taste of working from home, and a lot of jobs are now 100% remote. I've had many FAANG recruiters contact me about remote positions in fact. So that removes some of the last vestiges of “high cost of living areas” being the cause of high salaries. Though obviously there was always a chicken-and-egg issue with that claim, since the extremely high cost of living wouldn't have been able to exist without high salaries to begin with. So in a nutshell, I think that's a large part of the issue. We may have a higher raw number of tech startups as well, considering the lax employment laws that make hiring less risky for the employer. That would be another increase in relative demand in software engineers, and a corresponding increase in salary due to the supply and demand curve. Higher overall demand, plus the recognition that the very best developers are worth large multiples of average developers, serve to inflate the salaries of all of the developers. This is fundamentally an only slightly educated guess. There may be other factors at play that I am completely clueless about. I have seen the vast gap between developer skill and developer compensation, which is loosely correlated, but beyond that—I'm a software engineer, not an economist, so your mileage may vary etc.

Question: Which one is true, I can get a software engineer job without a degree or I need a degree to get a job? Why are there articles that contradict each other on this topic?
Answer: Some jobs will require a degree. This is even more true if you have fewer than, say, three years of experience. Not necessarily a degree in computer science. My degree isn't computer science and I've never had an issue, but I have also always done programming on my own and literally had a portfolio of games I could show off before my first interview after college. I also took enough computer science classes that I can pass technical interviews, which is where most people have trouble when they don't have a CS degree. College provides certain signals for employers. With a degree, you've proven that you're capable of performing arbitrary work that you've been assigned. That you have at least some ability to write in your native language. That you're willing to commit to something through to completion. So especially before you have a track record, a degree helps employers know that you at least meet a minimum bar. There is a local chat group that emphasizes helping the “average” developer find their first jobs, while providing them with encouragement and moral support, and they are really enthusiastic about some bootcamp programs. There are programs that boast 97%+ job placement in software development positions, and though I'm skeptical about the fine print for those claims, some people in the group did graduate from the bootcamp and do have software development jobs. So that alone proves it's possible. But what is your goal in asking the question? Really? Do you want to know if it's possible? Or do you want to know if it's likely? Are you hoping for a high demand, extremely high paying job? Or just trying to find an easy desk job with decent pay? The other thing that's endemic in the chat group I mentioned is complaints about how hard it is to find that first job. There are stories of repeated job applications to hundreds of companies over the course of more than a year, or even multiple years, before anyone hires them as a software developer. How much job mobility would you expect someone like that to have, really? If the job they eventually find is a living hell, what options will they have to switch? At a minimum they're likely to feel that they need to put in the time, maybe two years or more, to build up experience before they try to jump to another position. That's a long time to put up with abuse. What “those articles” aren't telling you is that there are effectively two distinct industries that are both described as software development. Some companies look for the least expensive developers they can find, and are not as picky about who they hire. Other companies are looking for really strong developers, but pay top dollar. The first category of company, in the Denver area where I live, will often pay as little as $48k/year to a junior developer, and will cap out at $75–105k/year for a senior developer. (Colorado has a wonderful new law that requires employers to include salary ranges with all job postings, so these are real numbers I just scraped off of Indeed.) This category often has dozens or even hundreds of applications for every opening, which is why some people struggle to find their first job. This is still decent money compared to many jobs, so I'm not knocking it, but I think that a lot of people join the industry because they hear about the high demand for and the numbers earned by the second group: $200k/year and up. Google and Amazon also both hire in the Denver area. I was just told that Amazon total compensation for a senior software engineer (SDE III) starts at $300k now (this includes stock grants, so if Amazon stock tanks, your total compensation would fall). I assume Google is similar or better. Even non-FAANG companies have good pay; one person I know works at a company in Boulder that you probably haven't heard of, and he makes >$250k plus stock options. His job search also only took a month and a half, if I remember correctly. And it only took that long because he was looking for a salary in that range. So to summarize, there is the group of developers who have a harder time finding jobs and who are paid in the lower range of salaries, and another group who excel at software development and get really great offers without needing to job hunt for months. With me so far? Here's the catch: The difference isn't the degree, but the aptitude and temperament of the developer. The high-paid group needs to learn most of the computer science fundamentals, but doesn't need a CS degree to prove they've learned what they need to know; that comes out in interviews. So in other words, you can't make your decision on whether to get a degree based on articles. If you're considered a programming genius by your friends and have been writing cool apps since you were 14? Then there's a decent chance you're in the second group and can pick up what you need to know of the CS fundamentals on your own if you put in the effort. If you haven't already shown aptitude? Then you just don't know yet. Strong developers don't form from whole cloth; they still need to put in the effort to learn. So until you've tried, you don't know where you'll end up. But if you end up in the first group, keep in mind how hard it is to find that first job for people who skip the degree. And even in the second group you'll need to build that portfolio before you will likely get that first job. So my conclusion is that you're likely best off getting a degree if you don't already have a degree (or “equivalent experience”). You can take a chance on one of the bootcamps instead, but that almost guarantees you'll only qualify for the first group of jobs, at least until you also spend the time learning the fundamentals. The amount of time it really takes to learn software engineering and build up “equivalent experience” just isn't that different from the time it takes to earn that degree. And while earning a degree you can also build a portfolio in your free time to better position you to get that first job. Also: There's no shame in taking the first two years of a degree at a community college. I took that approach myself due to lack of motivation in high school (and likely undiagnosed ADHD). Consider that you don't even need to put the community college on your resume: If you graduate from a four year college you can simply include the four year college and graduation date. Given today's extreme tuition costs, if you don't have parents who are willing and able to pay your way, you can work some job for those first two years to support yourself while filling taxes not as a dependent of your parents—and then get much more financial aid for your last two years since it will be calculated based on your income and savings instead of your parents’ or guardians’ when you fill out the forms. You might be able to get nearly all of your expenses covered and end up with only small college loans, in fact, though do your own research. (This is true for the US; other countries probably have different rules.) Good luck. And don't wait for anyone to tell you what to learn. There's no good reason to put off learning right now, and there are innumerable free options available online. Any degree or bootcamp education you eventually decide on will only be amplified by what you learn now. So what are you waiting for?

Question: Is it faster on average to have a balanced tree of if() else statements or to run through a bunch of if() else if() else statements?
Answer: This is part of what you learn when you earn a computer science degree. But you can also figure it out simply by counting. A string of, say, 16 if statements in series will take up to sixteen comparisons. If the statements require heavy calculations, then it could be 16x that you need to make that calculation. But if you instead can turn it into a perfectly balanced tree built only from if/else statements (meaning no if/else if situations), you can select among 16 results by using only four comparisons. Four is less than sixteen, so it would be faster. Whether that would matter in a real world program is another question. And if it does matter, it might not even be the fastest option. If you're checking if the same value equals one of a series of constants, a switch statement can sometimes be faster. Depends on the language and the exact situation, but in some cases the compiler can take it from four comparisons down to one. And a switch is easier to read. Sometimes what you really want is a table that maps states to behaviors. The speed wouldn't be any better than the perfectly balanced tree in some cases, but the clarity of the code would be vastly improved. Speaking of clarity of code, with too many branches of an if tree, you're probably doing something wrong from the point of view of design. Instead of calculating what should be done every time, for instance, you could use the strategy pattern[1] to assign an action to each object as appropriate. If you're looking at a series of thresholds to determine which gap a value is in, you should probably be traversing an array of the thresholds. Other patterns are available for other requirements. It's rare that you'd want to see 16 cases handled by as many if statements, no matter how your structure them.

Question: Why do developers hate project managers?
Answer: Developers hate project managers when they don't add value to a project. Let me tell you a (“based on real events”) story about a project manager I didn't hate, because he was awesome. I'll call him C. C spent months with the client before I was even involved with the project. He had to explain to me, sometimes in great detail, how things needed to work, and what the customers needed to accomplish. Whenever I had a question, he would go back to the client and drill down to what it was they actually needed, bringing me back clear instructions on how to proceed. He would work directly with the designer to create UI that was almost always perfect, but the few times that I would see a better way to present information to the user, he'd happily take the suggestion back to the designer and come back with new designs that were even better. Throughout this phase of the project I never even spoke to the client or to the designer. The team was able to focus 100% on the technical challenges. But time passes and C gets another job offer, and so he gets replaced by D. Unfortunately the frontend lead also left at the same time, so I'm the only one who is familiar with the full history of the project. D changes how things are organized. Standups now include the designer and the client. D didn't do all of that background learning about the project, and honestly doesn't understand how most of it needs to work. When D does work with the designer directly, the UI is just…wrong, and despite the fact that I'm backend lead, I end up needing to be the one who explains to the designer how things need to work, since the frontend developer just started. I try to be patient, but D never seems to really understand anything about the project. I try multiple times to explain the goals and strategies of the project—those same goals that were explained to me by C—and he just doesn't understand them. In fact, a lot of time in our meetings is wasted with these repeated explanations, with everyone else in the team also trying to explain the situation to him, since they understood it months ago. This shows up in meetings with the client, where D will make statements that don't make sense and we need to cover for him. He embarrasses us in front of the client regularly by revealing his ignorance of the product, in fact. He doesn't add tasks to the board unless one of the developers tell him we need it. He “runs” our meetings by asking what we're doing, which of course is what the task board says we're doing. There is very little that he adds to the project that an automated script couldn't handle. So that's why developers hate project managers. Not all project managers; as I said, C was awesome. But D added nothing to that project, and I was effectively doing the work of a project manager in addition to the backend work while watching him earn a crazy high salary for the work I was doing, while also criticizing my interactions with the client as not diplomatic enough. Yes, he complained to me once that I wasn't doing his job well enough. Am I bitter? Yeah, probably. Disclaimer: The above events are not strictly all from the same two project managers. I have creatively mixed events up to protect the innocent and to not publicly excoriate the guilty. If you have worked with me and believe I might be talking about you, know that you're not the only project manager I'm talking about, so I may actually be referring to something someone else did. But you should probably reconsider your life choices if you identify with D. So in other words, “This is a work of fiction. Any similarity to actual persons, living or dead, or actual events, is purely coincidental.” Except where it isn't. 🤷🏻‍♂️

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Why doesn't EcmaScript enable everything that TypeScript offers to JavaScript into JavaScript, so that TypeScript will no longer be relevant?
Answer: What does that buy us, exactly? I submit that there's no reason to bake TypeScript into the browser. TypeScript is complicated. Do we really need to add that complexity to every browser? If some browsers supported TypeScript and others didn't, we'd still need to transpile the code anyway. What are the odds that even if we got it into Chrome and Firefox and Edge that Apple would ever add it to Safari? TypeScript keeps getting better, with new versions being released all the time—but it sometimes breaks old code along the way. If one version of TypeScript were baked in, we'd be stuck with the features it could support and the language wouldn't be able to evolve as quickly. It's absolutely trivial today to precompile and package everything anyway. I've been using Vite, and it's really fire-and-forget. Everything just works, and is extremely fast. Or you can use this if you absolutely must import TypeScript in the browser: Paste that in your page and it can start to import TypeScript files directly. So they probably won't import all of TypeScript into ECMAScript. And we probably wouldn't want them to.

Question: What language get the most traction between C, C++, C#, COBOL, Elixir, Fortran, Go, Groovy, Haskell, Java, JavaScript Julia, Kotlin, Lisp, Lua, MATLAB, Objective-C, OCaml, Pascal, Perl, PHP, Python, R, Ruby, Rust, Scala, Smalltalk, Swift, TypeScript?
Answer: Assuming you're asking this question because you're trying to decide which one to learn: It. Doesn't. Matter. It's hard to learn to program. Once you learn, if you really learn and don't just memorize a few patterns in a bootcamp, then it's much easier to learn another language. The best money right now and for the foreseeable future is probably in Java, JavaScript, TypeScript, and C#. Swift and Kotlin are good if you want to write apps. Go is in a niche that is primarily backend development for less skilled developers. It's still pretty rare to encounter it in the wild, but it does exist. I don't think it's gaining much in popularity any more, though. COBOL might be a good choice for the next decade at least because of the number of older developers who are retiring, and the billions of lines of code that still run banks. Fewer people are learning COBOL, which means that if you can demonstrate skills in the language, you'll have less competition for jobs. This might also be an in for less talented developers who otherwise have a hard time getting jobs. C and C++ are languages that you should only learn if you don't need to ask what languages to learn. There will be jobs for them forever, but they also grind up and spit out developers who aren't as skilled. You've been warned. Fortran, R, MATLAB, Julia, and yes, Python, are really best if you know you need them—which means you're doing math, science, or machine learning. (No, I don't think it's a good idea to use Python for anything else. No, I don't want to debate that in the comments.) All of the above will probably be around for a long time in that niche. But you better have a strong advanced math background if you want to use one or more of these. The rest are dead, or dying, or on the decline, or obscure enough to be not relevant or worth learning unless it's out of curiosity. No, I don't want to debate whether Ruby or PHP or any other language is dying or on the decline. This is what I'm observing, and maybe it's a large part wishful thinking, but if you really want to tell me my answer is stupid, write your own answer. The best traction overall is the same as the best money paragraph above. I honestly thought Java would be on the decline by now, but it seems to be holding on while actually seriously improving as a language.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is the fact that Python doesn't support ++ or -- something developers consider when deciding upon a language?
Answer: I like ++ and - -, but I wouldn't avoid Python for excluding it. It's syntax sugar. Nice but not critical. I don't agree that it's an advantage that Guido ignored this useful feature, because I don't believe that language designers should infantilize developers, but neither is it a deal killer. On the other hand, I have a laundry list of complaints that do prevent me from liking Python. I'm using it for ML right now, and I can't wait to get back to a real language with static types and functional chaining, among other things. As a language it feels like a mess. The whole “there is only one way to do things in Python” is also a joke; for some things I've found three ways to do them, and they all suck. The entire philosophy is an anti-pattern anyway: Depending on what you're doing, some approaches are better, whereas for other tasks you might prefer a different approach. It's a beginner programmer's idea of what a great programming language should look like, as if where to put braces and semicolons is the hard part of programming. There really is no advantage to significant whitespace, and there are several reasons it's problematic, so it's a lose-lose design decision. P.S. I know Python 3 has type hints. I'm using them—and running into their limited flexibility and the near uselessness of the tooling. Half the time I don't even bother, since it has barely a tenth of the benefit of using types in other languages. See TypeScript for the right way to add types to your dynamic language.
