Question: Which is best combination for react app Nodejs or PHP?
Answer: If you're starting a new app today, there is no good reason to choose PHP. Node.js has a plethora of tools that make developing with React easier. React is distributed via npm, which is part of Node. You've got Next.js if you're making a single page app or blog. If you want more control over details, something like Vite will get you up and running on the frontend while you connect to servers using Prisma on the backend, for instance. And those are two options among dozens of strong choices. And TypeScript is a genuinely good language with stronger and more flexible static type support than even the newest PHP versions. If you use TypeScript on the front and backend, then your app can share code like type signatures, reducing interoperability bugs. PHP was great for making pages back when we wanted to install a counter on a page. Then people created monstrosities like WordPress and Drupal that effectively prove what a poor environment it is both for security and performance. There is nothing that still recommends PHP, and Node.js has some excellent benefits. The choice is pretty simple.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: What type of software benefits from being coded in Python?
Answer: If you mean how is the software better in some way because you used Python, well, it isn't. The opposite, in fact. The only exception is if the users will likely modify the software or extend it with scripts, and the users are beginner programmers who are more likely to know Python than other options. Even then it would be better to write the software in a better language and just embed Python in it. Python is slow. Python has poor support for threading. Python is big. And Python support for creating apps that aren't machine learning or web servers is extremely lacking. So comparing an app written in Python with an app written in just about any other language (except for Ruby, which is worse), it will be slower, more bulky, and have fewer options for user interface and graphics. And Python has an anemic type system that's barely ever used. This last point means that software written in Python is far more likely to have hidden bugs that were missed by testing, and is harder to refactor accurately and quickly, meaning it's more costly to pay down technical debt related to its architecture. I used to just not like Python because it used significant whitespace, which is bad enough. But the more I've been using it for a recent project, the more I've been finding broken about it. It's an old language with a lot of baggage and cruft (it's four years older than Java, if you can believe it—it predates C++ gaining templates or having an official standard defined, even!). It's cursed by design decisions rooted in the last century that predate any modern sensibilities. But it's somewhat easy for beginners to use. So I guess if the app is being written by inexperienced developers, it might benefit from being completed at all. Though even there, using JavaScript, or better, TypeScript, retains the same benefits of ease of use and a large number of available libraries, including many more application development frameworks, some of which are far better options than the few available for Python. And as a bonus, TypeScript doesn't have any of the drawbacks I listed above. If you need more speed than TypeScript, then you can graduate to C#, Java, or C++. But then you'll lose beginner-friendliness, and to dive degree, development velocity. There's always a tradeoff. Programming languages are tools. Choose the best tool for the job. If you need to test out machine learning models, Python may be that tool. Otherwise there are almost certainly better tools.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: What are the main differences between the MERN stack and other popular web development stacks?
Answer: There are four main differences: MERN stands for MongoDB, ExpressJS, React and Node.js. So the four main ways other stacks can be different is to not use MongoDB, or ExpressJS, or React, or Node.js. Some permutations of those are also possible, though if you don't use Node.js, you can't use ExpressJS. “Popular stacks” are overblown. It seems that web development bloggers are really bored and like to make up terms like MERN and LAMP and so forth. At least LAMP really was extremely common when it was coined. I even used it myself at one point. And I've never used a MERN stack. I've used the individual components separately. I'll probably never use MongoDB again, but I have used it. I do use the other three, but not because it's a stack but rather because they are good tools. Instead of MongoDB I've been using Prisma, which is database agnostic and gives you GraphQL, though I usually use it with PostgreSQL. I also often use Redis. Vite is another excellent tool that helps keep configuration more sane. Sometimes I use Fastify instead of ExpressJS as well. Depends on the goals of the project. And occasionally I write a backend in Java or Go. And that's the real answer: Today we build stacks with the best tools for the job. MongoDB isn't really the best at anything anymore, except possibly being easier to understand for beginners, but other databases really are just better. And there are so many tools in a stack today that trying to coin a word for each stack would get very confusing: “I'm using the VERPPLG stack.” “Oh really? I prefer FLIGDRAWS”… Yeah, stacks aren't quite as simple as they used to be.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How can we convert programming language from Lua to JavaScript? I am looking for some tools that convert from LUA to JavaScript.
Answer: Lua, not LUA. You got it right the first time. Lua is a word, not an acronym you need to capitalize. It's Portuguese for “moon” (think Spanish luna as a cognate). And other than trivial cases, a generalized automated tool would be more trouble than it's worth. Some aspects of Lua can't be converted to JavaScript at all. Other conversions would result in very ugly and suboptimal code. Example: Lua has a table data structure that simultaneously is optimized to be an array, a map, and a class. JavaScript has a function type that doubles as its class type, but there's a separate array. Oh, and Lua arrays are 1-based instead of zero based. Trying to automatically convert all possible usage patterns from Lua to JavaScript would end up with code so convoluted that you'd be better off using the WebAssembly build of Lua to run Lua directly in your web page. It was one of the first examples that I saw for the precursor to WebAssembly, asm.js, before the latter even got its name. I think they were calling it the Alchemy project back then. If JavaScript supported custom operators I could see how it could work. But it doesn't. Unfortunately, Lua does, and if your source Lua code relies on that you're fresh out of luck. So your options are WebAssembly or hand porting, like we had to do in the old days for everything. Or if your code is very homogeneous and follows similar patterns throughout, you could potentially write your own converter that could do some of the work, where you would go over it by hand afterward to finish the conversion. Good luck.

Question: A software engineer told me I shouldn't label myself as a programmer, I'm just a “coder” (I'm a web developer). What exactly is the difference, and should I remove the title programmer from my resume?
Answer: To me the distinction between coder and programmer is ability to deal with complexity. In the game industry, we used to call the people who wrote the extremely simple AI scripts “scripters.” These were creative types who were adding real content to the games, but beyond the occasional simple conditional, they were really unable to program anything complex. They knew their limitations, though. There was no polite fiction that they were programmers as well; they had enough technical skill to write scripts in a very controlled environment, and that was really the limit. My take is that the person who called the asker a “coder” may have meant something similar. After all, a huge percentage of the industry doesn't appear to actually have the skill to program. This isn't even a secret, and it isn't new: That article dates to 2007. So I have to disagree with many of the answers. There are a ton of people who have the job title “Programmer,” or even “Software Engineer,” who have been developing software, but who never seemed to gain the full skill and ability to program. Instead they tend to carefully assemble components, leaning heavily on examples and patterns, and more to the point, learning most actions by rote instead of through a deeper understanding. Someone like that can create apps or web sites, for sure. But parts of apps they work on will likely be less robust than they could have been if what I would call a software engineer were involved. The difference isn't about being a junior developer vs senior. A junior developer has a lot to learn, but I've worked with many, even interns in their first position in industry, who were quite skilled at programming. It's more about whether they really learned to program or instead learned enough of the shape of a particular flavor of programming to be able to do the work well enough to be employed. And the difference has long term consequences for the developers I'm characterizing as coders. I just wrote in another answer about how there's a huge division among software developers where one group complains about the difficulty in getting hired, either for their first job or later, while another group never seems to have trouble.[1] And, yes, the “coders” are the ones with long term career challenges. Enough so that there are dozens of answers to that question that assert that no one will hire a programmer after they turn 30 or 35. Despite the fact that other answers are from people in their 60s who have had no problem their entire lives getting jobs. I think that we really have a serious problem in the industry with a lack of well understood job titles or categories. We tend to use the title “programmer” for everyone from the person who barely knows HTML all the way to a top expert in compiler design or high speed multithreaded databases or critical real time systems where people die if the code crashes. And the level of skill in the industry is extremely broad as well, where higher skill developers not only are faster at complex tasks but can do some things that lower skill developers would simply never be able to complete. And on top of that there are different skill domains! It's like calling everyone in a hospital a medical worker, not distinguishing between a nurse and a surgeon and an expert in disposing of medical waste. Now it is rude of the other developer to use coder as an insult, if that's how it came across. And for all I know he's just being a jerk and a snob, and you're a great software engineer who likes to work on frontend. Working as a web developer tells me nothing about your skill at programming, after all. But that's the idea he's getting at, I think. And to the other answers that say all programmers are just programmers? Sorry, no. There there are programmers, and then there are software engineers—and there are also coders. And there are jobs for all of us, though jobs the “coder” tier may be oversaturated. Caveat Emptor.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Why do companies ask for Data Structures and Algo when we hardly use them in practical?
Answer: Listen. I've heard this assertion dozens of times. That CS classes are worthless. Data structures are something that they force you to learn in college, and that you immediately forget. That advanced algorithms are written by “other people,” and that the average developer will never need to write a sort professionally, and so it's useless to learn them. And finally, that the interviews that test potential employees in their ability to regurgitate these algorithms are completely bogus, and that they are a result of cargo cult interview practices that exclude all manner of perfectly good developers from getting jobs. It's both utterly false, and completely true. But I have bad news for you if you think it's true. I recently wrote a nice long treatment on whether developers can still be hired after they're 35-40. Similar to this answer, my answer there is also yes and no. The tl;dr with respect to this question is that there are some developers who put in the time to become minimally competent, and others who really shine. In order to shine you need to remember and use your data structures and algorithms knowledge, along with other CS fundamentals like algorithmic complexity. And the folks who are just competent? They’re the ones most in danger of being outsourced. Of being fired in their 30s and having a hard time getting a new job. Of seeing wages stagnate or even fall. So if you are one of the stronger developers who can shine, and your current job has you moving controls around instead? Then you’re in the wrong job and you should be searching for one where you’re not going to suffer from the “planned obsolescence” that makes so many people argue so vehemently about how no developers can be hired after they’re 35. Despite all of the abundant evidence to the contrary on that same question.

Question: Trump campaigned in 2015 on making America great again. When do Republicans think America was once great, when did it become less so, and what would make it great again?
Answer: Remember when you were a kid? You had no real responsibilities. All you had to do was go to school, do your chores, and do your homework. Life was simpler. In high school you maybe even had a sweetheart or two, and keeping them happy wasn't complicated. Wind back the clock to the 50s, 60s, and 70s, and the white men who now buy into MAGA had even less homework and fewer rules to follow. Life was good. High school may have been the absolute peak of their existence, since even more than today, having any kind of athletic ability meant you were in the popular crowd, while the “nerds” and “weirdos” were picked on and disrespected. Sexual harassment wasn't looked on as a bad thing, and casual racism was just how some people talked. I'm not quite that old—my high school years were in the 80s—but I'm extrapolating with the help of stories from older folks and some media representations. It's generally true that the peak of life for someone who never goes to college is often high school. And Trump brags about how well he does with the “uneducated.” After high school they really end up finding out how hard life can be, and it gets worse as they get older. All the smart and most of the weird kids they mocked and bullied in high school are now successful, and they are barely scraping by. The former nerds don't even think about them any more, but they've decided that the nerds are now mocking them in revenge. Classic projection. So back when MAGAs were kids, life seemed better. And when Trump comes along and says he will make America great again, it fires off rusty brain cells that remember happier, simpler times when they felt on top of the world. Long before their life fell apart, their jobs went away, and their family was broken. It's not logical. Of course they were happier as kids before adult responsibilities kicked in. They skipped college when everyone told them would hurt their earning power, which they ignored, and they're living the consequences. But it's a rare high school that teaches critical thinking, and most MAGA supporters never made it to college. So in what way do they want to make America great? They want that feeling back. The one where someone else is making money for them. That any problems weren't their fault. No responsibility. No one yelling at them for slapping an ass or using the n-word. And perhaps most importantly of all, seeing those nerds (“urban elites”) get bullied again, demonstrating that they're the winners. A lot of these people have lives that suck, making them vulnerable to the lies told by Trump. Anyone who does the most cursory research knows that Trump isn't to be trusted. That he's made a life of of grifting. That he specifically steals from the working class, the same working class that's supporting him now. But their lives suck enough that there's a desperation to believe in something that makes them feel like they're not losers. Belief so strong that no facts can break through their belief system. So strong that Trump can say one thing in the first half of a sentence and contradict it with a different lie in the second half, and they will somehow believe both are true. There's no coincidence that conspiracy theories are running rampant in the MAGA crowd. Even crazy ones like the “faked moon landing” and flat earth. Because people who believe in myths that don't stand up to the slightest rational reasoning are clinging to them as evidence that they know something those elites don't know. And that belief is a validation of how smart they are. So desperate are they to experience some kind of win over the nerds, they cling to nonsense and fantasy. A lot of words have been written about how life sucked for everyone who wasn't white and male in the times the MAGAs want to turn the clock back to. Other things like manufacturing leaving the US and workers later being replaced by automation are also contributing factors. I don't disagree with any of those points. But I think that it's more the visceral desire to return to childhood that motivates the MAGAs. Or maybe it's all of the above. Note that pro-MAGA rants will be duly deleted. Even if you claim to be “not a Trump supporter”. In my experience there is no point in arguing with anyone who won't agree to the existence of verifiable facts. So don't bother. As Chrysaor Jordan says, I dare you to instead prove me wrong in your own answer. Hint: That's the “answer” button, not the “comment” button. Happy writing!

Question: Self taught developers, how did you overcome the times of self doubt and self sabotage?
Answer: …by taking data structures and algorithms classes at a local community college? I've never been big on self-sabotage, though. And I learned pre-internet, so I didn't really have any idea how much I needed to learn until I took those classes. So I foolishly had no self doubt to start with either. But if I had known what I didn't know, I would have probably been even more motivated to take those classes. I'd been programming for years before I took any CS classes, and I thought I knew everything. But I was so wrong it's hard to fully express how retroactively embarrassed for myself I am. So if you don't know your data structures, algorithms, and other CS core concepts? And that's causing self-doubt and self-sabotage? Well, the solution is pretty obvious. Start learning the fundamentals! Even if you don't go for the full four year degree, you can probably find the basics at a local community college, or some online class, or something. It's possible, after all, that your doubt isn't irrational. But ace the CS sequence and you'll be able to bury any doubt related to having a CS degree. Keep learning!

Question: As of your experience, how much time will it take for 20 or more experts to make an online multiplayer game (for Android) which include chat, 1 big BR map, more than 50 players can participate in the match at a time and users more then 10 million?
Answer: I see you made an effort to add details, but you really haven't added enough detail to get a good idea of how long it will take. I haven't tried to create a battle royale game…ever. So I don't even know what's available off-the-shelf. It may be that you could buy assets from the Unity store, that they'll all work really well with each other, and you'll be mostly concerned with the polish of your app. In my experience, that's still a minimum of four months, and that really requires all of the stars to align perfectly. Six months is a better estimate, and 1-2 years is even better since it can handle the near inevitability of some critical bug coming up that takes forever to track down. I've talked to more than a dozen developers who use Unity professionally, and they all have stories of Unity breaking something between version updates, or just there being some bug that was incredibly opaque. For that reason I'd lean toward Unreal, but Unreal doesn't have nearly the quantity of ready-made assets, so it's a balance. And remember, if you do use publicly available assets, your game will generally look like all other Unity games. Your choice.

Question: I don’t know what to do anymore. I don’t want a future and I’m 14. I just want to be in a grave atp. I’ve asked for help over and over. I’ve tried hotlines. What do I do?
Answer: It can really suck to be 14. I had problems with depression at that age. I hated school. I was in conflict with my parents. I wanted attention, but when I got attention it was negative and it made things worse. Know that life gets better. It won't be like this forever. My life is awesome now, and I wouldn't want to have missed out on it for anything. Do what you can to put up with it. If there's something that you like, that you really resonate with, dive into it (as long as it's safe!) and let it distract you as much as possible until you finish high school. I'm thinking music, videos, hobbies, books, anime, clothing, makeup, animals, technology—whatever you can lose yourself in. And I know that high school seems like forever, but it really isn't. If you put your mind to it, you'll endure. You're stronger than you think. You haven't said if there are specific people bothering you, but there's a great quote floating around that goes something like: Revenge is outliving your enemies. If you can learn to live well, so much the better. If there are school counselors, talk to one. If you get desperate and nothing I've said works, then let a counselor know that you're having these thoughts, and they should get you the help you need. If the first counselor doesn't help you, then find another, or try the hotlines again, or as a last resort dial 911. That's better than making any decision that would be final. If you make it through, your life will change, and it will likely be for the better. You're in a period of transition right now, and that can really suck, but if you can hold on just a little longer, there's a better life waiting for you.

Question: Is it true that software engineers can only work until the age of 35/40 because they then get fired by their companies?
Answer: There are a huge range of answers to this question, because clearly there is a huge range of experience people have in the industry. There's one answer that goes as far as to claim that everyone in India over 35 has “aged out of the industry” because they can't learn new skills. That's a joke if I've ever heard one. I personally transitioned from game development in C++ to backend server development and scalable high performance architecture after I turned 35, and right now I'm learning all of the new machine learning tools. It also implies that junior developers are universally cheaper and can do the same work. Yet it's one of the top voted answers… Other answers insist that older developers who retain their jobs are only the lucky ones who never were fired. Many talk about how junior developers don't have a family and will therefore work 80+ hours per week, as if a developer can have a sustained workload of more than about 30 hours of programming per week without productivity going negative. But then there are answers that fit my own experience where people in their fifties and sixties have never had a hard time finding work. In the worst recessions I've experienced, I've never taken longer than about three months to find a new job, and that was right after 9/11 when no one was hiring. So what's the difference? I hypothesize that it's a “tale of two programmers.” Well, maybe more than two. Let's try three: Most of the answers talking about a “limit” at 35 seem to be in the first group. To be clear: There's nothing wrong with choosing a career for money. No implied criticism at all; we all work because we need to be paid, not just because we love the job. But software engineering is an art, a craft, and a skill with an aptitude, and by the time you've been in the industry for a decade, employers are right to assume that you're not likely to improve any more. And by that point in your career, you're asking for more money because of your experience—but if you've effectively repeated the same year of experience ten times, then those younger developers really are cheaper and offering the same results. One of the top answers seems to fall in the second group; by all indicators they seem to be a strong developer in their area of expertise, but demand in their industry is down. I'm sure they've moved to different industries, but it seems hard for them to ride a hot technology popularity wave. And the answers that say they're happily employed well into their later life? They all have signs they fall into the third bucket. As do I. My luck at choosing the next technology to study has been very good. I've chosen a few duds, but I learn enough new things that I've been able to jump from one technology to another as my career has progressed. So yes, there is some luck involved. But when you're using a shotgun, your aim doesn't need to be perfect, and if you choose to learn things that a lot of people are talking about, well, it's rare that a major new technology trend comes out of nowhere. So, is it true that software engineers have a harder time finding jobs after 30? For some it seems to be. There are ample examples of such complaints on Quora. For others it clearly isn't. The trick is to determine as early as possible which group you'll likely be in. My suggested strategy is that people who are trying to decide on a career should try programming. Really learn it. Find out if you have any talent for it. See if it catches your imagination. And if it doesn't? Then you can still make the attempt, but be aware that you may need to plan for a career pivot. Many software engineers I know have transitioned into management. If that's your plan, then you still need to learn, but instead of programming you need to learn more about managing people and projects. Having programming experience gives you a great background to understand the actual constraints that software engineers face. And it gives you enough context to know when a programmer is BSing you, which is also a critical management skill. 😉 As I implied above, there is a talent involved in software development. Companies don't owe you more money just because you put in the time; they aren't charities, and they expect more actual value for the higher paycheck that comes with many years of experience. I get that people get mad that companies won't hire them, but they need to accept the fact that their skills haven't kept up with their salary requirements—or that they're applying for jobs that are too junior for their career stage. Remember that companies hire junior developers with the hope that they will eventually become much stronger. No company needs a permanently junior developer. And yes, I have interviewed older developers who seemed to be very experienced junior developers. And please don't complain to me about the need to be constantly learning. I enjoy the learning, but if you don't, then you can choose whether you want to put in the effort. I'm simply the messenger here, communicating the consequences of stagnation as I see them. You're free to ignore me and move on, or to write your own answer about how the whole industry never hires people over 35, all of the evidence to the contrary. The best a person can do is to move forward. If you can't find a job now, then look for ways to pivot or to learn more. If you're trying to decide on a career, then dip your toe in as I suggested above and see if it's a good fit. If you're looking for somewhere to complain about the universe, though, please write your own answer.

Question: What's the point of JavaScript if TypeScript exists? Should I replace all my future JavaScript projects with TypeScript projects?
Answer: We're stuck with JavaScript existing for the foreseeable future. There's a tremendous amount of preexisting code, and browsers only know how to interpret JavaScript. But yes, all of your future projects should use TypeScript or another statically typed language. It's better software engineering all around.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How come that in 2022 developers have to waste hours writing HTML & CSS code just to center a component instead of using a framework that allows drag and drop?
Answer: I've actually seen a number of drag-and-drop tools for combining, for instance, React components visually. So these tools do exist. And if the code is properly formed, it shouldn't take hours to center a component. So that premise is also false. Finally, in general developers shouldn't be writing “HTML and CSS code” directly at all. Modern component frameworks like React mean that you're writing in JavaScript or TypeScript to specify the behavior of each component once, and there are excellent tools like Storybook that allow you to view and test each component in isolation. If you have a component that needs to center its contents, then you add the style information (and any additional containers, if necessary) to it once and you're done. That should take a few minutes. A long time ago, when drag-and-drop frameworks were more ubiquitous, a UI was really really static for the most part. At most you'd have a box or a list that could expand. Today it's expected that a web page work on all screen sizes and on phones. That it be “responsive.” And responsive is hard in a drag-and-drop context. Story time! Set the clock back to the early 2010s, when Android phones were starting to proliferate. There was a lot of FUD in the development press about “Fragmentation!!!”, which primarily focused on the fact that Android devices had different screen dimensions (and other features and Android versions as well, but much ink was spilled on how many screen sizes developers had to support). But now think for a minute about the web. There is absolutely no single screen resolution on the web, and to some degree every page really should support, or at least not look awful on, every reasonable screen size. The Android developer tools had drag-and-drop UI editing very early on, and within those tools you could add to each control to “magnet” it to different sides of the screen, or to scale it as the screen scaled, and even to select different layouts for different screen orientations and densities. This would trivially allow for an app to scale to every reasonable screen size. But everyone wanted to just drag-and-drop for one screen layout and be done, and people would whine endlessly about how hard it was to support different resolutions. Same thing happened on iOS eventually. “OMG! We have to support four screen layouts now! The world is ending!!” The whining was loud and omnipresent on developer blogs. No, it's not that we don't have the tools. It's that the world got more complicated than a simple drag-and-drop interface can support well any more, and a complex drag-and-drop interface is too complex for the people who really need them. And the people capable of using the more advanced drag-and-drop interfaces often end up preferring using code. Because just like in every other aspect of software development, beyond a certain level of complexity it's easier to write code than to use a visual programming paradigm. There's a reason we all still write code instead of dragging around boxes in a visual programming system, after all. But, given the fact that there exist multiple drag-and-drop website builders for React components[1] , at least some people must find them useful. At the same time, you're still modifying the components directly in code in many of them. But I'm sure at least some come with a container that centers the components you drop in it. It's not like a lot of code required.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is there a time when you join a software company and feel that the codes are too hard, the product too complicated, the framework and libraries too huge, and overwhelmed by the thoughts that you would never master them all? How would you overcome the fear, and train for the work? How long did it take you to master the code and make significant contributions to the project?
Answer: Hmmm… That's several questions. Note I'm a very senior developer, not a junior, so consider this an answer from experience. Do I ever find the code “too hard”? No. During my interview for any project I determine what expertise is required before I start, and no one so far has lied about what the requirements were. Do I find the product too complicated? Sometimes I find the architecture to be too complicated. Design is hard, and under development pressure, teams sometimes allow the architecture to grow organically. This kind of organic is not a good thing. Am I overwhelmed? Not really. On one project, the architecture was so bad that it took 20x longer than it would normally take me to accomplish anything, and that was stressful, but I always was confident that I could finish each task. Even on that last task I didn't fear it, nor did I “train” for it really. I asked questions and explored the different parts of the architecture to figure out how to accomplish the tasks they handed me. The other team members were only rarely available to answer questions, which was annoying, but I figured out ways to move forward. I made mistakes due to lack of information, but I was able to correct them when they told me the problems. And I was making minor contributions in a few days, and major contributions in a couple of weeks. I get that you're probably a junior developer. Keep learning and have faith you'll find the answers you need. It's a slog, but it's worth it.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: What game engine is good for a beginner? Don’t suggest Unity as it only gives me errors and nothing.
Answer: If you are getting stuck on Unity, then you need to step back and learn how to program rather than diving into a complex game engine while trying to learn to program at the same time. Or if you're impatient, there are tools like GameMaker[1] that allow you to use visual programming to implement simple logic. There's also RPG Maker[2]. Both cost money, of course. I'm sure there are more options out there, but as a general policy I try not to act as a Google search agent on Quora. I think there are a few beginner focused engines that are free, but I wouldn't expect the quality to be great. Try searching for beginner game engines, or game engines with visual programming. And definitely stick with 2d games to start with. 3d has a hundred ways you could break things and cause errors before you even get to programming.

Question: What is programming and coding, and how can one program or code as a beginner?
Answer: Programming is the process of telling a computer to do things. Coding is mostly the same, and some consider it a synonym, but it's somewhat pejorative; it implies less skill and complexity. How can you learn? Follow one of the approximately three zillion tutorials available online. Do the work. Don't just watch a YouTube video and think you've learned anything. Until you are typing code into an editor, you're not learning programming. You're at best learning about programming, which is as useful as learning about music when you want to become a musician. There are many free tools you can download. Any beginner tutorials should include instructions. If you only have access to a tablet (iPad etc.), then look for beginner tutorials that will work on your tablet. Search for things like “programming on an iPad”. Beyond that, you just need to do the work. It takes time to learn to think like a programmer. Don't give up too soon. You won't learn to program by asking questions on Quora. You won't learn by just watching videos or reading books. You can only learn to program by programming; find a book or tutorial and do what it says. Good luck.

Question: Is it hard to find a tech job in Boulder, Colorado?
Answer: Boulder won first place in a “Top Cities to Start Your Startup” list a few years back.[1] We have large employers like Google and IBM and a zillion smaller employers. There are also multiple startup accelerators and venture capital companies. Just outside of Boulder we have even more tech companies like Oracle and Seagate. Longmont to the north has their own tech community. And Denver to the southeast has its own large tech community (though the Denver Tech Center is unfortunately on the south side of the city, but some companies (like Amazon) are downtown, which is a much better commute). Boulder, Denver, and Longmont each have a “startup week” event that's free to attend every year. Tons of educational and networking opportunities in each event. Whenever I've looked around I've seen lots of opportunities. There are also a lot of great engineers in the area, but in general it doesn't seem that it's too hard to find great opportunities. It's always good to see if your particular skills are in demand in any area you're thinking of moving to, though. Boulder seems to be a bit heavy on Ruby on Rails and Python for my taste, though I've seen a full spectrum of different technologies in demand. So no, it's not hard to find tech jobs in Boulder.

Question: What is the use of learning high level programming language if future generation of computers can be programmed by using human language?
Answer: I answered a very similar question on Quora already: The underlying difficulty of creating software is entirely unrelated to the syntax of any particular programming language. I have to assume that whoever asked this question is imagining something like a computer on Star Trek, where you can just describe something you need, and the computer writes the program for you. Or you ask for a scene on a planet, and it just creates that scene for you. Credit: A very comprehensive and precise spec So, in their head, the asker is imagining describing an app in English, something like: “I want an app that will remind me of any appointments that I have, whether in my Google Calendar or on my office calendar, and it will take voice commands to add items to both calendars. I also want to share my calendar with friends.” I specifically describe an app here that could be developed with the proper team of developers. Even a team of humans would have a hard time with that English sentence, though. Problems: There are many more. But that last point makes a good transition: The real problem is that you need a computer (or a human development team) to ask all of these questions and understand the answers. In other words, the computer needs to be fully as smart as a human. It would need to understand human context, and what a calendar is, and what privacy is, and why some kinds of privacy might be important. And despite all of the recent advances in “AI”, we're actually no closer to “Strong AI,” an AI that thinks and understands like a human, than we were in the 1950s when they thought strong AI was only 20 years away. It's still at least 20 years away. And I wouldn't be surprised that it turns out to be 20 years away 50 years from now. I actually used to be more bullish on strong AI, but I feel the field has been stagnant for 20 years, despite all the advances in machine learning. Until you have strong AI, you will need programmers to do anything that hasn't already been done. There do exist drag-and-drop app creators (written by programmers) that can automate the creation of apps with specific features. Those will certainly get more advanced and capable. But there will always be a need for developers who understand the minutiae of how software works. And that minutiae is the domain of software engineers. Even when they're using increasingly advanced tools to assemble components. Tools that won't look like English in the foreseeable future, because English is terrible for precision specifications, which is what you're really writing when you're creating software. And the hard part is understanding the specifications, not the language. So the very premise of this question is misguided. More recently DALL-E has been giving people the idea that computers are starting to understand us. Nope. As soon as you dig a bit deeper you discover that it ignored half of the things you asked for and didn't quite understand the other half. So stop making excuses that don't have any basis in reality and start learning how to program. Or at least admit to yourself that you just don't feel like it. Making up unsupported reasons to avoid hard work is just a form of lying to yourself. See also: Tim Mensch's answer to In 2018 why are so many people fixated on programming/coding language/careers/minutiae when software engineering and automated code generation have been around for ages and will displace 80% of coding Real Soon Now?

Question: Are programmers new factory workers? It appears that glamour and prestige is gone from programming profession
Answer: There are many kinds of programming jobs. I've frequently pointed out that the range is as much as calling every employee in a hospital a “medical worker,” from the surgeons and specialists to the nurse assistants and, yes, even those who dispose of medical waste. Salaries vary just as much. So in software engineering, you will find developers who have been trained in how to perform relatively low skill tasks, on the order of factory workers (though, to be fair, more skilled than most factory jobs would have been). But you'll also find developers who are as highly skilled (and paid) as most lawyers, engineers, or even doctors in their own way. I can only speak to the attitude in the US, but here there exist pretty extremely highly paid jobs in software. A FAANG might pay a half million USD per year; a specialist might see over a million. And a software entrepreneur really doesn't have a cap on how much they can earn. In that respect, software engineering keeps the glamor here, even when there do exist “lower paid” programming jobs, since the glamor of the higher paid positions raises the perception of the lower paid jobs. Is the work itself glamorous? Work is work to a certain degree. I suspect that every profession has its less glamorous work that needs to be done. Finally, again here in the US, software engineers are treated with the same respect as those with other professional jobs. I've never really had a lot of contact with factory workers socially, so I honestly can't compare directly the relative respect for that as a profession. That said, my impression is that factory worker was a solid middle class but blue collar job. Programmer is absolutely white collar. And again, here in the US, there seems to be more respect given to white collar jobs. In one way it is like a factory job, though. If factory jobs in the 1970s had continued to go up in wages along with the economy and overall productivity gains, a factory worker would be making about as much money today as the lower end of the software engineering salary range. I talk about this in another answer: The high demand and low supply of programmers has pushed our salaries up to where they should be, in other words, while the factory workers are getting the short end of the stick.

Question: What does “best practice” mean in software development?
Answer: Instead of harping on the fact that we, as an industry, can't agree on what a complete set of best practices consists of, I'd like to answer the question. A best practice is a result the accumulated wisdom of experienced and skilled software engineers. It's a practice that, when you follow it, you will on average and over time end up with better results than if you ignore it. It's true that there are many conflicting “best practices” floating around. A common one I've heard is to use TDD, and in my experience a skilled senior engineer doesn't actually need the training wheels of TDD to write testable interfaces, and certainly doesn't need TDD to write good tests. But a loud group of advocates swear that no software can possibly be good engineering without TDD. I rarely use TDD, but I feel my work product is extremely robust and easy to extend reliably, so for me I feel I've proven that TDD isn't a requirement. Worse, TDD effectively requires a whole lot of fragile busywork that's prone to needing changes every time you update the code it represents, so it actually increases technical debt and decreases overall development velocity. So what best practices should you follow? If you're a junior developer, pick one programming pundit and follow what they say. There's no way to really choose between them until you have sufficient experience with one set of practices to get a feel for it. But remember the fact that you effectively picked that set of philosophies at random. If you can keep that in mind, then later, once you have more experience, go ahead and try other philosophies on for size. Because some really are better practices than others. A more senior developer should have enough context to judge the pundits and choose based on their own experience. It's still worthwhile experimenting with various practices until you find someone whose opinions you can really get behind, but it's no longer a random choice. Since I'm one of those pundits, you'd think I would advocate for my own opinions. No. My opinions work for me, and for developers like me. I've worked with dozens of developers who share my opinions on best practices, at least to the 95th percentile. But that doesn't mean they will work for everyone. Junior developers, as I alluded to above, may really benefit from TDD. Some developers may benefit from TDD over the long term, even. I don't know; it doesn't benefit me, but maybe it would be good for you. And the thing is, once you identify the set of best practices that work well for you, you can then identify the best companies for you to work for. Remember that when you interview with a company, you should be interviewing them as they interview you. If you can identify what practices work best for you, then you can ask your potential employer if they follow those practices. Personally, I wouldn't consider working for a company that didn't use statically typed languages for primary development, for instance. I certainly wouldn't approach one that didn't use source control, and I would hesitate if that source control weren't git. I would avoid companies that don't have any documentation for their internal APIs. I don't like projects that have no test coverage, though I'll work on them if I am supported in adding tests. And due to a nearly traumatic experience at a company that went 1000% in on isolated microservices and a completely custom ORM that didn't support joins, I realized that it was a personal value to me to not need to write 20x as much code to accomplish things on the off chance that it will be useful to expand the team someday. Not that they can hire anyone who can work on it at all at this point. Oh yeah, and they didn't have any integration test coverage either. Good times. So in summary, calling by calling something a best practice, the speaker is imparting that it's, in their opinion (and hopefully in the opinions of others) that the software engineering quality of your project will be impaired if you don't follow that practice.

Question: Why are senior software engineering interviews so tough these days?
Answer: So, this is one of those questions that was asked years ago, and it has plenty of answers. But I think that I have a slightly different take on the situation. The industry is maturing, and more and more companies are demanding actual skill from their senior engineers. For a long time, because of the perpetual shortage of software engineers, standards were reduced, and developers with two years of experience who were barely doing more than copying and pasting code from Google were being hired in senior roles. But many of these companies have learned that simply having “senior” on their resume doesn't mean they can actually do the job. That if you do hire without extensive screening, you can end up with a developer who reduces the overall team velocity. Negative productivity is a thing. So for better or worse they've been adding various kinds of programming challenges to their interview process to try to avoid this problem. But then we get tons of formerly senior engineers who can't find a job posting questions about how hard it is to get through the interview process. This parallels the dichotomy between the “I always can pick up a new job quickly” crowd and the “no one is using reasonable criteria for hiring” crowd. The former have the skills required to be a senior software engineer in today's market, and the latter don't. Yes, jobs that don't require programming tests do still exist. By all means, they should keep applying for them and post self-righteous screeds about how they won't lower themselves to taking such tests, as if their real reason is some kind of high principle and not that they just can't write the code. But as the industry matures, more and more jobs will require actual skills. And people who write questions like this will find it harder and harder to get jobs, since they're competing with the many others who are lacking in programming competence. In summary: Senior software engineering interviews aren't tough at all if you have the right aptitude and experience. If you finding them to be tough, then you should try applying for a lower-than-senior role, or pivot to a role that's programming adjacent like QA or management. Because acting as if employers owe you a job even when you can't prove you can do it isn't a good look. If you want to comment on how unfair programming tests are, please take your complaints to this answer: Because I'm really sick of repeating myself. I've also already heard all of the arguments, and they all sound like “I can't write code and so therefore I'm going to claim that it's not relevant.” And considering the job is programming, being able to demonstrate that you can program at all seems like a reasonable test. If you're going to claim a programmer shouldn't need to have that skill, the proof is really on you.

Question: I need a freelancer to help me code. I'm willing to pay as high as $1200 for the job. Can anyone help?
Answer: My general rule as a freelancer is to never take projects that are too small. With a funding limit like that I'd generally assume that, even if I could crank out the code I'd promised in a day, that you'd be asking for tweaks and additional features for weeks. By the end of any nontrivial project my hourly compensation for it would rapidly approach minimum wage or less. I'm fast, and can accomplish a decent amount in a day or two, but I can't finish an entire project of any complexity in that time, and the odds are good that what you initially request won't be what you actually need. There's a reason most projects take hundreds of thousands of dollars to complete, and that many end up in the millions. Here's a hint, though: If you could find someone to do what you're asking for $1,200, then it's probably possible for you to spend a few months learning and to piece together existing components to accomplish your goal. If you still can't even tell where to begin, then odds are good that $1,200 will be a drop in the bucket. Because the only things even marginally substantial that a freelancer can do for $1,200 are to assemble existing components (for instance, with WordPress) or to use a site builder like Wix or SquareSpace (or many other options; please don't take this as an endorsement), and you can do those yourself with only a small amount of effort. Prebuilt solutions like that have significant drawbacks, but with that kind of funding limit, it's the best you can likely do. And if you learn to do it yourself instead of hiring someone, then when you inevitably need to make changes you'll be able to make them yourself.

Question: Do rockstar software engineers dig deep and understand the implementation of programming languages and libraries that they use?
Answer: Controversial labeling aside*, the strongest engineers, in my experience, do understand at least how languages and libraries could be implemented. And often they understand the performance and memory characteristics guaranteed by the language or library as well. The phrasing “dig deep” isn't exactly how it works though. Forming a solid understanding of the fundamentals means that you can build up a mental model of how things probably work simply from the API. So it's not as if you need to spend hours reading source code of every library and programming language that you use, but instead just learning how something is intended to be used grants a mental model of how it likely works. Only when there is ambiguity do you need to dig deeper. And sometimes that digging is nothing more than checking the documentation. C++ standard library containers, for instance, let you know the expected performance and memory characteristics of each of the container options, so if you need to know the effect of a particular operation, you can look it up. That said, it's not too rare for a strong engineer to dig more deeply into a library when confronted by unusual behavior. I've submitted patches to many different open source projects either to fix bugs or to add features that I needed. One thing common to strong engineers is that we write our own code instead of relying on example code, so we're more likely to do things in ways that haven't been fully tested by the community. That means we often find obscure bugs where libraries don't work as expected. But in the general case, no, we don't dig into every tool we use. I've been using a lot of TypeScript on Node.js, for instance, but haven't tried to understand exactly how the JIT compilation of V8 works. I have read about how it works at a high level, but that was mostly out of curiosity rather than for concrete benefits. And that's the final piece of the puzzle, in my opinion. In addition to a strong grasp of the fundamentals, a strong engineer needs curiosity. You don't get to the point where you're strong if you don't have the drive to learn what you don't know about how something works. * Hardly anyone uses “rockstar” in a non-ironic manner any more. The label 10x is far more common. The other answers, as I write this, are all making fun of the term “rockstar” rather than making any attempt to answer, though at least one doesn't seem to believe that strong developers even exist, as if software engineering is the sole human endeavor where all humans are magically exactly equal in skill, unlike every other skilled endeavor from writing books to art to advanced mathematics.

Question: Does skipping unit tests give a false impression to a software engineer that they are progressing fast?
Answer: As usual, it depends. When I'm working solo on a project, I can crank out a lot of code without unit tests and without worrying about breaking things. If I do break something, I typically find out quickly and can fix the issue in minutes, so the existence of unit tests for all code doesn't actually provide much by way of benefits for me. That said, there are some routines that are sufficiently complex that I feel unit tests are valuable. I'll write them after the code, usually (so not TDD), but at that point I'm in a better position to understand what boundary conditions I need to look out for. Also, consider that I'm talking about unit tests here. Unit tests aren't system or integration tests. I do like to see system or integration test coverage of every major API entry point in any backend I'm working on, which provides a much more reliable measure of the functionality of the backend than twenty times the number of isolated unit tests. And “did someone break the code” is what I want to know. Isolated unit tests often don't reveal the breakage that fewer systems tests would catch. This is especially true if the unit tests are extensively mocked. If you've mocked all of your database and service calls, all your tests are telling you is that the types are wired up mostly correctly, which you shouldn't even need if you're using a typed language. And yes, you should be using a typed language. Not all unit tests are created equal, and some parts of the code likely don't need unit tests at all. Even if you prefer to use TDD as part of development, you'd likely be better off throwing away any unit tests that you create as part of that process if you don't think they will have a long term value for the product; otherwise the unit tests themselves become technical debt, in that instead of supporting progress they can become an impediment, often simply becoming “change detectors.” If you now need to make a change in twenty places because a new behavior is desired instead of updating two or three tests, that's another way superfluous unit tests are slowing you down. So back to the original question: Does a developer get a false impression of higher programming velocity if they skip unit tests? Not if they have coverage of systems from a higher level, and in fact they may end up with higher overall velocity over the longer term due to less technical debt.

Question: Is a software engineer constantly judged by the quality of code that they produce?
Answer: It depends a lot on the company. Some companies get it right, which means, in part, raising the overall code quality over time. This means code review, and what is code review but judgement of the quality of code? Some (many? Most?) companies really don't get it right. There are managers who aren't code savvy directing programmers, and there are no processes in place to review code before it's integrated. A developer will still be judged for poor code, but not constantly. Instead the judgement will be reserved for when their code causes problems that come to the attention of management, or that other developers are assigned to fix. When one team member who contributes for three months and then leaves the project turns out to be responsible for 80% of the bugs needing to be fixed over the next eight months (true story), then is that programmer going to be judged? I don't see how we could avoid feeling that judgment without being saints. And then there are the users of the product. If I'm using, say, the Quora app, and it operates in some unreasonable manner or has really annoying bugs that haven't been fixed in years, will I judge the programmers harshly? Yes, I will. I know there is time pressure and deadlines and so forth, but many of the problems shouldn't have existed to begin with, so yes, I judge those programmers. But are they being judged by their employer? Who knows. Maybe they are being praised for meeting deadlines and achieving goals. Not all companies actually care about quality, after all. So I guess if you're wary of being judged by your employer, you should try to join companies with crap software. Odds are good your code won't be judged by anyone who pays you, though the users might post passive-aggressive insults on the very product you're creating. Just saying.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: When and why did the humanities become viewed as inferior majors for highly motivated students?
Answer: There are brilliant students who are highly motivated in the humanities majors as well as in every other department. A highly motivated student should find the major that best fits their own aptitudes and interests and ignore those who denigrate one major or another. I think there may be several reasons for this myth, though. Someone who can excel in a STEM major can almost certainly at least pass a humanities course. It may be harder for a person with STEM skills to do good work in the humanities, and we may not do as good of a job as someone who is genuinely skilled, but we can pass the class. But the reverse isn't always true. STEM majors often have weeder classes that some percentage of students simply can't pass at all. Even simpler “intro to programming for humanities majors” classes can completely stump some students; I had a roommate in college who switched majors to avoid needing to pass such a class after making an epic attempt. I think that's the key to why STEM is seen as more rigorous; in a liberal arts college, everyone has to take humanities courses, but only the STEM majors have to take engineering courses. And the students who are a bit more challenged in the intellectual domain who are looking for a major that is easy enough for them to graduate with at all will certainly end up in the humanities. This doesn't mean that humanities majors are inferior, though. I suspect that is a rumor started by insecure STEM majors.

Question: Why aren’t developers passing coding tests despite being given lots of study resources? What gives? They look like seniors/principals on paper, then fail.
Answer: A significant fraction of the industry doesn't have the skill to qualify for senior, much less principal. But some are good enough at faking it that, at a non-technology company, they can achieve lofty titles. They can talk the talk, but they can't really walk the walk. Ever notice how questions about whether there is a programmer shortage have a mix of contradictory answers? Where some say they always find a job quickly, and others claim that they have been looking for work for a year or more but can't find a job due to “unreasonable expectations”? Yeah, same two groups: The skilled and the unskilled. You can see the pattern in the answers to this question as well. Many claim that the problems being asked are unrelated to the real world problems they need to solve. In fact, I use the same skills as a professional programmer that I do when I'm solving interview problems. If I didn't have these skills, many of my “solutions” would end up causing more problems. One comment on a similar answer claimed that all a programmer really needed to know was how to iterate over an array and how to concatenate strings. Maybe as a web developer who only creates simple web pages from database queries? But even then, really understanding the computer science side can mean the difference between a page that takes 30 seconds to load on mobile and one that is snappy. No, the objections to understanding algorithms all fall into the pattern, “I already have my hammer, and I can solve all the problems with it, so why do I need to learn how to use that screwdriver, much less any of those complicated power tools or jigs?” So that's the answer. You're trying to hire someone who is adept at the full suite of tools, and people who only know how to use a hammer keep applying, because they're the ones who are having a hard time finding any work at all, so they dominate the applications. It also might be that you're not offering enough money for the position. The good developers probably won't even talk to you if you're offering “market” rates, because the market rates for the best developers are above the market at large. Note: There also exist bad coding tests. Not every interviewer or company is competent. A good test should be an algorithm to see if you can program; something on the order of an easy Leetcode problem, and at this point they should offer some kind of IDE for you to use to code it. P. S., to those commenting how terrible coding tests are? You can see the large number of strong developers who have written comments in support of this answer. You can see the upvotes. When you comment about how wrong I am, you're basically outing yourself as a mediocre or worse software engineer. None of the questions I would approve of should be at all hard for a competent programmer. I am tired of responding directly to all of your denial, so I'll block those who employ insults and leave the rest as a wall of shame. Please, knock yourself out! Advertise how poor your skills are that you can't write a dozen lines of code without looking at a reference. And if your job isn't primarily about programming, then why are you applying for software engineer positions? That one stumps me.

Question: As a software engineering manager, how do you deal with a senior software engineer who always needs to be told what is needed to be done?
Answer: It really depends on the team size. I generally work on small teams. There's not a lot of room for people who aren't pulling their weight. Another answer suggests pairing an hour per day, and if there's another engineer who has time, that could help, at least if the problem is only around a few specific challenges. But my gut reaction is that a senior engineer who is “always” needing assistance is an engineer who was promoted to, or hired for, a senior role before they were actually qualified. At least at tech companies, the hallmark of a senior software engineer is that they can work independently. There is disagreement about many of the other details of the role, but self-direction is pretty universal. So a senior engineer who isn't hitting that threshold is exactly what “performance improvement plans” and the like were designed for. And while pairing can help, the odds are good that the engineer isn't going to be able to bridge that gap with a little guidance over a month or two. In fact, I've read something here on Quora that I believe is true: A developer with the potential to become a senior engineer is already acting like one after only one to two years of experience. Maybe they need to learn more before they're promoted, but they're already mostly working independently. On a smaller team, where we don't really have “extra” developers who can cover for the underperforming engineer, the answer is likely to be more brutal: Let them go. Odds are good they won't improve no matter how much we help them, and productivity of a senior engineer who can't carry their weight can rapidly approach zero or negative. Caveat: A new developer on a large existing code base is likely to need to be “told what to do” for potentially months if you keep sending them to new parts of the code. Especially if the code is a mess. From what I understand, many developers take months to really get up to speed. But in this case you'd see a decrease over time in the questions asked, as they got up to speed with the code patterns and architecture. So as usual, the real answer is “it depends.”

Question: How can I write scalable code? What are the best practices?
Answer: This is why we have computer science and software engineering degrees, and even graduates need years of experience to truly have the right context. You can't summarize all of the best practices down to a single Quora answer. You probably can't distill them enough to put them into a single book covering a single domain. I'm sure that such books exist, and reading good ones would probably help. But the path to scalability is understanding the problem, understanding the algorithms that can solve the problem, and understanding algorithmic complexity. Short of all of the above you're just rearranging deck chairs on the Titanic. Buy books that look relevant to your situation, and books that cover any fundamentals that you don't know. Read all the things. Also read code that already is scalable. What you need for scalability isn't patterns, it's understanding.

Question: 13 (f) who wants to be successful in life like business and has many dreams. Yet I’ve got poor motivation and I don’t know how to change that or what to do. I need someone to talk to that can change my mind-set to better. Any help or tips?

Question: In developing countries, wouldn't it make sense to push the smartest medical doctors, engineers, mathematicians, architects into political leadership positions?
Answer: In all countries, it feels like the best results would be obtained if, in order to qualify for a political position, you needed to pass psychological tests that showed you didn't really want the position for its own sake or for your own profit. The best leaders are those who lead because they're needed, not because they're trying to accumulate power. Which means they have interests and skills outside of politics. Like scientists and engineers and doctors. Today in the US at least, we're seeing the direct results of a large number of “leaders” who are clearly there 100% in pursuit of power, prestige, and profit. Who have no care for those who they govern, and instead value hurting people they don't like or respect over helping those who need it. Who retain power by lying to their base and keeping them afraid, while at the same time exploiting their ignorance to retain their power. I will refrain from naming parties in a vain attempt to discourage partisan debate in the comments, but to be clear, I don't believe the two big parties in the US are “equally bad.” One has its faults, and I could spend pages enumerating them. But the other lacks any redeeming qualities and seems to have become the party of fascism and theocracy. If we don't get the country on track, the US may be doomed to become one of the “developing countries” that needs to be run by scientists and engineers just to pull us out of our decline. Yes, there is some value to have leaders with experience being leaders. It would be nice if democracies could have some defense against being taken over by sociopaths, though.

Question: I failed a programming interview, which I feel I should have passed. I feel like a fraud after that. Should I quit programming altogether or should I just practice more?
Answer: Maybe you're trying to get answers that boost your ego and tell you it's not your fault. Well, you've gotten those answers, so let me provide another perspective. To be frank, we don't know and can't know from that information. I don't believe in encouraging everyone regardless of skill to continue to seek employment in a skill based industry. That said, failing one interview is not sufficient evidence of your skill to know if you're a “fraud,” as you put it. Everyone fails interviews. I have one of the best interview success rate I know, and toward the highest levels of programming skill, and I fail interviews. You need to have more resilience than to give up after one failure. If you told me that you'd failed 20 straight interviews, then I'd say you at least have something you need to work on. That something could be interview practice, or programming practice, or even social practice. But you implied that you really don't trust your programming skill. I can't tell you if that's impostor syndrome, or if you're really not skilled enough to succeed. Impostor syndrome is a thing, but I've been lucky enough to not be cursed with it, so I don't have much good advice for dealing with it. If you've already been working in the industry successfully, and you weren't let go for performance reasons, then odds are good you're at least good enough to work in the industry. One way to test this ”skills” hypothesis is to interview a bunch more. Another thing that could help is the book Cracking the Coding Interview. Good luck.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is there a gap between how software engineers think compilers work and how they actually work?
Answer: All abstractions are leaky. If a developer has no clue at all how a compiler, or more to the point, the low level assembly code could work, then ignorance of the lower levels can cause just as many problems as not understanding how a framework, an ORM, or even how a service like AWS could work. You don't need to implement AWS to have some idea how it would be implemented, and therefore what the drawbacks or performance characteristics might be. You don't need to step through every line of source of the ORM you're using to understand what it must be doing with respect to its actual queries. You don't need to know the implementation details of your framework to know what the performance characteristics of your design decisions might be. You don't need to know exactly how the compiler you're using works either, but knowing that it's more expensive to compare strings than integers, knowing the dangers of comparing floats, and knowing and internalizing the kinds of computational complexity a compiler can and can't help you with is extremely useful in creating code that isn't unintentionally pessimized (the opposite of optimized). Treating any aspect of infrastructure or your tools as magical black boxes is a path to creating code disasters, because if you don't understand what you're doing, you're far more likely to make stupid mistakes.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How often do you think about computational complexity in your software solutions?
Answer: I can't not think about computational complexity. That doesn't mean that I do the most complicated algorithm I can come up with because it's fastest. Some data is guaranteed to be a small enough n that the exact algorithm will never matter, and readability totally trumps optimization in that case. In fact, some kinds of “optimization” will hurt performance if you always have a small n . I also think about computational complexity when designing a database schema. Taking into account what will be needed when and why can mean multiple orders of magnitude of performance difference. I've even seen the effects of computational complexity in frontend code. In an attempt to keep components completely isolated, it's really common to see each section of a site doing its own queries, and if one section relies on the results of another, you can end up with a so-called N + 1 query pattern, which can hurt performance significantly even for relatively small n . If you want to be a software engineer, you need to think about performance. If you don't, then the work you're doing is likely to be outsourced to an AI in the next decade. No AI can replace a developer who is capable of understanding the problem they're working on, but if all you're doing is mindlessly connecting components? That's exactly the kind of work that can be automated. In fact, with the Github “code completion” tool it already is predominantly automated, as long as you have at least one developer who does know what they're doing involved. Learn your computational complexity. Internalize it to the point where your brain just naturally sees the complexity of everything you write. Understand your tools. Keep learning. This is an industry with high demand, but that also has high standards, at least at some companies, and I imagine that some people reading this question are wondering whether they need to learn about (or refresh their knowledge of) computational complexity. There do exist jobs that don't have that as a requirement for certain, but those are the same jobs that you're competing with every bootcamp graduate for. If you want to stand out, you should strive to be better.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Why is MySQL used rather than NoSQL MongoDB?
Answer: I agree with Adam D’Angelo’s post from 10 years ago, where he describes why MySQL can be scaled manually using partitioning, though to be fair I think MongoDB has improved in stability since then: There are other options than MongoDB for automatic horiztontal scaling today as well. CockroachDB and YugabyteDB are both full SQL databases that can scale their load as well as MongoDB and they can perform JOINs across shards. There’s an extension for PostgreSQL that enables automatic sharding as well (search for “CitusData”—links outside of Quora seem to flag answers as spam at this point). There are really very few advantages to using MongoDB. I’ve also written elsewhere on Quora about why MongoDB doesn’t really live up to its hype: MongoDB is often touted as having two major advantages: The ability to have a flexible schema and the ability to scale horizontally. I’ve touched on the second above, but for the first point, PostgreSQL and MySQL both have JSON data types to support flexible schema components, giving you the power of SQL and a flexible schema in the same database. Today, PostgreSQL is used in more new custom backend projects than MySQL, in my experience, for a number of reasons. Among the strongest developers and architects I work with it’s simply the default choice because of its increased power and better conformance to the SQL standard, and under most loads it’s as fast as or faster than MySQL now, so there are few advantages to using MySQL. Oracle purchased MySQL as well, meaning that it’s no longer considered fully “free” by some, while PostgreSQL is a completely free and open source solution. (Yes, MariaDB exists as a fork, but again, PostgreSQL has its other advantages.) In my opinion, MongoDB was a bridge technology: It existed for a time to ease horizontal scaling complexity, and now it’s obsolete as a result of better and more powerful tools that can do what it promised and much, much more. MongoDB is the fax machine of databases, in other words: Very useful for a short time until newer technologies turned it into a dinosaur, but still used in those niches where it was firmly established. At this point Mongo’s continued popularity is largely due to momentum and the ease of learning MongoDB compared to SQL—at any time, roughly half of all developers have less than five years of experience (the number of developers doubles every five years), and so there are many who value ease-of-learning over actual utility and leverage of tools. So existing projects that already use Mongo aren’t likely to change, and developers without much experience with SQL find it easier to learn (and then recommend) MongoDB. It’s better to learn SQL and database theory than to choose MongoDB for a new project today and advertise the fact that you don’t know how to use SQL.
