Question: Which programming language produces binaries that are the most difficult to reverse engineer?
Answer: Probably anything that goes through a modern optimization backend like gcc or LLVM. And note that gcc is now the GNU Compiler Collection, a backronym that they came up with after adding a number of frontend languages. In addition to C, there are frontends for C++, Objective-C, Objective-C++, Fortran, Ada, D, and Go, plus others that are less mature. LLVM has even more options. The Wikipedia page lists ActionScript, Ada, C#, Common Lisp, PicoLisp, Crystal, CUDA, D, Delphi, Dylan, Forth, Fortran, Free Basic, Free Pascal, Graphical G, Halide, Haskell, Java bytecode, Julia, Kotlin, Lua, Objective-C, OpenCL, PostgreSQL's SQL and PLpgSQL, Ruby, Rust, Scala, Swift, XC, Xojo and Zig. I don't even know what all of those languages are. In some cases they may include enough of a runtime to make it easier to reverse engineer the underlying code (I'm guessing the Lisp dialects and Haskell would, among others), but in general, once compiled to a target architecture with maximum optimization, all of the above would be more or less equally difficult to reverse engineer. Languages that are more rare (like Zig) may have an advantage by virtue of doing things differently enough that existing decompilers would have trouble. But that's only an incremental increase in difficulty. There exist libraries that you can add to a binary to make it much more difficult to reverse engineer. Tools that prevent trivial disassembly or that make code fail if run in a debugger, for instance. If you really need to protect code that you have to distribute, then using one of those products might be appropriate. But overall the only way to be sure that no one can reverse engineer your code (aside from nuking it from orbit, which has the negative side effect of eliminating your customer base) is to never distribute your code: Run anything proprietary on servers and only allow people with active accounts to use it. Generally, though? 99.9% of code isn't worth reverse engineering. If you're not being paid by some large company doing groundbreaking research (and you're not if you would ask this question) then no one will ever bother to reverse engineer your code. This is a really, really frequent “noob” question, though: Because it was so hard for a new developer to write an app, they fear someone will steal the code and use it in their own app. As if anyone would want to steal code written by a junior developer. 🙄 More to the point, stealing your app and distributing it illegally can generally be done without reverse engineering it at all; I guarantee that many apps on the Play Store are hacked and republished with different art without the thieves even slightly understanding how the app works. It's only if you embed some kind of copy protection/DRM into your app that they'd even need to hack it, and if you're not clever about how you add the DRM, hacking it won't take much effort or any decompiling at all. If you can point a debugger at the code, you can simply walk through the assembly language and find where it does the DRM check—and disable it. I managed to figure out how to do this as a teen, on my own, pre-Internet (for research purposes, of course). I guarantee I'm not unique or even that skilled at it, but start to finish I disabled DRM in a couple hours at most. So generally, don't even bother worrying about how difficult something is to reverse engineer. No one cares to see your code, and you can't stop them from hacking the app if you add DRM. So unless you can keep your unique code on a server and charge a subscription, count on the fact that if your app gets popular, it will be stolen. People will also share subscription accounts, so you need to worry about that as well when you design your server architecture.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Why do programming interviews require strong competitive programming skills rather than good software development skills?
Answer: Before you ask why, ask whether. Do programming interviews require strong competitive programming skills? The point of a programming challenge in an interview isn't to demonstrate competitive programming skills. It's to demonstrate that you can program. You don't need to be able to rank on Leetcode to get a job, but you do need to know how to create code. That is part of the job description, after all. And who says that they aren't requiring good software development skills? In stronger tech companies at least, I've always been asked questions that probe my software engineering skills in addition to any coding challenges. Aside: Reading other answers, I get the sense that there may exist non-tech, consulting, or outsourcing companies that really only have you answer competitive programming challenges. I doubt that is universal, but it could be a contributing factor as to why outsourcing is so commonly awful, as well as why most non-tech companies have such awful software. “Enterprise development” is mocked for a reason, after all. But back to the original point: They don't force you to write Quicksort in college because you'll need to implement it in your career. You write Quicksort because it's an example of a non-trivial algorithm, and you're demonstrating that you can write non-trivial algorithms. The entire point of hiring programmers is so that they can create novel algorithms. All code is algorithms. There are programmers who understand how to write a more complex algorithm, and those who copy and paste algorithms from the internet and then loosely glue them together. The latter is profoundly worse than the former, and so companies that are aware of this fact will require that an applicant demonstrate programming ability. There clearly exist a large number of software developers in the industry who actually lack most of the basic skills and aptitude to be a competent programmer. That's why we have to ask applicants to prove their ability. If there are companies that rely completely on competitive programming ranking for hiring, or require that you've memorized a ton of specific algorithms in order to pass their tests? Well, as with the outsourcing companies, it's probably because they don't know any better methods, and they've heard that FAANG companies have programming challenges, so that's what they use, and without any real understanding of why or which problems to select. There's a saying in the industry: “A developers hire A developers. B developers hire C developers.” If you have a non-expert attempting to hire experts, then they don't have the context they need to judge potential hires. And a lot of companies hiring people are not run by technology experts, so they use the only measure they can understand—a score on a test. I generally focus on the competent technology company side of the industry because that's what I'm familiar with. I guess it would be ironic if I tried to apply at a non-tech company and was rejected because I didn't know some specific algorithm for their programming test, even though I have passed FAANG interviews. That hasn't actually come up, though, and I am almost entirely a freelancer at this point, so I don't think it will.

Question: A private company asks your software company to develop a database of information obtained from government records. Would you accept the contract and develop the system? Explain the options/alternatives you have and justify them.
Answer: This question smells of being a homework problem. You won't learn anything if you post your homework problems on Quora and use someone else's answer. Worse, it seems like a question from some kind of course on ethics. Someone who would cheat on homework for an ethics class…let's just say that I may have a guess as to why they're being forced to take an ethics class. Finally, the question doesn't actually contain all the relevant information. There are tons of public records that are legal to acquire and index. There are also records that are free and legal to acquire but restricted in how you can use them. There are records you can pay to acquire from the government as well, with various restrictions placed on what you can do with the data. And there are government records that are illegal to possess. What kinds of data are we talking about? And what country are we in? Laws about public data certainly vary by jurisdiction. Presumably we'd know from the context of the question if we were taking the class. If it's not homework? Then you should think more carefully about what information someone would need to answer your questions. And you shouldn't make rude demands of the people kind enough to answer those questions for free, as you did in the last sentence of your question. Not unless you're paying someone to do research for you. There are a range of answers possible depending on the details. I personally wouldn't work on anything that didn't align with my own sense of ethics, but if a company were indexing legally acquired traffic data for purposes of making recommendations for road changes with an eye to reduce pollution, for instance? What could possibly be wrong with that? Of course I would only accept the contract if it were appropriately compensated. I do need to eat, after all.

Question: Any good advice/insight about hiring mobile developer who are good bang for the buck (smart and competent enough with good judgement but doesn't have firm premium price wise) locally or via online?
Answer: There's a conflict in your request. You see, most of the best developers, the ones you really want to hire, and the ones who are the absolute best bang for the buck? Those developers tend to also have premium prices. This isn't a contradiction. If a really good developer can spend an hour doing exactly the right thing, creating code that is easy to modify, having understood your requirements due to carefully discussing them with you, then they've spent one hour of your contracting time to achieve a good result. Compare to the developer who costs 1/5 at much, and who then takes five hours to produce inferior code that doesn't actually satisfy your requirements, so they need to spend another five hours replacing that code with code that actually does what you need. If you're lucky. I've seen this pattern repeat four and five times, to the point where I begin to wonder if they're intentionally working on the wrong solution, or if they're really that incompetent. Software is expensive to produce. There is no silver bullet that will get you a good product for cheap. The only real exception is if you find a new developer who is brilliant and naive, and you take advantage of them. Hint: If you're willing to do that, it doesn't reflect well on your morality or ethics. If you convince a kid straight out of college to accept a (large!) share of your company in exchange for working for less money, that's a different story, but the question phrasing makes it sound like you're looking for someone to cheat out of a fair wage for their labor. And that's not cool. So acquire the funding to actually pay your developers a fair wage, or pivot to a new business plan. Any attempt at working with an outsourcing team that will “make your product for cheap” is likely to end in pain. The scammers outnumber the genuine outsourcing teams by seemingly thousands to one, and the better outsourcing teams will seem really “expensive” by comparison, even though the reality is they're quoting you the real price of creating an application vs. selling a fantasy low price to get your business and then pumping you for money until you give up.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is functional programming designed to waste programmer time on theory and subjective beauty instead of writing another practical program?
Answer: Designed to? No, of course not. Does it waste time on theory? Only for those who feel the need to wax philosophical about category theory and endofunctors, or those who are trolled into trying to understand what that group is actually talking about. Is it subjectively beautiful? That depends on what you're trying to use it for. When you can use functional libraries to transform data, it can be extremely clean code that's almost certainly correct. That's beautiful, at least to me. But when you try to take that beauty to the extreme in a pure functional language? I'm sure if the app you're developing matches the functional model in an elegant way, it can still be beautiful. But the problem comes when your app needs to do more than a few things. And all hell breaks loose when you also need to add animations. Some applications are inherently stateful. Worse, they would really benefit from aspects of OO development, but those in the pure functional camp have typically thrown OO out with all things stateful, meaning that the app code will be awkward and unsafe compared to an OO implementation. The real world isn't pure and clean. It's usually messy, in fact. Using a language that's capable of using functional techniques but that also supports other paradigms can not only get you to a finished product more quickly, but it can also make that product more robust and easy to extend than if you jump through the pure functional hoops in an app that doesn't match that paradigm.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: As a software engineering manager what would you do when a highly skillful software engineer in your team habitually deletes code developed by other developers and writes their own implementation which is much more superior?
Answer: This is a skilled developer who is otherwise getting their assigned work done and working as a team player? And the changes are really improvements and not just minor aesthetic changes? Then I’d encourage them to work on communication skills, and possibly encourage individual team members to not feel as proprietary about their code. Beyond that, poor question grammar aside, it sounds like you’re asserting that the replacement implementation is superior to the code that’s been replaced. Unlike other takes on this, I’m going to say that if a developer is reducing overall technical debt on a project without impacting their ability to get their assigned work done, that’s a good thing. But at the same time, since this question comes up at all, there must be some kind of conflict. What comes to mind is that other team members are feeling offended by this developer’s actions. So where are the communication issues I mentioned? The developer should take many of these changes as opportunities to teach other team members better ways to approach problems. Just changing code every time they see it isn’t the “correct” structure actually makes more work for them, and ideally they should be motivated to teach their techniques to other team members. Now I wouldn’t demand heroic attempts to teach the rest of the team; some programmers are less amenable to learning from coworkers, and if they aren’t interested in learning, that’s their issue. As to the likely motivation for this question: You aren’t your code. Developers need to realize that, once their code has been released to the team that others may come in and change it. If you’re going to be on a team with a skilled developer and you don’t want to hamstring that developer, then you need to put on your big-boy or big-girl pants and accept that sometimes your code will be improved when this developer happens to make changes in its vicinity. Now if the developer is spending half of the week going through and rewriting every line of code released by the remainder of the team? Or if the extra rewriting is causing their own responsibilities to slip? That’s a problem. And if the project doesn’t have sufficient test coverage that you can be confident that any changes made by the skilled developers are producing substantially the same (or better) results? That’s a different problem. But if the project has sufficient coverage that rewrites of blocks of code are known to produce valid results when they’re complete, and the developer is able to quickly rewrite the blocks of code required to work on the tasks they’re working on anyway? I see absolutely no reason to ask them to stop, and anyone who has a knee-jerk response to tell them to stay in their lane should not be surprised when all of their skilled developers leave the team for greener pastures.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is it hard to build a good app if you don't have a good idea or money to hire a developer?
Answer: Is it hard? You don’t have a good idea, which means what? You have no idea what to build? You don’t have money to hire a developer, either? And presumably you don’t have the skill to build an app yourself? And you’re asking is it hard?! Sounds pretty well impossible to me given those constraints. You want to build an app yourself, but don’t know how to program? Look for no-code and low-code solutions and learn one. Play around with it until you’ve build several “apps” (they’ll be pretty trivial) and have a sense of what you can do with the no-code/low-code solution you choose. Then brainstorm for an idea that you can accomplish using those tools. Then at least you have a chance of getting the good idea you’ll need at a minimum to build a good app.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Who makes more money in freelancing, a graphic designer or a coder?
Answer: A person skilled in graphic design can make more money at graphic design than doing a crappy job at coding, or taking race-to-the-bottom “low skill” coding gigs. (Hint: There are tons of people offering $10/hour “coding” services.) A person skilled in software engineering can make more money doing software development freelance jobs than a typical graphic designer can make. If you're skilled in both, then “software development and design” can pay quite well. But it's more likely the skills and aptitudes you have that should determine which path you take. You won't do anyone any good if you try to freelance at a task you're not actually skilled at. And you can't learn either graphic design or software engineering overnight. Either will probably take at least two years of learning and practice before you're actually qualified to freelance. Good luck.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is becoming good at Googling a skill that every software engineer must develop?
Answer: Googling is a core life skill at this point. But is it necessary to learn software engineering? Obviously not! Many of us learned how to program well before Google was an option. In fact, I'd propose that learning to program without Google makes you stronger. So many posts and answers imply that programmers can't survive without Google or StackOverflow. It's a common programming meme, in fact. I can tell you right now, though, that there's zero possibility that most short blocks of code could possibly be found and modified as fast as a strong programmer can type in the correct code. And that correct code can be better than the first block of example code you happen to come across in your search. I can't tell you for certain that learning to code without Google will make your stronger. But I can tell you that strong programmers barely use Google for much more than obscure error messages and for finding docs. And any actual skill “at Googling” is more about learning the proper keywords to find what you need. But that skill is a very small part of what you need to learn to become a programmer.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Are 10x programmers naturally geniuses or did they just practice a lot to get to that level?
Answer: I wouldn't use the word “genius.” In addition to being poorly defined, at least in common usage, I'm not sure that full-on genius is required to be 10x. Instead, I usually use the word aptitude. A 10x developer was born with the correct aptitude for software development. Would love to see some good studies on this; I suspect there may be multiple relevant aptitudes, and that the more you have, the better your performance can be, and the more domains in which you can be 10x. Because all 10x really means, when you come down to it, is that you can quickly analyze problems and write out exactly, or nearly exactly, the right code. There are a ton of problems and domains where I can do that. And I've encountered a few where I'm no better than anyone else with domain experience, but others with different aptitudes were able to write out exactly the code required. So that's one thing I'd like to point out: 10x isn't just a binary state. A developer may be 10x in their core domain(s), and 1x in other domains. Even within a domain, as complexity increases, a 10x developer can drop down to 1x in speed and skill. (Which is why it's always good to minimize complexity. But I digress…) As with most human traits, aptitude exists on multiple axes. On the second part of your question: I know that I needed to spend a lot of time to learn to program, but I'm not sure that I practiced any more than most developers as they learned. Programming just came to me easier than for most of my peers, and I may have even needed to practice less. I know I worked really hard for the first year or so, but after that I was just stronger than, well, most everyone I encountered. There was still plenty for me to learn, but that just improved my skills. I did write code a lot after I'd learned, but that's natural when you've discovered you're good at something and not how I became good. One last thought: I have a suspicion that some developers could be 10x, or at least more capable than they are now, if they were to force themselves to do more “programming thinking” rather than pulling all answers from StackOverflow. The strongest developers I know all do their own thinking about software development, and few use StackOverflow for more than tracking down obscure problems or as a substitute for documentation. There is a chance that some people today may be leaning too much on the internet for help, and therefore not forming the necessary neural pathways to get really good. So there may be a grain of truth to the idea that people aren't working hard enough—though I suspect that aptitude is still a factor, since even back when I was learning and there was no StackOverflow, the dropout rate from CS was extremely high.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Do some software engineers focus too much on becoming a “10x” programmer?
Answer: Probably? But not because they shouldn't improve themselves. Your goal should be to improve yourself to the best of your ability. Be the strongest developer you can be. There is plenty of room in the industry for many levels of skill, and if you're doing your best to maximize your own personal potential, that is as much as you can hope for. I do think many developers are not trying hard enough to realize their potential, though. I've had comments here on Quora where someone was asking me “how did I gain my skills.” I always have to respond that, to some degree, it has to be some flavor of aptitude that sets me apart. But, there was a period of time where I wrote a lot of code with little help from others. I was forced by my circumstances to do my own thinking. That may be a necessary component? With help available on the internet for every little question you might have, and code to copy from StackOverflow, many people today may not get the practice in “how to think like a programmer” that everyone was forced to back when I learned. And that's the key difference in programming skill, from what I can tell. The ability to model complex interactions in software in your head is what allows you to write code 10x faster than others—because you can simply write out code and it works, or mostly so, almost all of the time. The more complexity you can model, the more problems you can type out that will just work when you're done. So if you want to have a chance at developing at 10x speed, take off the training wheels and code increasingly complex tasks without StackOverflow to help you. Try to picture what's happening in your code, and do what you can to get everything to work the first time. As I said above, I don't know that this is actually a prerequisite, but it is something a “10x” developer can do, and so directly practicing it might help. As I implied above, older developers had no choice but to do this. It could take a half hour between writing code and being able to test it, and another half hour before I could be editing code again, and I didn't have a debugger or even a console to print out debug messages to. The code would either work or it wouldn't, and I had to determine why it failed simply by observing its behavior. I had no choice whether or not I modeled the code in my head: If I couldn't form an accurate model, my game would never work. And at the time, I simply didn't consider failure to be an option. So give it a try. Code like it's 1985 (but with better tools), and make your brain work harder. It may be the only way to improve your skill. Just stop worrying about labels like 10x.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How many hours does a senior programmer study per day?
Answer: Study implies direction. Like there's a curriculum that we're working our way through or something. I will spend maybe a 15–30 minutes in a day glancing at Hacker News to see what new technologies people are talking about. If there's something that catches my eye, I might read about it (or follow links down a rabbit hole) for another 15–30 minutes. Sometimes I'll learn something new in that process. I've also gone through periods of listening to software engineering podcasts regularly. That happened a lot more when I had a regular commute, but sometimes I just feel like listening to podcasts again. Sometimes I'll learn something new that way. Periodically I'll work with technology that I don't know every corner of yet, and I'll spend time in docs to learn how to accomplish something new. I'll certainly learn new things that way. When I'm working with a larger team, there are often other developers who do things differently than I would have. I'll often adopt their methods. That certainly counts as learning. And occasionally I'll come across a genuinely complex problem that I feel could use a bit of more obscure CS knowledge to solve in an optimal manner, and I'll do research and/or ask questions of relevant experts to see if there are existing algorithms that are relevant. I'll almost certainly learn something in that process. So when we say that senior programmers need to constantly be learning, that doesn't mean that we set aside “study time.” We just do things that seem interesting to us, and approach life and work with curiosity. It means we don't feel that the things we learned in college and our first job are the end of our education. That we never simply copy and paste code we don't completely understand, because we're driven to know how our software works. That we don't accept extremely repetitive work as inevitable, and instead look for ways to automate that work away—even when that automation requires that we dig for the proper tool to use. We don't just sit around “doing what we're told.” We are just driven to learn the next thing because it's interesting. P. S., I anticipate that some programmers will be motivated to post irate comments about how “Some of us have lives!” This is a common theme for comments on related topics on Quora, and I have this to say to you: Please write your own answer that explains how you, and people like you, learn new things instead of trying to argue with my experience. If it works differently for you, then please, enlighten us…in your own answer. And if you never learn new things? Then I almost certainly wouldn't consider you a senior programmer as much as a junior or mid-level programmer with X years of experience, and if you don't want to out yourself as a mediocre developer, you probably shouldn't post to say that you haven't needed to learn new things in X years. Just saying.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: This may not be a very easy question to answer, but what is the minimum amount of programming I need to know to write a game? I know it would depend on the quality and complexity of the game.
Answer: Think of it this way: What's the minimum amount of Spanish you'd need to learn in order to write a novel in Spanish? (Assuming you don't know Spanish already) You'd likely need to know all of the grammar, and most of the common words, but you'd also need to look up more words that you weren't sure of. But that's not a complete analogy, because you've presumably already read novels and have a general idea how a novel is shaped, but when writing a game, you also need to understand how to assemble the parts and ensure they will work well together. So to extend our analogy, let's say that the novel you're writing also needs to be written in iambic pentameter. That's the meter that Shakespeare used, and while anyone can do it, to do it well takes skill, practice, and much more effort, at least at first. Oh, and imagine that if the novel has even the slightest plot hole, the whole thing will fail. There's no way to quantify “the minimum amount of programming to write a game.” As far as knowledge of the main programming language, you really need to know all of it (except for C++, for which you'd need to learn some complete subset of the language, though for anyone who would ask a question like this, I would just recommend not using C++). The libraries associated with a language you can learn as you go, but the core language is important to just understand. And as for techniques that you'll need to learn to write your game? That depends 100% on the nature of the game. But here's the real trick: Stop procrastinating and just start trying to write your game. First you should pick a game engine, and then look at tutorials. Pick an engine with tutorials as close as possible to the game you want to write. You can learn as you go. Type in as much of the code as you can instead of copying and pasting. You'll learn much more quickly that way. Now get busy! I expect you to give me a status report in two weeks. The clock is ticking. 😉

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Do some software engineers fall into the trap of copying code from Stack Overflow that solves their problem without understanding how the code actually works?
Answer: I think that “copying code” is extremely rare among stronger developers, but it seemingly must be something that happens given the number of memes that reference it. I've also seen people post that “it's faster to copy the code than to write it.” This frankly shocks me. I can't even imagine how a search for the exact bit of code that you need could possibly be faster than just writing the code. I mean, there do exist some pretty hairy algorithms that would be hard to get right in one go. And if you can't find a library, then in those rare cases starting with working code might make sense. But I'm talking a once per year kind of exceptional experience, if that. And given that I've also seen people claim that all software developers really need to know is how to iterate over lists and concatenate strings, I really doubt any of the really complex algorithms are what people are picking up. So hear's the deal: If it's faster for a developer to look up the code than to write it, what are the odds they will actually be able to fully understand it? They didn't write it, so they certainly don't understand it as well as if they did write it. One final note: A few times recently I've seen a comparison between copying and pasting code and using libraries. It's profoundly different from using a library. A library I would choose would: I think that one of the major anti-patterns common in the PHP world is to copy and paste code in preference to installing libraries. You end up with millions of copy-pasted security holes that are literally millions of times more difficult to find and fix. So no, it's not the same by any stretch. Copying code from StackOverflow is an anti-pattern. Looking at code to see how a library or method is intended to be used is fine. Looking for docs on a language is fine. I'm not against using the internet as a reference.

Question: Should I use MERN stack or Next.js?
Answer: Next.js, because you probably shouldn't use MongoDB. Tim Mensch's answer to Is MongoDb ideal for big scale projects? Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How do web programmers divide the running part of code between the server-side and the client-side more efficiently nowadays? Is it always better to run more code on the server-side if too many requests are coming?
Answer: That's two very different questions. Second part first: That's pretty much exactly wrong. If you want to scale more easily, then you want to run as little code on the server as possible. As to how to “divide” the code? That's a matter of design, and the accumulated wisdom developers gain that grants them the intuition to ensure the right code is in the right place. You need to understand the goals of the system you're creating. And that includes the security requirements. When you understand what you need to create, how to “divide” the code becomes obvious. And until you understand what you need to create, no pithy advice that can be offered on Quora will help.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How common is it to have weak engineers on a team?
Answer: It varies a lot by industry and between companies. I've been on teams where none of the members could be considered weak. I've encountered some teams where it seemed everyone on the team was weak. And every permutation in between. The worst offenders are often smaller non-technology companies where a non-technical manager hires one or more developers to work on their web site. There's a saying that “A developers hire other A developers, while B developers hire C developers.” It's very rare for a team to ever get a really strong developer when it's dominated by weak developers. The reality of software engineering is that the demand for developers exceeds the supply, or at least the supply of strong or average developers. And someone who isn't an expert won't be able to tell a weak developer from a strong one. Even experts may eventually need to hire someone to fill a role. Not all tasks require strong developers, after all.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Do Docker and Kubernetes make obsolete all conventional web design in the near future due to fast response speed?
Answer: Docker is a container technology. Kubernetes is a container orchestration technology that helps you run code on your servers. Web design involves HTML, CSS, and maybe JavaScript or a language that compiles to JavaScript, but more to the point, it runs on your web client. There are a ton of ways to make web pages more responsive. None have to do with Docker or Kubernetes, at least not directly. If you're talking about the architecture of the servers that serve the web pages? In the modern JAMstack, depending on your needs, you may actually want your HTML, CSS, and optional JavaScript to be hosted on a CDN. That's how you get the best response speed. Note that in neither case did I mention containers. In fact, the code that generates pages could even run in cloud functions, or offline where it uploads the newest files to a server like S3, no containers necessary. Alternatively, having your servers or functions that generate pages cached by a CDN is the second best option. If you're talking about API servers that the web page relies on? That at least would be reasonable to run in Docker and Kubernetes, but that's just one option of many. Docker and Kubernetes allow you to deploy and potentially scale your servers, but they don't actually make the servers faster. For some operations they will actually be slower than running your servers directly on hardware instead of in containers. Don't get me wrong. I love Docker. I find Kubernetes to be really useful. I typically use them both with every project. But I make that decision based on actual benefits, including enabling scaling of servers by allowing Kubernetes to actually request more VMs whenever the load becomes too high on the existing servers. Cool features, yes. But not directly to do with response speed. Only indirectly via autoscaling, and technically you don't need either Docker containers or Kubernetes to achieve autoscaling. One modern alternative I'm aware of is Nomad, which can autoscale with containers or with direct hardware.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Would I be fine taking cognitive science major even though I’ve never had any experience in science, math, or CS field?
Answer: This is a question you should be asking of an advisor at the university where you're considering applying to the cognitive science major. The answer will depend on your goals in taking cognitive science, as well as the requirements for the program itself. I majored in cognitive science at UCSD, and I leaned heavily on the science track, but I remember there were other options. What I don't know is how much of the computer science track I took was mandatory. There was one “weeder” computer science class that I took that would have filtered out anyone without the right aptitude. The requirements may have changed significantly since I graduated as well, so whether it was mandatory for me doesn't say anything about the degree requirements today. Talk to someone who can ask you key questions to determine the answer for your situation. Generic questions without enough information to answer them help no one.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How is getting into programming-heavy occupations even possible off of being purely self-taught if computer science in college is infamously difficult?
Answer: I would hypothesize that most strong developers are effectively self taught, and that those who also have a CS degree are enriched by the experience rather than taught how to program in college. Even the college experience didn't really ”teach” programming as much as saying “here are problems—go solve them.” Anecdotally, I have found this to be near universal. I did almost all of the computer science sequence plus a couple of the harder electives (compiler design, for instance). My degree says cognitive science, but I effectively learned everything in the CS degree as well. I didn't find most of it to be hard at all. Computer science degrees are hard for some people. And getting a degree simply isn't that hard for others. Some are born with or develop an aptitude that allows them to understand the fundamentals without much work. Others have a harder time. Al Klein mentions music skill as an analogy, which seems really apt. I actually love playing piano, but I will never be a pianist. I could put in the same amount of effort as a professional musician, and maybe I'd get to be decent that way, but I know I just don't have the right aptitude for music performance. I doubt I'd even be able to put in that many hours without my brain eating itself: I just don't have the patience. Visual arts are another example. I tried to learn to draw when I was younger, but even my very best efforts were underwhelming. I've spoken to artists who insist that all you have to do is practice, but I've also seen the results of extreme amounts of practice, and it can vary from decent illustration to amazing creations at a young age. Aptitude has to be a defining factor. Software engineering isn't just learning a language and typing code. It's systems design and visualization of complex interactions and understanding what's going on at a deep level. It has a creative component that many don't recognize, and it requires a very logical thought process. It's an art and a science and a craft. And someone who teaches themselves how to program and who spends the time to learn the computer science concepts, and who has the right aptitude? They would be as skilled or more so than a college graduate with the CS degree. So that's why some companies will hire them even without a degree.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Will employers totally not consider you for an interview the moment you fail a coding test?
Answer: If you fail a coding test, and the job requires programming skill? That's probably a hard no from the employer. No one will consider you for a job that you've just demonstrated that you can't do. The only exception that comes to mind is if they gave multiple tests, you passed some, and then they gave a more advanced test that was beyond your current experience which you failed. In that case it's possible that they were trying to determine if they were going to offer you a junior or a full programmer position. Depending on how badly you failed, they might only offer you junior at that point. But if it was the first screening test, and it was something really simple? Then failing you is doing you a favor. Programming jobs require that you know how to code. If you don't know enough to write code for a very simple problem, then you're not ready for a programming job. Keep learning. Keep practicing. Focus on a single language so that you don't get confused by syntax or patterns from several. If you have done all of that and have been learning for years and still can't solve simple problems, then it's time to consider pivoting to another career goal. Software engineering isn't for everyone. Don't give up early; or does take time to learn. And don't ignore algorithms and data structures; learning them on your own can take the place of a degree, but do learn them. But if you've been trying and failing for two years or more, then do yourself a favor and pivot to a new career goal. It's not about how hard you've worked, nor is it a personal failing. It just never really clicks for some people. Unfortunately, the bootcamp industry and the popular press frequently imply that “anyone can learn to program.” This is only true in the same sense that “anyone can learn to write” is true: Not everyone can learn to write well enough to be a professional editor or novelist or technical writer. Choose your career wisely. Good luck.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Why is Stack Overflow so overwhelmingly hostile?
Answer: It's not. There's a saying that if everyone is treating you badly, that maybe you should consider whether you're the one being an asshole. And I would be willing to bet that whoever asked this is talking about asking low-effort beginner questions and having someone treat them badly. But by going to StackOverflow and asking a question that you didn't even bother to search for an answer for, that you didn't make the first attempt to understand what is happening, that you didn't post even a fraction of what was necessary to answer the question? That was actually you being rude. StackOverflow pretty much has every beginner question in every on every popular topic answered, probably at least three ways. If you're a beginner and you're considering posting a question, instead search some more. If you don't find anything, then ask your teacher. If you don't have a teacher, get a teacher, because StackOverflow isn't the right place to ask for help as a beginner. Beginners simply don't know enough to know what they need to ask. There's effectively an infinite number of ways a beginner can misunderstand software development, and the model of professionals volunteering their time to write answers on obscure topics doesn't scale to them answering questions for millions of beginners. Yes there are jerks on the internet. Sometimes they will post harassment even on good questions. But 99% of the time a good question will get a friendly answer.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: A question for software engineers: how often do you Google how to code something during your daily work?
Answer: How to code something? Very rarely. There are times when I'm working on a new library or framework, and Google may be better at finding docs than the canonical doc page. Or I might start with a working skeleton app so I can avoid all of the setup boilerplate. But after I'm up and running, it goes back to rarely. There are times when I'm trying to do something that I don't do every day and I similarly find the docs page through the use of Google rather than searching directly. PostgreSQL table migration is the most common search, since I don't write enough SQL to have all corners of the syntax memorized. But both of those are syntax, really, not “how to code something.” Almost all of the time I know exactly what I need to code, just not the specific syntax. In fact, the memes about “StackOverflow is down; programmers everywhere can't work” never really resonated. Yes, sometimes there's a weird error message that I will Google to try to track down a root cause in less time than a brute force search. Again, that mostly happens during setup, but it can happen at other times. Ultimately, other than when I'm starting a new project or working in an unfamiliar domain, I might Google something once every week or so. I would expect that to be true of most competent developers with more than a few years of experience.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How do you deal with a technical interviewer who just wants to show off how smart they are?
Answer: Apparently I end up arguing with them. I don't necessarily recommend the approach. OK, here's what happened. I refer to this experience as “the worst interview of my career.” Apologies if you've read my story about this elsewhere on Quora. It started badly: I was late. I didn't realize how far the interview location was from BART (this was in San Francisco), and it took me far longer to walk than I expected. So I started out off balance. Then the interviewer presented me with a puzzle. You know, the kind that are no longer in fashion because they test more for IQ than for actual job skills. The funny thing was that I'd just seen the exact same puzzle two days before at a different interview, where I'd nailed it immediately, and instead of going through the same thought process, I tried to remember the answer. Bad idea; between being out of breath and flustered from being late, I couldn't remember the answer. So I had to work my way through it slowly and deliberately, eventually getting to the answer. I may have even needed hints. Ironically this may have helped my case somewhat. I'll explain below. Next, he asked me to write a factorial function. I wrote the standard recursive code out quickly. He then asked if I could write it without recursion, and this is where things went really south. I said something like “yes, but I wouldn't for this function.” Well, it turns out the interviewer had, at one time, written a recursive function that had taken a ridiculous amount of time to run compared to the iterative version, and he therefore had decided that made recursion bad in all cases. He was absolutely convinced of this wisdom. But stupidly, I had to argue about it. You see, factorial gets big. Quickly. If I needed to make a factorial function that returned 32-bit integers faster, I would have used memoization (effectively a lookup table generated at runtime), since it would only need to remember 12 values (13! Is larger than an int32 can hold). So it seemed silly to write code to optimize a function that I could write a couple lines of code to create a much much better optimization for. But no, he was certain that his answer was correct, and wanted to prove to me that he knew what he was talking about because of the bad recursive algorithm he'd written in the past. One other curious thing that I remember from the interview was that he wanted to know exactly when I started programming. I was older than he was, you see, and it seemed he felt that he needed to have “more programming experience” than me in order to manage me. Well, yes, since he started programming at 7 and I started at 13, it turned out he'd started before I did. This actually satisfied him, as if the 15 subsequent years of experience we'd each had meant little. Pretty sure there were a couple more disasters in that interview, but it was roughly two decades ago at this point, and those were the only frustrations that managed to stick in my memory. Oddly enough I ended up getting a call back about the job, and I apologized for ever doubting his wisdom about recursion…and ended up getting the job. I actually partially credit not being able to solve the IQ puzzle instantly, since the seemed to need to feel smarter than me, and if I had just provided the answer right away, he might have either felt intimidated or assumed that I'd seen it before—so if I'd not seen it recently and therefore messed it up, he might have assumed I had seen it before and was therefore cheating. The job did have its good points, though I never did really stop arguing with him, so it was a bit of a mixed blessing.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Should I be concerned that my web and mobile development teams are mostly people with electrical/mechanical engineering and embedded software backgrounds?
Answer: Not really, no. Now, I have noticed that some electrical engineers have been among the worst programmers I've encountered, as evidenced by extremely poor embedded development they've done on projects they were involved with. But those are electrical engineers who do have full time jobs as electrical engineers. They aren't claiming to be great programmers. Just because someone started out their career on that path doesn't mean they can't have discovered they were actually strong programmers, which could have motivated them to pivot to a new career. Some of my earliest experience was in electronics and embedded work. I discovered programming early and stuck with it, but I could imagine having taken the advice of effectively every adult around me to instead pursue a “real” career and get an engineering degree. So you should judge the development teams around you by their results, not their history. If they're producing great results, then you're golden. They have learned more about the hardware underneath the software as a result of their backgrounds, after all, which can help to avoid some problems that might be caused by developers who have only used higher level languages like Python, JavaScript, and Ruby.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Why are Android phones better to be used by developers/programmers than iOS phones?
Answer: You shouldn't ask why until you ask whether. I use Android phones. I'm a software developer. The two are pretty much unrelated except for when I'm developing software for Android. I know software developers who like Android, and others who like iPhone. None that I'm aware of use their phone when they're programming, unless they're using their phone…as a phone. And both kinds of phone work fine as a phone. Thing is that any actual development is much better accomplished on a desktop or laptop. People will argue all day whether that should be a Windows, Mac, or Linux based computer, but what phone they use always comes down to personal preference.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: As a student, you build software in 20 days, and in an industry, you do the work in 60 days. Where do you think this extra time and resources are spent?
Answer: You'd need to be way more specific for this to be a useful question. For one thing, there are very few projects in a college CS sequence that take 20 full-time days of work to complete. Probably the only thing close was the compiler in the compiler design sequence. That's 20 weeks of classes on the quarter system. I think that I may have spent a bit more than 20 full time days on it, but let's say for the sake of argument that it was 20 days. What would a professional compiler take to create, then? Well, if I were to start one today, I'd likely use LLVM as a backend and a more modern parser compiler for the frontend. For a really simple language like the one I created for the class in college, that might mean I'd have an entire compiler, one of much higher quality, functional in about a week. Maybe two. So call it 5-10 days, including an elaborate test suite, something that I didn't create in college. But it wouldn't be ready to sell yet (for the sake of this discussion we'll ignore the fact that almost no one sells compilers any more). First, I'd need to create documentation for it. It would need a web site that describes its features, and maybe offers the ability to buy the product. It would likely be a good idea to spend a few more weeks in hard-core testing, adding more tests to the suite as we find issues. It would need better error messages, and more command line options. Would that push the process out to 60 work days, possibly spread across several developers? We've likely blown past 60 days already. In industry they generally do want multiple developers, who then would need to spend time communicating. Say the team is seven developers, a technical writer, and two project managers. Due to the exponential growth of the communication requirements and time spent planning and changing designs, talking to customers, and making multiple chances based on updated requirements, now the project will probably take a year of calendar time to complete, or 2500 work-days spread across the whole team. And that doesn't begin to count time lost from team turnover, conflicts, developers performing in a subpar manner that needs to be fixed later by other developers, communication issues, and time off by critical team members that blocks progress of other members trying to get things done. Software is hard. Shipping software is much more work than getting a well-defined simplified toy project to pass a few tests at school. Industry doesn't like to have only one programmer who understands and can extend a product (see: Bus factor), and so teams get bigger. The larger the team, the more overhead to communication. And productizing an app may take 90% of the development time; 60 days is likely a vast underestimate, especially if the app is targeted at consumers, though even the compiler example would really need a lot more work than it would take to get a basic compiler up and running. So I don't know what answer your teacher wants. A 3x factor of development time doesn't really seem to me that it would be enough to go from ”toy project” to something that can be sold. So if you want the right answer, you probably should have gone to class and taken notes, as well as done any assigned reading. It's the only way to be sure.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is MongoDb ideal for big scale projects?
Answer: The niche that MongoDB is ideal for is pretty rarefied. Once upon a time, MongoDB had “horizontal scalability and speed” as its primary advantage. Some people also liked the fact that it was schemaless, which is still touted as a feature. So what are the advantages of MongoDB today? Mongo still has horizontal scalability as an advantage over the biggest relational database players: PostgreSQL and MySQL don’t really support completely transparent data sharding natively. But PosgreSQL at least has an extension that enables transparent sharding. And there are two other options: The fully Postgres-compatible YugabyteDB that is actually running a set of modified PostgreSQL servers under the covers, and the PostgreSQL-wire-compatible CockroachDB. So MongoDB can’t really claim that as a complete advantage over SQL databases. For SQL databases I’ll use PostgreSQL as an example from this point forward, since it’s the leading open source example. So what about schemaless? I assert that having no schema simply pushes a lot of complexity out of the database and into the hands of the application developers, where it enables many kinds of bugs that simply can’t exist in a database with a schema. Lacking a schema doesn’t mean you can just throw “any” data into your database; the application code needs to know what to look for, after all! And so now your application needs to handle not only the current schema everywhere, but every schema that still exists in every record currently in the database. So to my mind, lacking a schema on the database side, one that can prevent errors in data, is a strict disadvantage. So that leaves speed; here the advantage only goes to MongoDB in the narrow case where you simply need to look up a single object or set of objects, either via its key or as a result of a search. And given the amount of performance engineering that has gone into PostgreSQL in recent years, there is no guarantee that MongoDB will be much faster, if at all. But hypothetically it could be faster in some use cases, so we can grant that point. But speed falls apart entirely if what you really need to do is what’s called a “join.” In relational data, when you need to look something up, some of the fields in the first record you’re looking at may refer to another table of data. For instance, say you have a user record that is associated with some number of project records that are shared with other users. In a relational database you can trivially query for a user and all that user’s associated projects and it can look up who is associated with which project and return all of the data as one block. Or you could query for a list of “users that share projects with me along with the project we have in common.” Or maybe it’s a store web site and you want to see how many users logged in each week, by week, and for users that logged in, how many made a purchase vs. just shopped without buying anything. Again, the proper query can pull all of that data from the database quickly and easily. MongoDB did get the ability to do the most trivial kind of join, but it’s limited in its functionality compared to a SQL join. Worse, in my opinion, it’s not SQL, and as such it is yet-another-syntax to learn, with its own limitations and performance characteristics, compared to the SQL standard which works across many relational databases. For comparison, the MongoDB query language isn’t compatible with the Firebase query language, nor is it compatible with the DynamoDB query language…and all three of the above are NoSQL document databases. Learning one helps you almost not at all with learning another. It’s hard to overestimate how fast a well-written SQL query can be compared to the typical MongoDB approach of querying one table after another. In fact, the MongoDB documentation discourages you from using its join feature, instead encouraging you to “spread the data around to where you might need it.” This is called denormalizing the data, and by doing this you’re now making your application a lot more complicated. In the project example, every time some detail about a project changed you’d need to find every user that shared that project and update the appropriate record. If a user was added to or removed from a project, you’d then have to search for other users associated with their project and change their “associated user” list. Make a mistake or have the server crash mid-update and the data can be corrupted. (Yes you can use transactions. But that adds still more to the additional complexity required on the MongoDB side of the equation, because if you have a transaction then you need to take some action if the transaction fails, which can happen even if the underlying operation should have succeeded…) In PostgreSQL at least, the SQL query is effectively compiled and optimized based on a lot of factors. It can be very fast, at least if it’s supported by the correct indices. So overall, having SQL is generally faster and better than dealing with the custom query language and limitations available in MongoDB. So with the following constraints: …you can say that your workload is better handled by MongoDB. And that’s the only place where MongoDB still wins as a technology. (And it’s worth noting that very few projects that need a database have data that’s not at all relational.) Very rarefied indeed. Though if you’re a less experienced developer who doesn’t know how to use SQL yet, doesn’t know what your schema should look like, and aren’t willing to put in the time to learn either? Then MongoDB may start looking quite good. I suspect the latter is the real reason for MongoDB’s popularity: It’s said that the number of developers doubles every five years, so at least half of all developers have less than five years of experience. There was even a time before I’d used it that I thought NoSQL and MongoDB was a great idea; I learned otherwise. And “my developers aren’t very skilled” is rarely a good reason to choose a technology, if only because the lack of skill will show itself in many ways throughout your project. Better to find developers who have realized that MongoDB is simply almost never the right choice; they’ll be superior for almost every aspect of your project. I know that the strongest developers that I work with have come to similar conclusions about NoSQL vs SQL databases, similar to how they’ve all come to respect static typing over dynamic typing. So I guess the short answer is “In most cases, no, Mongo is not ideal.”

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: As a software engineer, how do you keep from getting bummed out troubleshooting issues in poorly documented, needlessly complex code bases?
Answer: I've done this so often that I ended up branding my consulting company as “Rescues small businesses from code disasters.” Like everything else, it takes practice. And sometimes you need to make the professional call to dump large portions of the code base. But yes, sometimes you just need to deal with diving into crap code bases. Read as much code as you can to get a taste of the patterns (and anti-patterns) being used in it. Ask questions when the code is completely opaque. After you understand enough to have a feel for how things work, start on whatever changes you need. Try to understand what you can about whatever immediate problem domain you’re looking into, and endeavor to make minimal changes to prevent breaking things. And yes, I would worry about that even if there’s a test suite. Because poorly documented, needlessly complex code bases can’t be trusted to have sufficient code coverage to protect you from breaking things by accident. But the real answer, if the above doesn’t work for you, is to change jobs to one where you interview the employer: Ask about their code base. Drill other engineers about documentation and code architecture. Ask them how long it takes to add a typical feature. And when you find a job where everyone actually seems competent? Try to work there. And then you won’t be bummed out by bad code, because you won’t have to deal with any. Good luck.

Question: Are interviews harder than the job itself in software engineering?
Answer: I say no, with a helping of probably not. There's a myth that floats around that interviews are really hard, and that they require the candidate to solve these crazy hard problems, only to have their developers duct taping code together, never using the skills they needed to get the job. There are probably jobs out there that fit that description. I mean, it's a big world, after all. But most jobs today do benefit if you have the right skills to be able to solve a few relatively simple problems in about a half hour each. I think that most of the myth comes from the fact that people are actively training, even memorizing, common interview problems. It's fine to practice on Leetcode, don't get me wrong. Especially if you're using the time to learn new ways to think about algorithms! But memorizing fifty algorithms and interviewing dozens of times until you get an interview that happens to use the solution that you remember? That's cracking the interview in the sense of cheating to win, deceiving the interviewer about your skill because you happened to have memorized the question they used. It's worse when you look up what problems specific companies usually use; that's just straight up cheating. And once that programmer is hired, assuming they haven't been caught, they will quickly find the job is either completely beyond them, or they'll be delegated to simpler tasks (or in some cases unintentionally litter the code with small disasters). So in that respect, the interview may have been harder than the job. But it wasn't harder than the job they wanted the applicant to be able to do. They just decided to keep the programmer rather than firing them because firing someone is hard. Listen. The programming test exists to see if the candidate can create a novel bit of code. It shouldn't exist to see if the candidate memorized something. The current trend of studying hundreds of algorithms with the intent to memorize as many as possible simply perverts the whole process, because a regurgitated answer is a false positive in the interview. And I get that someone who studied CS really wants to get a job in software, and so they're motivated to do whatever it takes. But it sucks to be interviewing people who have turned our one measure of actual programming skill into a game they're trying to hack to give incorrect results in their favor. So if you're good at software engineering? The interview, including the programming test, should be easy compared to the job. And if you spend hundreds of hours trying to hack the interview process in your favor, the job may still be harder for you, unless you find that one company that gives hard problems but has really low actual job requirements.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Why is it becoming so common for senior software engineers to intentionally drop out of hiring processes that require coding tests?
Answer: I think that the truth isn't pleasant. First: A useful programming test shouldn’t make you implement some arbitrary algorithm you have memorized. And it shouldn’t involve some “trick” you need to see to get it right, unless they’re fine with talking you through the trick and seeing if you can understand and implement it. A programming test that actually tests programming ability should rely purely on programming skill; not something obscure a candidate has memorized. But the sad truth is that there are tons of senior developers who can’t themselves code worth anything. They’ve accumulated years of experience via leaning on coworkers and/or duct-taping code together that they don’t fully understand. And that’s who the tests are intended to filter out, if they’re well-designed. That there are interviewers who pick some cargo-cult-inspired “hard” question that most developers wouldn’t know the answer to off the top of their heads, I don’t dispute. People suck at interviewing. Picking an Leetcode problem that requires you to know a trick and failing a candidate when they don’t see it? That sucks as an interview process. But some coding tests really are needed to validate that the developers can really code. A resume doesn’t prove anything. It doesn’t filter out older developers, as some have claimed. It filters out “developers” who can’t code. Having survived in the industry for 20+ years doesn’t guarantee that they haven’t been skating by and “Wally”-ing through their career; unless they’ve done amazing solo work, a resume isn’t proof of even basic competence. I’ve worked with developers with “amazing” resumes who couldn’t code their way out of a box without copying and pasting that code from a StackOverflow answer, and even then it would likely have problems. And entirely too much of the industry seems to fall into this category. It’s why we get comics like this: Reference. Our entire field is bad at what we do, and if you rely on us, everyone will die. Unfortunately it’s too true—with notable exceptions. Frequently in FAANG companies and equivalent, and that’s in part because they require people who are claiming to be programmers to pass programming tests. So why do they drop out of the hiring process when confronted by a programming test? Because they know, or at least fear, that they won't be able to pass. Saying they feel insulted by the test is just an excuse. Edit: A comment points out that I'm answering with respect to in-interview programming tests. That was how I'd interpreted the question, but it could also apply to take-home tests. With respect to take-home tests, unless they're really short and/or I really want the opportunity, those are asymmetric in time requirements: One company can send out hundreds of such tests that require eight hours each and literally ignore the results of all but a few, which they spend can minutes to review. That is BS of a high order, and should be rightfully scoffed at. If everyone did that, then looking for work would be more than a full time job, and that's totally bogus. If the prospective employer is paying an employee to interview me, then they have skin in the game. If they're instead just spamming out programming tests, they don't. Only the most attractive employers can afford to behave like this, but sometimes you see it with tiny little companies that no one has heard of. Those companies are unintentionally filtering for the most desperate employees, which means the best developers, who are almost always in high demand, will simply pass them by.

Question: I need to choose Ruby, Java, PHP, or Python as the coding language of my website. Which is more SEO-friendly?
Answer: An odd selection of languages for 2022. But first: The backend doesn't have an effect on SEO except if the language slows the site down. SEO is mostly content, tags, and page structure—which is defined in the HTML and CSS of the page. Google at least also cares about the page's performance, though. And selecting a language for the backend doesn't itself tell me how fast your page will be. If you pick any of the above languages and have your backend generate pages on request, then if your site is busy when the search engine hits it, expect to be marked down for slow page generation speed. Just about the best SEO recommendation for today is to keep your page light and prerender as much of the page as possible. Design your pages so that the time to first render and the time to first interaction are as low as possible. Ditch as many external advertising libraries as you can manage; they can slow down the render and limit your SEO. For my simpler websites I've been using generators. Hugo works well, but it's a bit hard to configure. Next.js has a code generation mode. In both cases, the templates include a lot of SEO-specific optimizations. In neither case would you be using any of the languages you listed Good luck.

Question: How will you free the allocated memory in C++?
Answer: What allocated memory, exactly? Memory allocated and stored in a smart pointer…just gets deallocated when you leave the final scope of the last object that's holding it (or otherwise release it). If it was allocated with malloc, you use free. If it was allocated with alloca, you just leave its scope. If it was allocated with new (with or without square brackets), you use delete (with or without square brackets, respectively). Unless it was handed to a smart or otherwise managed pointer, in which case it's probably back to leaving a scope or deleting a containing object. Beginners asking questions they don't really understand (or pasting incomplete homework questions) on Quora is rarely a great idea. Better to ask a teacher for help.

Question: Why can't JavaScript add 1 to 9007199254740992 and other big numbers that have been converted from strings?
Answer: To manipulate really large integers, you need to be using a type that can support integers that large. The number type in JavaScript is a double precision floating point value. This is true of floating point numbers in most common languages, so your question isn't unique to JavaScript. The solution in JavaScript is to use BigInt, though. The regular number just can't hold values that large.

Question: What is the best way to learn a programming language fast without quit?
Answer: I'm going to guess that you're trying to learn to program, which isn't entirely the same as learning a programming language. Question: In the software engineering profession, is it common to omit semicolons in JavaScript and rely on automatic semicolon insertion?
Answer: It's common, but in my opinion, it's ugly. It marks you as a JavaScript-only noob. JavaScript is a C-family language. One of the hallmarks of C-family languages is that they terminate every statement with a semicolon. JavaScript requires a semicolon at the end of every line. Omitting them and relying on ASI is like throwing trash on the street and relying on someone else to clean it up. Yes, someone will clean it up for you, but that doesn't make you any less of a slob. There are even cases where you can end up with code that doesn't behave the way you expect, and in the “standard” approach they have you add semicolons at the start of lines to fix the error (!!!). Considering the argument is that it makes things prettier, that seems a particularly poor resolution. Just use semicolons. It's not that hard, and if you use Prettier, it will add semicolons for you, so you don't even need to learn the habit of typing the character. Not that it's actually hard to type. I mean, C, Java, C#, and C++ developers have been adding semicolons for decades without their pinkies falling off, after all. It's a home row key! (At least on most Qwerty US English keyboards; YMMV). Everyone should be migrating to TypeScript as soon as they can anyway, and in TypeScript, the predominant standard is to use Prettier and require semicolons.

Question: As a software engineer, is it recommended not to write code that you think you might need in the future, but don't need yet?
Answer: YAGNI[1] is often good advice. It apparently originated with the Extreme Programming movement, one of the first examples of agile development. But. As with every “rule of thumb,” there are always exceptions. This particular rule comes out of the “agile” movement, along with the idea that “Big Design Up Front” is a de-facto Bad Thing. Sometimes, though, you really do know in advance what you’re going to need. I frequently operate like this, and I’ve been around the block enough to know what we’ll need next, so when I think particular will be needed somewhere, I usually include it. And it usually is needed eventually. And sometimes you’re creating a complex system, either in library form or simply an application that needs to be more complicated than average. This is where the typical agile approach completely fails. Where you really do need a robust design in advance. Because if you just look at the features immediately in front of you, you’ll end up with a code disaster that no (reasonable) amount of refactoring will save. So my recommendation? Think carefully before adding features before you know you’ll need them. But do be sure to think in advance about the kinds of features you might need, and, at the very least, design as if you will eventually need to be able to implement those features. The agile movement helped us think less rigidly, but many of its practices are actively harmful if taken too literally. I really think there should be a better compromise approach that isn’t quite agile and isn’t quite waterfall, but I’ve yet to see one that captures the advantages of both.

Question: How does a debugger break down code and show what's happening?
Answer: For an assembly language debugger, this is one of those questions where, if you have to ask it, you are pretty much guaranteed not to understand the answer. To actually answer it, one would need to explain how a CPU works, how memory works, and how machine language instructions are encoded. Once you understand all of that, it's obvious how a debugger can display the current (disassembled) code around the program counter as well as displaying all of the registers. If you're talking about a higher level compiled language, then you're unintentionally asking the wrong question. The debugger doesn't “break down” code. It shows you the point in the source code where the current execution is paused. It can also show you the value of variables. How does it do those things? When the code was built, debugging information, including source code line numbers and variable names, was saved with the code, and the debugger uses that to display the various values. For a script language like JavaScript or Python, a debugger can either just show you the script directly or show you the source code. Otherwise it's similar to the complied code debugger.

Question: How do all-inclusive resorts make money?
Answer: By charging their guests more than the services and goods cost to offer. This is basic economics. How can they give you so much for so little? They are typically in lower cost of living areas, so cost of employees, food, and alcohol is probably lower than you'd expect. Some entertainers may take a lower paycheck in exchange for free access to the resort when they're not entertaining. Land can be practicality free or extremely cheap, so they just have the cost of construction, which is of course lower because everything there costs less. Mostly it's cost of living arbitrage.
