Question: How would you go forward if you wanted to convince your boss to use Haskell instead of TypeScript?
Answer: I think I'd need a lobotomy first. Better to just use TypeScript. The religion of pure functional doesn't pay the bills and instead harms your boss’ ability to find experienced developers. TypeScript is a great language with strong types and excellent type inference. Its ecosystem is unparalleled. It is easy to integrate with existing JavaScript libraries. Most experienced web and Node developers already know TypeScript. The rest know JavaScript and can get up to speed with TypeScript extremely quickly. The “problems” of JavaScript can be 100% avoided by using TypeScript and a linter, so all of that JavaScript hate? Irrelevant. TypeScript also supports functional programming, so you can effectively have all of this additional power along with flexibility to use advanced functional techniques. Haskell has…strong types and excellent type inference. It's pure functional, so people used to TypeScript, JavaScript, C++, Ruby, Python, Perl, or PHP (or really most other languages) are going to have a difficult learning curve. Hiring for Haskell will therefore be a significant challenge and almost certainly require more training. Haskell doesn't have nearly as strong of an ecosystem, so you'll either have to reinvent the wheel a lot or interface with other languages with more robust ecosystems. If you must, play with Haskell on your free time. There are good reasons Haskell has remained a niche programming language, even losing ground, whereas TypeScript has launched past Haskell to become more and more of a standard for Node development. Given the tendency for this topic to provoke religious discussion, I'm preemptively closing comments. I really don't need the pure functional advocates telling me yet again why Haskell (or Elm) is better for…. Reasons….

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Are JavaScript and Lua similar? If I learned JavaScript will Lua be easier to learn?
Answer: In some ways they are similar. They look different. JavaScript is a C-family language and looks kind of like C. Lua…looks different. But really, the differences are mostly skin deep. The hard part about learning to program is in learning to think like a programmer. If you're memorizing exact syntax and regurgitating it, you're doing it wrong. So once you learn how to think like a programmer, picking up another language should be easy. Under the surface, Lua and JavaScript function in similar ways. Both use “prototypal inheritance” to create objects. Both have a single number type. Both use objects as dictionaries (in JavaScript objects are also functions; in Lua you can make them act like functions, but they're different beasts). The differences are really just aesthetic for the most part, though JavaScript has a much bigger standard library. Though why Lua chose one-based arrays I'll never understand. It was a mistake at at the start, and will always be.

Question: I want to learn Lua in college. What should I major in to do so?
Answer: You should major in computer science or software engineering. You won't likely learn Lua in college even then, but you'll learn how to program. Which is the hard part of learning your first language, no matter the language. Once you know how to program, it's about a weekend of effort to learn Lua. Maybe a bit longer if you're planning to embed it yourself in a new game you're writing, though I'm betting you want to learn it because you want to use it in an existing engine. Roblox perhaps? It's especially easy if you learn JavaScript first, since both languages have a similar foundation (prototype-based inheritance, at least). And it's a bit more common to find classes in web development that use JavaScript, though you'd also be learning HTML and CSS in a class like that. Maybe better to just learn Lua once you can program? That said, learning CS or software engineering will actually be useful for you to get a well paid job later. Most people can't make a living writing Roblox games, after all. But who knows? Maybe you'll strike it rich. Good luck!

Question: How do you attract software developers?
Answer: Money and good working conditions. And have an interesting problem to work on. You probably need a good senior engineer to manage the project in order to achieve the other three conditions. A solid engineer to start with can reduce the amount of repetitive code your developers need to write, and will make it easier to add features, allowing your engineers to focus on the interesting challenges and less on the minutiae. But here's the catch: Distinguishing between good senior engineers and crappy senior engineers that talk a good talk is really hard. It's a Catch-22: You need to be good to be able to tell the good from the poor developers. And that is a problem that I don't know how to solve.

Question: Is the Coding Ninjas certificate valuable?
Answer: Most certificates are of questionable value. I challenge the concept that “industry” is aware of the value, since I've been in the industry for 30+ years and I've never heard of them. Question: Why is a programmer’s life very boring?
Answer: There's an entire category of question here on Quora for which the answer is “ask the person in question!” In every case, the answer is to just ask. If a programmer has a boring life, you should ask them about their life to determine why it's boring. It's certainly not boring just because they are a programmer, which can be quite challenging and fulfilling for the right person. Many programmers are quite engaged by their job, and many also have hobbies outside of their job to keep them engaged. Maybe your bored programmer has a job that isn't challenging, or maybe they really hate programming, or maybe they are putting in too many hours and don't have any free time. Maybe they aren't even bored but scared; many programmers suffer from impostor syndrome, after all, and that can be debilitating. So ask the programmer about their life. It's clearly not a boring profession, looking at the many other answers to this question, so it must be something specific the bored programmer.

Question: As a software engineer, do you apply for a position only if you are confident with your preparations or do you apply anyway and request for 3-4 weeks to prepare once your resume is shortlisted?
Answer: Prepare…for an interview? I really don't like this idea that someone “should” spend several weeks “preparing.” I'm guessing that means practicing programming problems on Leetcode or out of Cracking the Coding Interview or similar? I'll admit that one time I pulled out the latter book and spent a few hours on practice problems. But it only convinced me that I didn't need to spend more time on practice problems. When you're in school and you “cram” for a test, how long do you retain the information you've learned that way? Hopefully long enough for it to be useful on the test, but after that? Not very long, correct? Now CtCI has a good point: If you're going to be using a whiteboard to write code, it's good practice to actually write code on a whiteboard before the interview. Now it's been many years since anyone asked me to write code on a whiteboard, but it could happen. Usually today you get a mini-IDE, or sometimes can use your own IDE/editor with a screen share. But beyond that, trying to memorize a bunch of algorithms in 3-4 weeks before an interview will likely at most deceive your interviewer into thinking that you're better than you actually are, and that only if you happen to get a problem sufficiently similar to one you practiced. And deception isn't the best way to start a new employment relationship. If you want to practice Leetcode problems to try to up your coding and algorithm game in general, by all means practice. But spend a year or two doing that in your free time; don't try to cram in a bunch right before an interview. Software engineering isn't about memorization. It's an art as much as a science, and memorizing the rules of perspective won't suddenly make you a good artist.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: What is a software developer versus a software engineer?
Answer: In some senses, there is no difference. There is no board of engineering that will approve your title. Anyone who is able to get a job as a programmer can legally use the title “software engineer” with no repercussions. But we have a dearth of titles in our industry. You can have someone who only knows how to assemble web pages with HTML and CSS, and they're a developer, even though they're not even programming. You can also have a brilliant developer who is the software equivalent of a Mozart, and they are also a developer. This is roughly equivalent to having a hospital where every employee from a nurse assistant to a surgeon was simply called a “medical worker.” And lacking any kind of official distinction or licensing, people hire the “nurses” (who are perfectly competent at their nursing jobs, don't get me wrong!) to perform surgery, with predictable results. So I would suggest that software engineer should be reserved for those developers who are capable of performing software surgery—and at least some software architecture design. It’s true that at present it’s a meaningless title, but that we should start pressuring developers to self-segregate into using titles more appropriate to their skills. But until then? It only has as much meaning as invested into it at a particular company where you are assigned the title.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How should I position myself as a software engineer to a prospective employer at the age of 60? My part time freelancing shows me that my wisdom and decades of engineering experience should make me quite valuable, but I'm not getting interviews.
Answer: I'd encourage you to keep consulting, at least provisionally. I'm not quite 60, but I'm getting close, and at this point I plan to keep on consulting unless someone makes me an offer I can't refuse, so to speak, to become an employee again. If you really want to get a traditional job, then I'd try updating your resume so that it's not quite so obvious how old you are. Eliminate the graduation date from your university degree(s). Delete any experience from more than 15 years ago or so. Update the language with the help of a younger friend who can reword it to sound like a younger peer. Focus on newer tech if you can. You didn't say where your focus is; that's part of the “provisionally” above; some domains really are only reasonable to find full time employment in. Beyond that you might need to work with an expert to help guide your career. I'm not such an expert; I'm just a software engineer/consultant.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: I chose software engineering as my bachelor’s program and I know pretty much nothing about programming. What is the best trick to understand the topics and tricks to being a programmer?
Answer: Spend a lot of free time learning programming. ASAP. If not yesterday, then today, and continually throughout your college career. Don't wait to be “taught.” The secret that they don't like to talk about is that programming really needs to be learned the hard way, by pushing through the difficulty and forcing your brain to form the right pathways. If you know programming before you get your degree, the degree will actually have much more value to you. Otherwise you end up learning things by rote if at all, and brains tend to forget things they don't have proper context for. Which results in the hundreds of answers and comments on Quora and elsewhere that imply a CS degree is worthless. It is worthless unless you put in the extra work. Yes you can sometimes find a lower skill coding job that will support you for a while, even without really learning software engineering. But at that point you're competing with the vast majority of barely competent “developers” out there. Whereas the high salaries? The ones you really want to find if you're pursuing the degree? Those are available to the actually skilled developers. And most of those started their degree with some programming skill, or they put in the extra time to learn more than the minimum during their degree. Good luck.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: If someone uses artwork that another bought as an NFT, what can the buyer do?
Answer: Nothing. When you buy an NFT, you're buying a token on a blockchain. That's it, unless there are specific other rights granted by the original owner of the artwork. Most of the time you're just getting bragging rights, though. You generally don't even have the right to use the art yourself! The token may contain a link to the art, but if you weren't careful, the token may not even be authorized by the artist. I was just hearing about several artists who were spending time trying to fight to get their art taken down from where it was stolen to create NFTs with it. There's no guarantee that it's the only NFT that links to the same art, either. As far as I can see, it's all a scam. Sorry you've been taken in by it. Hope you didn't waste too much money.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: How can I go about finding companies who support individuals who are currently learning how to code?
Answer: Companies expect employees to be able to contribute to their bottom line within a reasonable period of time. If you're “learning how to code,” they may not see a return on investment for two years or more. And frankly not everyone has what it takes, so they may never get a productive programmer from the hire. You're not looking for a company as much as a college. If you can find any job where you can contribute, and where the job will grant you educational stipends, that can help, but in general if you are still learning to code, no company will likely want to hire you to code.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is it normal for a developer with 2 years of experience to still be a junior developer?
Answer: Two years of working professionally? After being educated in software development for some number of years before that? That's about the latest point where you'll be expected to either become a full developer or be asked to leave. In some companies it's more like one or one and a half years. Now there's no real standard in the industry as to what “junior” really means. There's probably a company somewhere that will allow a junior developer to contribute at a junior salary indefinitely. But typically “junior” means that they're still being trained. Meaning a more senior developer is doing less work because the junior can't do work fully independently. Other developers need to spend extra time during code reviews to explain how the junior needs to fix their code. Net productivity is very low or even negative. If this isn't the case, then the junior should be promoted, and possibly should have been promoted months earlier. The company in question is paying a junior salary for a full developer, which isn't fair to the developer. Some companies will promote a strong junior after six months or less. If it is still the case that the developer needs extensive help after two years, then they should probably look for another career. Perpetual junior level developers do exist; not everyone has the right skill set to become a full developer, and it will become increasingly difficult for them to find a job in the industry. Hiring managers will look at their resume and decline based on insufficient trajectory.

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Is backend going to be obsolete while frontend becomes full stack via cloud technologies like Firebase which ensure basic server functionality?
Answer: Hahaha! Thanks for the good laugh… I'm involved with a Firebase project right now. It uses the newer Firestore database. Yes it's cheap. Yes it guarantees that the server will be up and that it will scale. It's a pretty simple project that doesn't need anything complicated. It's just about the poster child of projects that should work well to use with Firebase. I swear I will never recommend Firebase again for any project that needs anything beyond a simple user configuration data store. It's been that awful in every conceivable way. Some of the problems I remember: And the advantages: I usually use Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL on the database side for simple projects. It gets #2 in spades, and isn't actually that expensive. It's just not quite as cheap. I actually suspect that developers who are happy with Firebase are simply not actually adding any security, meaning that anyone who spends the time will be able to trivially hack the data or even delete it all. So the above is why Firebase isn't the end-all of databases, but you could imagine a database that has full relational and SQL ability that's also scalable. CockroachDB is one that's now available as a service, for instance. But I still think there's value in wedging backend server logic between the database and the frontend. First, because it makes security so much easier. Second, because it enforces separation of concerns. And third, because writing the database backend logic requires different skills than writing the frontend. I've worked with frontend engineers who did an excellent job of making the frontend do exactly what it needed to do. Pixel perfect everything. But they really weren't to be trusted anywhere near business logic. And I know backend engineers (myself included) who never want to touch the UI code, and as such we don't know all the tricks to make browsers jump though all the necessary hoops to make the clients happy. We're facing a perpetual software engineer shortage in the industry. Forcing excellent frontend engineers hack together backend code they're not good at, or vice versa, is not the best use of engineers in my opinion. If I can go out on a limb here, I'd say that a good percentage of developers who call themselves “full stack” are more likely to actually be frontend engineers who are barely able to write secure, robust backend code—and that includes the code needed to configure Firebase to be secure. Now I know personally some full stack engineers who are perfectly competent on the backend, so don't start yelling about how some full stack engineer is actually competent at both. People absolutely can be. But since there exist frontend engineers who can't do backend well, maybe it's a better use of resources to assign those folks to frontend so the rest of us can focus on the backend?

Name: Tim Mensch
Question: Should I switch my tech stack to web 3.0/NFT/metaverse/blockchain from .NET core, given its massive future scope?
Answer: In the 1950s it was thought that strong AI (the ability of a computer to think like a human) was about 20 years away. Today it's still thought to be 20 years away. Fifty years from now that still may be the case. Blockchain is looking like one of those technologies, only for a different reason. Instead of being because of a technical challenge, it's a technology in search of a use case. I mean, it's not a currency. Web3 and NFTs are scams. Heck, crypto's best usage as far as I can tell is as a punch line. The only use case I've seen that actually feels substantive is in trading tokens that represent ownership of an item or share of something with real value. NFTs don't count because they're not real ownership of anything other than the token itself. And ironically, this use case isn't at all dependent on the crypto technology, at least not beyond the existence of secure signatures. Because any time there is something with real world value (like shares of a company), there is by definition a centralized authority that could be tracking the token ownership. Boom, no “crypto” required, and in fact blockchain makes every aspect of the situation strictly worse, except for the part that people are writing software to manage the trading of the tokens for you. So what I'm saying is that literally all of the genuine uses of blockchain could be trivially replaced by a simple standardized API that multiple apps could communicate with. Every other use case is a scam to get people to invest in companies or products to inflate a bubble. So no, you shouldn't throw away learning in a real stack for learning in one that will pop any year now.
